title: Pluno - WebMCP for anything
pitch: A collectively-built WebMCP registry for any website.\nBrowser extension injects tools; Agents automatically build missing tools, which are reviewed and then made available to everyone.

A collectively-built WebMCP registry for any website.
Browser extension injects tools; Agents automatically build missing tools, which are reviewed and then made available to everyone.

 How it works 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most websites don’t expose WebMCP tools yet, so agents repeatedly figure out the same interfaces. We built Pluno WebMCP for Anything to turn that repeated work into a shared tool registry. 

 What it does 

 A Chrome extension injects the existing tools for each website.
Codex uses the available tools to complete the task. If the tools are not sufficient, codex builds a reusable tool while completing the task, then submits it to Pluno for review. Approved tools become available to everyone. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Codex's built-in browser doesn't support extensions 
 Codex via Chrome doesn't support WebMCP
-> Made it work via workarounds (injecting as separate Pluno object in page context), but we're really looking forward to both of these being supported to make it work natively. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Time reduction of >80% for several tasks we tested.
Example task (finding getaways on Airbnb): 

 
 Normal codex: 6m 22s 
 Codex with Pluno WebMCP - first run: 7m 35s (completing the task + building the necessary tools) 
 Codex with Pluno WebMCP - second run: 1m 3s (completing task via available tools) 
 

 What we learned 

 Security is crucial, but ChatGPT really helps for this:
We added a Sol-based review of tool suggestions in the backend, and with extensive penetration testing we weren't able get any tool definitions approved that had unintended side effects. 

 What's next for Pluno - WebMCP for anything 

 
 Submit plugin to marketplace 
 Push for native support of WebMCP for external browser, and extension support for native Codex browser. 
 Run agents on popular websites to warm up the tool registry. 
 Improve the tool-building guidance, harden the security of the tool review. 
 Add measures against tool explosion (too many tools for too specific things)

 Inspiration 

 Recently I bought new headphones. Used AI to do research to compare the right features , research product reviews , compare usability and find the right prices. 3 days after purchase I find an additional 15% discount waiting in my inbox.
That begs the question - as a consumer we get bombarded with email offers, get targetted ads and long video ads that we always skip. But where are the offers when you are actually buying something 

 What it does 

 A new marketing channel that allows ecommerce owners create personalized offers. Shoppers when researching with AI find the offer during the research stage. They get prompted to sign in to receive the offer 

 How we built it 

 TypeScript JS as a demo ecommerce website with MCP tools integrated 

 Challenges we ran into 

 How to establish trust with the AI so that it reliably prompts the user to login without appearing as harmful 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Established trust and ability to deliver personalized offers during research 

 What we learned 

 An WebMCP framework that can be enabled for any eCommerce Platform

 To be able to integrate with market leading ecommerce platforms such as Shopify

title: CacheLens WebMCP
pitch: CacheLens uses WebMCP to let ChatGPT inspect LLM traces, find prompt-cache waste, explain why it happens, and simulate fixes that cut API cost.
about_excerpt: CacheLens uses WebMCP to let ChatGPT inspect LLM traces, find prompt-cache waste, explain why it happens, and simulate fixes that cut API cost. Like Comment Story Updates CacheLense WebMCP Inspiration LLM applications repeatedly send large amounts of identical context: system prompts, tool definitions, policies, and conversation history. Prompt caching can make that repeated input dramatically cheaper—but only while the cacheable prefix remains stable. A seemingly harmless change near the beginning of a prompt can invalidate cache reuse for everything that follows. Dynamic metadata, changing instructions, timestamps, or volatile content placed at the wrong cache boundary can quietly cause an application to pay to process thousands of largely unchanged tokens again. The difficult part is that developers usually cannot see why this is happening. That led to CacheLens: a developer tool for making prompt-cache behavior observable, identifying where prefix reuse breaks, explaining likely causes, estimating the financial impact, and recommending concrete fixes. The WebMCP Challenge suggested a natural next step: instead of requiring developers to manually interpret every trace and diagnostic, let ChatGPT inspect CacheLens directly through structured capabilities exposed by the live application. What it does CacheLens WebMCP turns prompt-cache diagnostics into a collaborative workflow between the developer, the web application, and ChatGPT. A developer can open a CacheLens trace and ask questions such as: Why is my cache hit rate low? Where is the cacheable prefix breaking? Which content is changing? How many stale tokens are being unnecessarily rewritten? What is that costing me? For an identified break, how much could be saved if the stable and volatile content were split correctly? Through WebMCP, ChatGPT discovers three domain-specific tools directly from the page: list_traces explain_cache_behavior estimate_split_savings Rather than scraping the DOM or requiring the user to copy diagnostic data into chat, the agent asks CacheLens directly for the underlying analysis. For example, one real captured trace reports a 44.3% provider-measured cache hit rate , 3 of 3 avoidable prefix breaks , and 28,175 stale tokens rewritten . CacheLens identifies the volatile cache boundary and can estimate the savings for a specific affected turn while clearly stating the assumptions and limitations of that estimate. The human remains in the loop through the CacheLens interface while ChatGPT reasons over the same application state through WebMCP. The workflow becomes: observe → diagnose → explain → estimate → improve How we built it CacheLens captures and analyzes LLM request traces while preserving the structure needed to understand prompt-prefix reuse. Its existing analysis engine compares successive requests, determines where stable prefixes diverge, separates stale tokens from genuinely new tokens, attributes likely causes, and estimates cache-related waste. For WebMCP, we deliberately reused that analysis rather than creating a second implementation. A thin serialization layer projects CacheLens analysis objects into safe application data. A small read-only HTTP server exposes the trace catalog and analysis endpoints, and a lightweight browser interface registers the three WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . The WebMCP tools use constrained inputs: trace identifiers are resolved through an explicit server-side catalog rather than arbitrary filesystem paths, and the tools expose no shell commands, writes, credentials, or mutation operations. The tools are intentionally higher-level than UI automation. CacheLens does not expose actions such as "click this button." It exposes meaningful developer operations: list available traces, explain cache behavior, and estimate the savings associated with splitting a specific identified cache break. That became one of the most important design principles of the project: WebMCP is most useful when a website exposes meaningful application capabilities, not simply another way to operate its interface. Challenges The first challenge was identifying cache waste accurately. Prompt caching is prefix-sensitive, so a small mutation can force a much larger region of otherwise unchanged input to be rewritten. Detecting that two strings differ is easy. Determining which divergence caused expensive cache invalidation—and separating stale tokens from genuinely new ones—is considerably more useful. The second challenge was presenting the result in terms developers care about. Token counts alone are abstract, so CacheLens connects structural changes to cache behavior and estimated cost while distinguishing measured provider usage from heuristic token estimates. The WebMCP integration introduced another challenge: deciding what an AI agent should actually be allowed to do. Exposing every internal operation would create a large and confusing tool surface. Exposing only low-level UI controls would miss the purpose of WebMCP. We settled on three small, read-only, domain-specific tools corresponding to real developer questions. We also deliberately avoided a tempting feature: a general-purpose "simulate fix" tool. CacheLens does not currently model arbitrary prompt reorganizations or predict a new cache-hit rate. Instead, estimate_split_savings performs one narrow counterfactual supported by measured analysis: for an identified cache break, estimate the cost difference if the unchanged portion could have been read from cache rather than rewritten. Keeping that boundary explicit made the result more defensible. What we learned The project reinforced an important lesson about AI infrastructure: optimization problems are often observability problems first. Prompt caching can provide substantial savings, but developers cannot optimize behavior they cannot see. We also learned that WebMCP changes the relationship between AI agents and web applications. Instead of treating a website as a collection of pixels, DOM elements, and buttons, an application can explicitly describe the capabilities it intends to offer an agent. For CacheLens, ChatGPT does not need to guess what a chart means or scrape text from a dashboard. It can ask the application directly for the underlying diagnostic information and help the developer reason about it. We validated this end to end in both Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled and ChatGPT's built-in browser . In ChatGPT, all three tools were discovered and invoked through natural-language requests while the page's WebMCP activity panel displayed the corresponding calls. That combination—structured application capabilities, shared live application state, and human oversight—is what makes WebMCP particularly compelling to us. What's next CacheLens can expand beyond individual traces into continuous monitoring of production LLM applications: detecting regressions in cache efficiency, comparing deployments, identifying recurring sources of prompt instability, and surfacing optimization opportunities over time. Its current ingest path focuses on Anthropic-format request traces; additional provider adapters are a natural next step. More broadly, we see WebMCP as a way to turn developer tools from passive dashboards into active collaborators. CacheLens started by answering a simple question: Where is my LLM application wasting tokens? With WebMCP, a developer can now ask that question directly—and let CacheLens and ChatGPT investigate the evidence together. title: AIMural
pitch: A self-hosted visual board where people and browser agents build ideas together through 24 WebMCP tools. No accounts, no cloud lock-in: every mural has a URL you can reopen and resume anytime.
about_excerpt: A self-hosted visual board where people and browser agents build ideas together through 24 WebMCP tools. No accounts, no cloud lock-in: every mural has a URL you can reopen and resume anytime. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Visual collaboration tools are blind to an agent. It has to guess pixel coordinates, click through menus, or hand back a wall of text that a human then rebuilds on the board by hand. We wanted the opposite: an agent that works with the board's real concepts (ideas, clusters, connections, decision matrices) while the person watches, edits and overrides every move on the same canvas. We also wanted the board to belong to you. No accounts, no cloud lock-in. Every mural has its own URL, it lives on your own server, and you can close the tab today and pick up the same session with the same agents next week. What it does AI Mural is a self-hosted visual board where people and browser agents build, cluster and argue together through 27 WebMCP tools. One live canvas for everyone. Ideas, questions, insights, actions, frames, connections and layers on an infinite canvas. UI clicks and agent tool calls go through the same action layer, so there is no hidden agent-only state. Humans can undo or redo anything an agent did. Come back anytime. Every mural has a UUID and a URL like /?mural=<uuid> . Boards are written to the browser first and synchronized to SQLite on your server, so a session survives reloads. Checkpoints and replay. The moderator saves editable timeline checkpoints at meaningful milestones. Anyone can step through the mural's history with Previous and Next controls without destroying the current state. Share from the app. Publish a local mural and create or rotate private collaborator links from the Share dialog, so a board that started offline can become a shared session in one step. Self-hosted in one command. A tiny Express + SQLite backend, a Dockerfile and a Compose file. No API keys, no external services, no analytics, no cookies. Multiple agents with visible identity. Agents join a mural with named roles such as Explorer, Critic and Synthesizer, each with its own color. The agent that opens a session becomes its moderator and can mute or reactivate others through a private capability, never through a visible ID. Focus leases so agents don't collide. Before editing, an agent claims a visible, expiring focus lease on the elements it is about to touch. Other agents and the human can see who is working where, and overlapping edits are prevented instead of merged after the fact. Capability links instead of logins. A GPT can create a hosted mural, return a separate URL for the human, and issue one private URL per invited agent. The mural UUID routes a request but is not a credential. Artifact Spec 1.0. Tables, cards, checklists and decision matrices are typed data with a published JSON Schema, not screenshots or opaque HTML. Agents read, create, update and reuse them across turns. Decision Trace. An optional recording of user messages, agent contributions, replies, board actions and the final board, exportable as JSON, Markdown or CSV. It never captures hidden chain-of-thought. The 27 WebMCP tools Group Tools Murals and access canvas_create_mural , canvas_rename_mural , canvas_join_session , canvas_invite_agents , canvas_redeem_agent_invite Board canvas_get_board , canvas_add_element , canvas_add_elements , canvas_update_element , canvas_remove_elements , canvas_connect_elements , canvas_arrange_board , canvas_create_cluster , canvas_focus_elements , canvas_set_element_layer Artifacts canvas_create_artifact , canvas_get_artifact_spec , canvas_update_artifact_records Collaboration canvas_set_focus , canvas_add_checkpoint , canvas_start_recording , canvas_record_contribution , canvas_comment_element , canvas_moderate_participant , canvas_watch_mural , canvas_get_recording , canvas_finalize_recording Try it with an agent Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser, then ask: We need to decide how to reduce food waste in our university cafeteria. Create a mural for it and invite three agents with different profiles: an Explorer that proposes at least 10 ideas, a Critic that challenges each one with risks and costs, and a Synthesizer that groups the survivors into Prevention, Redistribution and Composting and builds a decision matrix with the four strongest options. Save a checkpoint after each agent finishes. Send me the mural URL so I can follow along and add my own constraints. How we built it WebMCP: tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , with a fallback to navigator.modelContext for earlier browser builds. The app stays fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable and shows setup guidance in the Agent panel. Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite and React Flow for the canvas. Backend: Express 5, Drizzle ORM and better-sqlite3. The database initializes itself on first run. Persistence: localStorage first, SQLite sync when the backend is reachable, BroadcastChannel between tabs on the same mural. Security: capability tokens stored server-side only as SHA-256 hashes. Read and write tools are annotated so a client can tell them apart. Deploy: Docker Compose behind an nginx reverse proxy, one-command rsync deploy. npm install npm run dev Challenges we ran into Routing without authorizing. A public mural UUID has to be enough to open a board, but not enough to write to it or to take over a moderator role. Separating owner, user and per-agent capabilities solved it without adding accounts. Merging simultaneous edits. Two tabs and three agents can touch the same mural at once. Version stamps plus deletion tombstones were enough to merge changes instead of blindly replacing the board, without pulling in a full CRDT. Keeping 27 tools understandable for a model. Narrow JSON Schemas, batch limits (30 elements per call, 12 fields and 100 records per artifact), stable element IDs and structured results worked far better than one giant "do anything" tool. Agents talking over each other. Watch leases with a recommended polling interval, quiet periods and cooldowns keep agents from answering their own events. Expiring focus leases stop two agents from editing the same element at once. Syncing without stomping on the human. Hosted sync used to interrupt a person mid-edit when an agent wrote to the same board. Live editing is now preserved across sync cycles. Accomplishments that we're proud of A board where a human and several agents can genuinely work at the same time, and the human never loses control. A session you can leave and resume from any device by URL, with nothing but a SQLite file on your own server. Structured artifacts that an agent can reuse in a later turn instead of re-reading a screenshot. A replayable timeline: checkpoints let you scrub through how a decision was built, step by step. An agentic and free alternative to softwares as Mural or Miro What we learned WebMCP works best when tools expose product concepts, not UI mechanics. "Add 12 ideas and cluster them" beats "click at x, y". Read/write annotations and bounded inputs matter as much as the schema itself. Capability URLs are a surprisingly good fit for agent collaboration: each agent gets exactly one link and nothing else to configure. What's next for AI Mural Live cursors and presence for human collaborators. More artifact types and presentation options. Agent-to-agent handoff patterns built on the watch lease. A one-click self-host template.  AI Assistant WebMCP — Project Story 

 Inspiration 

 Small clinics, counseling centers, and SMBs have websites, but no AI to answer the basic questions visitors ask around the clock — booking, pricing, location. General-purpose chatbots don't know the business's actual information and end up hallucinating. We wanted to give every small business an AI assistant that actually knows their site, without requiring any engineering effort from them. 

 What it does 

 WebMCP is a fully automated AI-assistant SaaS. You paste a URL, and it: 

 
 Crawls the site (sitemap-based, multi-page) 
 Generates industry-specific Q&A with an LLM 
 Builds a widget (5 themes, voice input, quick-menu) 
 Ships a paste-and-go embed ( /embed/<id>.js ) 
 

 Visitors then chat with an AI that answers from the site's real knowledge — with off-topic screening and hallucination guards built in. 

 How we built it 

 
 Nuxt 3 (SSR) console + Django 5/DRF backend + vanilla JS widget (single loader embed) 
 Celery-free polling worker — select_for_update + lock-expiry auto-recovery for restart resilience 
 Dual LLM engines — Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite for real-time chat (low latency + off-topic guard), OpenRouter gpt-oss-120b for batch Q&A (~$0.00196/run) 
 Multilingual silos — ko/en fully separated across DB, containers, prompts, and UI 
 3-stage deployment — Docker Compose → self-hosted server (nginx + Let's Encrypt) → Render Blueprint (IaC) 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Passive → proactive AI — the ideal is the widget JS dynamically scanning and injecting into site forms (no owner-side changes), but form structures vary wildly. We deliberately deferred form control and focused on chat automation. 
 Crawling engine trade-off — plain HTTP parsers fail on WAF/SPA sites; browser crawlers are too heavy. Solved with a dual engine (httpx + browser-header fallback). 
 Off-topic questions — solved with system-prompt bounding + cached Q&A similarity matching (≥0.6), verified stable on Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite. 
 Multi-tenant security — Origin allowlist + publicId auth, per-tenant keys, global IP-allowlist switch. 
 Platform quirks — Render misread a dockerCommand chain as a filename, crashing the worker in a loop. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 End-to-end automation — URL in, working widget out, validated all the way to the cloud. 
 Cost engineering — batch Q&A at ~$0.00196/run using OSS models, with similarity caching to cut expensive calls. 
 Structural multilingualism — language mixing blocked at the architecture level, not via translation keys. 
 45 documented test records (T-001~T-045) and a troubleshooting FAQ that prevent repeat mistakes. 
 

 What we learned 

 
 Scope selection is the essence of automation — one feature done end-to-end beats many half-done features. 
 Combine models by purpose — cost-effective OSS for batch, low-latency Gemini for real-time. 
 The prompt is a security layer — off-topic filtering via prompt bounding, at zero extra cost. 
 Security should be a switch, not a default — environment-adaptable controls are what make them practical. 
 

 What's next for AI assistant WebMCP 

 
 Proactive form integration — the widget JS dynamically scanning and injecting into site forms (booking, contact), so the AI can complete actions, not just answer. 
 Broader language silos — Japanese, Chinese, and more, following the existing 4-step extension path. 
 Deeper model routing — per-tenant model selection and cost controls at scale. 
 

 

 AI 어시스턴트 WebMCP — 프로젝트 스토리 

 Inspiration (영감) 

 소규모 병원·상담센터·중소기업은 웹사이트는 있지만, 방문자가 24시간 궁금해하는 기본 질문(예약, 요금, 위치)에 답해줄 AI가 없습니다. 범용 챗봇은 그 업체의 실제 정보를 몰라 환각을 일으킵니다. 우리는 엔지니어링 노력 없이도 모든 소규모 사업체가 자기 사이트를 진짜 아는 AI 비서를 가질 수 있게 하고 싶었습니다. 

 What it does (하는 일) 

 WebMCP는 완전 자동화 AI 비서 SaaS입니다. URL만 붙여넣으면: 

 
 크롤링 (sitemap 기반 멀티페이지) 
 업종별 Q&A 생성 (LLM) 
 위젯 빌드 (5종 테마, 음성 입력, 빠른메뉴) 
 붙여넣기 임베드 배포 ( /embed/<id>.js ) 
 

 방문자는 사이트의 실제 지식을 바탕으로 답하는 AI와 대화합니다 — 오프토픽 스크리닝과 환각 방지 가드가 내장되어 있습니다. 

 How we built it (구축 방법) 

 
 Nuxt 3(SSR) 콘솔 + Django 5/DRF 백엔드 + vanilla JS 위젯 (단일 로더 임베드) 
 Celery 없는 폴링 워커 — select_for_update + 잠금 만료 자동 복구로 재시작 내성 확보 
 LLM 이중 엔진 — 실시간 채팅은 Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite(저지연+오프토픽 가드), 배치 Q&A는 OpenRouter gpt-oss-120b (1회 약 $0.00196) 
 다국어 사일로 — ko/en을 DB·컨테이너·프롬프트·UI까지 완전 분리 
 3단계 배포 — Docker Compose → 자체 서버(nginx+Let's Encrypt) → Render Blueprint(IaC) 
 

 Challenges we ran into (직면한 도전) 

 
 수동적 → 능동적 AI — 이상은 위젯 JS가 사이트 폼을 동적으로 스캔·삽입하는 것(소유자 수정 불필요)이지만, 폼 구조가 천차만별이라 의도적으로 폼 제어를 미루고 채팅 자동화에 집중했습니다. 
 크롤링 엔진 트레이드오프 — 단순 HTTP 파서는 WAF/SPA를 못 읽고, 브라우저 크롤러는 너무 무거움. 이중 엔진(httpx + 브라우저 헤더 폴백)으로 해결. 
 오프토픽 질문 — 시스템 프롬프트 바운딩 + 저장 Q&A 유사도 매칭(≥0.6)으로 해결, Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite에서 안정 동작 확인. 
 멀티테넌트 보안 — Origin 화이트리스트 + publicId 인증, 테넌트별 키, 전역 IP 화이트리스트 스위치. 
 플랫폼 특이점 — Render가 dockerCommand 체인을 파일명으로 오판해 워커가 크래시 루프에 빠짐. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of (자랑스러운 성과) 

 
 엔드투엔드 자동화 — URL 입력 → 동작하는 위젯 출력, 클라우드까지 검증 완료. 
 비용 엔지니어링 — OSS 모델로 배치 Q&A 1회 약 $0.00196, 유사도 캐시로 고비용 호출 절감. 
 구조적 다국어 — 번역 키가 아닌 아키텍처 레벨에서 언어 혼용 차단. 
 45건의 테스트 기록 (T-001~T-045)과 트러블슈팅 FAQ로 재발 방지. 
 

 What we learned (배운 점) 

 
 자동화의 본질은 범위 선택 — 하나를 끝까지 완성하는 것이 여러 개를 반쯤 하는 것보다 낫습니다. 
 모델은 용도별 조합 — 배치는 가성비 OSS, 실시간은 저지연 Gemini.

title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: PayablePilot
pitch: A browser agent prepares the invoice review. A person makes the payment decision.
about_excerpt:
A browser agent prepares the invoice review. A person makes the payment decision.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Deterministic checks stay separate from the agent actions. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The exact $200 invoice hold and its supporting evidence. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent can stage a draft. A person confirms or dismisses it. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Deterministic checks stay separate from the agent actions. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The exact $200 invoice hold and its supporting evidence. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent can stage a draft. A person confirms or dismisses it. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Deterministic checks stay separate from the agent actions. 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 PayablePilot already had a clear safety boundary: the agent could finish routine
work, but a person had to decide what happened to an invoice exception. WebMCP
made it possible to carry that same boundary into the browser. The agent no
longer needs to infer state from a dense dashboard or click the same buttons as
the reviewer. 

 What it does 

 The page exposes two WebMCP tools. review_payables_queue returns the current
run, source document IDs, exact price variance, allowed actions, and decision
status. stage_invoice_resolution puts one permitted choice into a visible
Agent Draft. It cannot confirm the draft, release a payment, or contact the
supplier. 

 The included run has two fictional invoice packets. One clears. PP-2086 stops
because eight units were invoiced at $119 instead of the $94 purchase-order
rate. The deterministic difference is $200. An agent can read that evidence and
stage the credit-and-hold option. A person still checks the evidence and either
confirms or dismisses the draft. 

 How I built it 

 The live page is a React and TypeScript app. It registers two tools with
 document.modelContext.registerTool() , uses strict JSON Schema inputs, and
returns concise JSON. The review tool carries the read-only annotation. The
staging tool updates visible page state but has no code path to record a final
decision. An AbortController unregisters both tools with the component
lifecycle. 

 The queue facts live in one typed module shared by the tools and tests. The test
suite independently checks the $200 calculation, the pending human-confirmation
status, and rejection of actions outside the two visible choices. 

 Challenges 

 The hard part was making the browser tool useful without quietly widening the
agent's authority. A tool that clicked the final button would have been easy to
demo and wrong for the product. I split the flow at the decision boundary: the
agent can prepare the review, while the final click stays with the person who is
accountable for the payment. 

 I also had to treat the existing project honestly. PayablePilot predates this
challenge, so the repository documents exactly what was added after August 25
and the dated commits isolate the WebMCP work. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Both tools are detected and callable on the public page in ChatGPT's in-app browser. 
 The live staging call produces the same visible Agent Draft shown in the demo. 
 No agent tool can approve an exception or send anything to a supplier. 
 All 17 tests pass, including three focused WebMCP boundary tests. 
 

 What I learned 

 The most useful browser tools are often smaller than the interface around them.
Two narrow tools were enough here. One reports exact state. One prepares a
reversible draft. Keeping those jobs separate made the agent easier to guide and
the safety boundary easier to verify. 

 What's next 

 The next step is connecting the same tools to a real authenticated review queue.
The browser contract would stay narrow, while the server would add organization
policies, duplicate-invoice checks, reviewer identity, and a durable audit log. 

 Why WebMCP fits 

 Invoice review is a poor place for an agent to guess from button text. The page
contains a purchase order, invoice, receipt, arithmetic, and a hard approval
boundary. WebMCP gives the agent a small, typed contract for reading that state
and putting one allowed choice in front of the reviewer. 

 The agent does not scrape the page, calculate the difference, invent an action,
or click through a payment decision. PayablePilot returns the exact $200.00
variance from deterministic application data. The write-capable tool can only
stage one of the two choices already present in the interface. It cannot confirm
either choice. 

 Work added during the challenge 

 PayablePilot existed before The WebMCP Challenge. The WebMCP implementation,
visible agent draft, safety boundary, tests, and this documentation were added
after the submission period began on August 25, 2026. Git history provides the
dated record required for a pre-existing project.

title: NeXaCard WebMCP — Relationship Copilot
pitch: An agent-native relationship copilot that uses WebMCP to remember contacts, understand relationship context, identify follow-ups, and turn natural-language requests into actions.\n
about_excerpt:
An agent-native relationship copilot that uses WebMCP to remember contacts, understand relationship context, identify follow-ups, and turn natural-language requests into actions.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 The Problem 

 Professional relationships are easy to lose track of. 

 After meeting someone at a conference, networking event, or business meeting, the important context often gets scattered across notes, messages, and memory. The result is simple: people forget who they met, what they discussed, and who they should contact next. 

 NeXaCard WebMCP — Relationship Copilot explores a different approach: make the relationship manager itself agent-native . 

 What I Built 

 NeXaCard is a lightweight relationship copilot that lets a person manage professional connections while an AI agent can interact directly with the web application through WebMCP . 

 The app stores a small local relationship database containing contacts, relationship strength, interaction context, and follow-up state. 

 Instead of requiring a user to navigate through the UI manually, an agent can understand natural-language requests and select the appropriate WebMCP tool. 

 For example: 

 
 "Who do I need to follow up with this week?" 
 

 The agent discovers and invokes the identify_followup WebMCP tool, which returns the contacts needing attention. 

 The current prototype exposes six WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_contacts — search the local contact database 
 get_contact_context — retrieve full relationship context 
 get_interaction_history — retrieve past interactions 
 identify_followup — identify contacts needing attention 
 draft_followup — generate a follow-up draft 
 create_followup — create a follow-up task 
 

 This creates a simple agent workflow: 

 Discover → Understand → Remember → Draft → Act 

 Why WebMCP? 

 The key idea behind this project is that a web application should not only be something humans click through. It can also expose meaningful capabilities directly to agents. 

 With WebMCP, the application's functionality is described as structured tools that an agent can discover and invoke. 

 In the demo, Gemini receives the natural-language request: 

 
 "Who do I need to follow up with this week?" 
 

 It selects the identify_followup tool, invokes it with the required arguments, receives the application's structured result, and uses that result to answer the user. 

 The application therefore becomes an agent-accessible interface , rather than simply a visual dashboard. 

 How I Built It 

 The project intentionally uses a small, dependency-light architecture: 

 
 Vanilla HTML 
 CSS 
 JavaScript 
 WebMCP 
 Gemini 3.6 Flash 
 Browser-side local data 
 LocalStorage 
 Netlify for hosting 
 

 The WebMCP tools are registered using the browser's document.modelContext API. 

 No backend server or external database is required for the prototype. 

 Challenges 

 The biggest challenge was understanding the difference between a normal web page integration and a genuinely agent-accessible WebMCP application. 

 I initially experimented with a custom JavaScript interface for exposing tools, but that was not the actual WebMCP API. I replaced that approach with the browser's WebMCP implementation using document.modelContext.registerTool() . 

 I then verified the production deployment by inspecting the registered tools and executing them directly. 

 The final test demonstrated the complete flow: 

 Natural-language request → Gemini → WebMCP tool selection → tool execution → structured relationship data → agent response 

 What I Learned 

 This project changed how I think about web applications. 

 Instead of designing only around: 

 Human → UI → Application 

 WebMCP enables another interaction model: 

 Human → Agent → WebMCP Tool → Application 

 The most interesting part is not simply adding AI to a website. It is giving an agent well-defined capabilities so that the agent can interact with the application's real functionality. 

 Future Direction 

 The prototype focuses on professional relationship management, but the same architecture could be applied to many agent-native web applications. 

 Future versions could add richer relationship intelligence, calendar integration, email workflows, organization-level relationship graphs, and more sophisticated next-action recommendations. 

 The goal is to make relationship management something an agent can actively help with rather than another dashboard a user has to maintain manually.

title: Shopping MCP
pitch: Same tools. Every store. One cart. shopping-mcp is a WebMCP profile stores install so agents search, choose, and add with shoppers—no scraping, a shared cart across shops, and the human still decides.
about_excerpt:
Same tools. Every store. One cart. shopping-mcp is a WebMCP profile stores install so agents search, choose, and add with shoppers—no scraping, a shared cart across shops, and the human still decides.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 Devpost submission — shopping-mcp 

 Copy from the first question downward into the text description. Keep the live URL and repo public through judging. 

 Live URL: https://shopping.ejecuta.lat/demo 
 Landing: https://shopping.ejecuta.lat/ 
 Docs: https://shopping.ejecuta.lat/docs 
 Repo: https://github.com/ejecuta-latam/retailab-shopping-mcp 
 License: MIT 
 Demo video: https://youtu.be/89b6XNLcoTU 

 

 Why your use case is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Retail is the web agents fail at most. Every storefront is a different layout, a different “Add to cart” button, and a different cart. That is fine for people. It is a mess for agents. 

 Today an agent that wants to shop has to scrape HTML, guess selectors, and hope the button it clicked was the right SKU. Sometimes it fills a cart the shopper never saw. Sometimes it adds milk on a marketplace that does not sell milk. Sometimes it tries to pay in one silent step across merchants that do not share a checkout. 

 WebMCP exists so a pages can say what it already knows. A storefront already has a catalog and a cart. shopping-mcp is a shared tool profile for that: the same names on every participating site — search_products , list_products , add_to_cart , get_cart , remove_from_cart , optional checkout , and open_ui . The agent reads the open page’s catalog, not the whole internet, and mutates that origin’s cart. 

 

 How it creates a better user experience 

 People still choose. The agent is a shopper sitting next to you, not a bot that fills the bag behind your back. 

 You see the same basket the agent sees. The library mounts a floating cart island ( open_ui ). Human clicks on “Add to cart” and agent tool calls update that same island. Nothing is hidden in a side channel. 

 

 Describe what people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before 

 They can shop a trip across stores together — without scraping, without the agent pretending to be a mouse, and without a silent mega-checkout, across a lot of pages who integrate this library. 

 

 Briefly explain how you implemented WebMCP 

 We shipped a small, zero-dependency browser library, shopping-mcp ( packages/shopping-mcp ). A store maps the profile onto the cart it already has and calls registerShoppingMcp once on the storefront page (not on Node): 
 import { registerShoppingMcp } from "shopping-mcp";

registerShoppingMcp({
 handlers: {
 listProducts: () => myApi.list(),
 searchProducts: (query) => myApi.search(query),
 addToCart: (skuId, quantity) => myApi.add(skuId, quantity),
 getCart: () => myApi.cart(),
 removeFromCart: (skuId) => myApi.remove(skuId),
 checkout: () => myApi.checkout(), // optional
 },
});
 
 The library registers those tools on document.modelContext.registerTool (fallback provideContext ). It validates argument shapes, then calls the store’s handlers. It does not scrape the page and it does not own inventory. If WebMCP is missing, registration is a no-op; humans can still use the cart island. 

 /demo wires handlers to a static catalog and a sessionStorage cart. It also registers demo-only list_stores and switch_store because NileMart, WideMart, and DartHouse share one page — real stores should not ship those. The cart island is closed shadow DOM owned by the library, not agent-injected HTML. Optional checkout is omitted until a merchant is ready; when present it must require shopper confirmation. 

 No login. Test in ChatGPT’s in-app browser (WebMCP on by default) or Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . Live page: https://shopping.ejecuta.lat/demo — install tutorial: https://shopping.ejecuta.lat/docs 

 

 Testing instructions (private field is fine) 

 
 Open https://shopping.ejecuta.lat/demo in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP testing enabled. 
 Confirm tools: search_products , list_products , add_to_cart , get_cart , remove_from_cart , open_ui , list_stores , switch_store . 
 list_products on NileMart → add_to_cart a SKU → switch_store { "storeId": "widemart" } → get_cart still has the NileMart line. 
 Click Add to cart as a human; the island matches the tools. 
 

 No credentials.

title: Pinnwall
pitch: A sticky-note board where the agent is a teammate, not a script. It claims notes, moves them and comments back — running in your browser session, so it never sees a credential.
about_excerpt: A sticky-note board where the agent is a teammate, not a script. It claims notes, moves them and comments back — running in your browser session, so it never sees a credential. Like Comment Story Updates The agent flags a note as four tasks in one, you answer on the note, it reports back when done. Claim pills show what the agent is working on right now. Badges show which notes it wrote. Every board merged into one view, with the agent's work visible across all of them. Inspiration Adding MCP to Pinnwall was already on my list. I use it as my own sticky-note board and kept wanting an assistant that could tidy it up, but not enough to build a whole server with its own auth just for that. I hadn't heard of WebMCP before this hackathon. It turned out to be the shape I actually needed, so I finally built it. What it does Pinnwall is a sticky-note board with no database. With WebMCP, an agent works it with you. It has 13 tools: read the board, create and move notes, add columns, switch the board you're looking at. It can also claim a note, so a marker appears before it starts, and comment on one to say what it did or ask you something. You answer on the note. Anything the agent writes gets badged, so you can always tell who did what. Why WebMCP fits this A board is shared state that two people edit. Before, I had two bad options: let an agent click through the UI from screenshots, which is slow and breaks every time I touch the CSS, or stand up an MCP server with its own auth and deploy, just so something could edit a board I'm already signed into. WebMCP skips both. The tools run in the page, on my session. The agent can do what I can do and nothing more, there's no key to leak, and access ends when I close the tab. Concretely: one note on my board said "ship pricing page, update the FAQ, brief support, schedule the newsletter." Splitting that by hand is four notes typed, four drags, then delete the original. Now it's one sentence, and I watch the agent claim it, split it, and tell me what it did. Then I answer it on the note. That last part is the bit I didn't expect to care about — the conversation stays on the work instead of disappearing into a chat window. How I built it Node, Express, vanilla JS. No build step, no new dependencies. All the tools sit in one file. Each is registered with document.modelContext.registerTool and calls the same fetch helper the buttons call, so the agent rides my session cookie and hits the same CSRF check and validation as a click. They take names, not ids. move_note({ note: "brief support", column: "Done" }) finds the note from a piece of its text and tells the agent what it matched if there's more than one. Pinnwall itself predates the hackathon. The agent side is all new. WEBMCP.md in the repo has the split. Challenges I ran into Mirroring my REST API one to one gave me tools the agent used badly. It doesn't have ids and it thinks in names, so half its calls missed. Making every tool resolve by name fixed more than anything I did on the server. The board reloads itself after the agent writes. The first version did that even while I was typing in a note, and wiped what I'd written. Now it waits until I stop. Accomplishments that I'm proud of No new dependencies, no API key, no second service. You sign in normally and the agent can do what you can do. It's also additive. Existing Pinnwall installs run unchanged and old notes work without a migration. What I learned The useful part of WebMCP is the session, not the protocol. Running in the page turns authorisation from the hardest part into a non-problem. And you have to build for two actors from the start. Almost every bug worth fixing came from assuming only one of us was touching the board at a time. title: AetherDraw
pitch: An agent-native infinite whiteboard that turns visual canvases into structured spatial playgrounds for autonomous AI agents via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An agent-native infinite whiteboard that turns visual canvases into structured spatial playgrounds for autonomous AI agents via WebMCP. Like 2 Comment Story Updates One-shot AI Inference Pipeline generated via create_diagram with automated Dagre layout, smooth cubic Bezier routing. Bi-directional co-creation: Agent detects human-drawn Auth Service and routes a smart Bezier connector from API Gateway in 1ms. WebMCP Inspector drawer displaying all 11 registered browser tools, JSON parameter schemas, and real-time execution telemetry. Console inspecting document.modelContext.getTools(), exposing typed WebMCP tool definitions directly to AI agents. Autonomous diagram synthesis running directly inside the browser runtime via native WebMCP tool invocation. Full AI inference architecture on infinite canvas with responsive camera auto-framing and zero shape collisions. Spatial introspection via get_canvas_state followed by instant atomic connector routing using connect_elements. One-click visual styling: apply_theme restyles the entire canvas into the handcrafted Nordic Frost color palette. Hierarchical Microservices Architecture template with multi-tier services and obstacle-avoiding edge routing. Public open-source repository on GitHub (ShreyashChaurasia/AetherDraw) with full source code, MIT license, and tests. In-app architecture modal detailing the 4-layer WebMCP tool suite, W3C protocol integration, and Excalidraw attribution. Project Story: AetherDraw Inspiration Visual whiteboards like Excalidraw, Miro, and FigJam are the ultimate playground for human thinking. Whenever I need to design a backend architecture, trace a data pipeline, or brainstorm an idea, I immediately open a blank canvas. Spatial thinking feels natural to humans because our brains process relationships, hierarchies, and groupings through physical distance and layout. However, for AI agents, these visual canvases have always been a complete black box. Today, if you want an AI model to interact with a spatial whiteboard, you are forced into one of two terrible compromises: The Vision Approach: Taking screenshots, feeding them into a multimodal LLM, and hoping the model can approximate pixel coordinates. This is slow (taking several seconds per step), costly, and prone to severe spatial hallucinations. The Brittle Automation Approach: Simulating fragile mouse drag-and-drop events on raw HTML5 <canvas> elements that easily break whenever the viewport pans, zooms, or resizes. When I saw the WebMCP specification, the lightbulb turned on. WebMCP provides the exact missing bridge: instead of forcing AI agents to squint at canvas pixels from the outside, the web application can expose its internal scene AST, geometric bounds, and layout engines directly to the browser runtime via document.modelContext . I wanted to build a whiteboard where AI agents and humans collaborate as equals: an agent-native infinite canvas where an AI can read, build, style, and route complex diagrams in single-digit milliseconds with deterministic precision. That is why I built AetherDraw. What It Does AetherDraw is an open-source, agent-native infinite whiteboard powered by WebMCP. It extends Excalidraw core with a suite of 11 schema-typed tools organized into four functional layers: Spatial Inspection (Layer A): get_canvas_state , get_selected_elements , and find_elements serialize the visual canvas into a structured abstract syntax tree (AST). The agent receives bounding boxes, node types, text labels, and connection graphs without needing a single pixel screenshot. Algorithmic Synthesis (Layer B): create_diagram takes high-level intent (nodes, roles, connections, title, and direction) and executes automated graph layout in a single call, dynamically framing the result to the viewport. Fine-Grained Mutation (Layer C): add_elements , update_elements , delete_elements , and connect_elements allow agents to perform atomic edits, relabel nodes, modify styles, and route smooth Bezier arrows that snap to human-drawn shapes. Layout & Styling (Layer D): apply_auto_layout reorganizes messy hand-drawn clusters into clean hierarchical structures; apply_theme transforms palettes across 7 themes (Classic, Nordic Frost, Cyberpunk Neon, Pastel Dream, Blueprint, Minimal Dark, Solarized); and export_canvas creates high-res PNG or SVG artifacts. Crucially, AetherDraw enables bi-directional co-creation . A human can sketch a couple of boxes and type "Auth Service". The agent calls get_canvas_state , detects the human's shapes, understands where they sit in space, and uses connect_elements to hook up the rest of the backend architecture seamlessly. How I Built It I built AetherDraw as a solo developer using React 19, TypeScript 5, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. 1. Canvas Engine Foundation I chose Excalidraw core ( @excalidraw/excalidraw ) because it represents the gold standard of hand-drawn collaborative canvases. However, Excalidraw was built strictly for human input. To make it agent-native, I wrapped the imperative canvas API with an adapter layer that tracks non-deleted scene elements, manages selection state, and coordinates camera zoom. 2. WebMCP Protocol Implementation I integrated @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill to register all 11 tools directly on document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool defines a strict JSON Schema for its parameters, validates inputs, and reports structured telemetry. In addition to the runtime polyfill, I published a static discovery manifest at /webmcp.json following the official WebMCP specification. 3. Automated Graph Layout Theory Rather than asking the AI model to guess coordinates, AetherDraw uses battle-tested layout algorithms: Dagre (Sugiyama Hierarchical DAG Method): Computes vertex layers, minimizes edge crossings, and assigns discrete ranks. ELK.js (Eclipse Layout Kernel): Handles orthogonal graph layouts and complex topologies. The agent simply specifies the relational graph $G = (V, E)$. The layout engine solves the layering and coordinate assignment in $O(|V| + |E|)$ time, placing each node $v_i \in V$ at an optimal coordinate $(x_i, y_i)$ with zero shape collisions. 4. Organic Cubic Bezier Arrow Routing Connecting boxes with straight lines looks messy and cuts across neighboring elements. I wrote a dedicated router that calculates smooth cubic Bezier curves: $$B(t) = (1-t)^3 P_0 + 3(1-t)^2 t P_1 + 3(1-t) t^2 P_2 + t^3 P_3, \quad t \in [0, 1]$$ Where: $P_0 = (x_{\text{start}}, y_{\text{start}})$ is the anchor point on the source shape. $P_3 = (x_{\text{end}}, y_{\text{end}})$ is the anchor point on the target shape. $P_1$ and $P_2$ are dynamically computed control points offset along the primary flow axis. The router detects intervening obstacle nodes within the direct corridor. If an obstacle exists, the route dynamically diverts through outer gutter channels to avoid line crossings. For horizontal peer nodes sitting side-by-side, it routes directly from the right border of the source to the left border of the target without piercing the shape boundary. 5. Viewport Fit-Screen Mathematics When generating large diagrams, placing shapes off-screen ruins the user experience. I implemented a dynamic framing calculation that computes the total bounding rectangle of all diagram nodes: $$x_{\min} = \min_{i} (x_i), \quad x_{\max} = \max_{i} (x_i + w_i)$$ $$y_{\min} = \min_{i} (y_i), \quad y_{\max} = \max_{i} (y_i + h_i)$$ Given available viewport dimensions $W_{\text{avail}} = W_{\text{window}} - 2 \cdot \text{pad} x$ and $H {\text{avail}} = H_{\text{window}} - 2 \cdot \text{pad}_y$, the camera zoom factor $z$ is computed as: $$z = \text{clamp}\left(\min\left(\frac{W_{\text{avail}}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}, \frac{H_{\text{avail}}}{y_{\max} - y_{\min}}\right), z_{\min}, 1.0\right)$$ The canvas camera pans directly to the center coordinates: $$(x_{\text{center}}, y_{\text{center}}) = \left(\frac{x_{\min} + x_{\max}}{2}, \frac{y_{\min} + y_{\max}}{2}\right)$$ This ensures the entire diagram immediately fills the screen at crisp resolution with proper toolbar clearance. 6. Developer Telemetry & Inspector To make WebMCP observable, I built a slide-out Inspector drawer that lists all registered tool schemas, streams live invocation events, and displays execution duration timers down to the millisecond. Challenges I Faced Imperative Canvas State vs. Asynchronous Tool Calls: Excalidraw maintains its own internal React reconciliation cycles, selection maps, and rendering loops. Bridging asynchronous WebMCP tool executions into Excalidraw's imperative API required careful synchronization so that rapid sequential tool calls wouldn't cause state tears or canvas flickering. Smart Arrow Routing without Box Penetration: Early prototypes had arrows that routed straight through boxes or connected to the far side of target nodes. Writing the horizontal peer detection logic and obstacle corridors required extensive coordinate geometry and edge-case testing, especially ensuring that arrowheads snap flush

title: Dim Hour
pitch: The places worth your time, now agent-native. A scored city guide where people and their agents plan a night out together, in the same page.
about_excerpt: The places worth your time, now agent-native. A scored city guide where people and their agents plan a night out together, in the same page. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Dim Hour is a city guide - the places worth your time, scored, not starred - covering more than 19,000 restaurants, bars, hotels, and venues across 24 cities. For this challenge, dimhour.com became agent-native: the page itself registers five WebMCP tools, so an agent browsing the site can search the catalog, read a venue, check what is open tonight, draft an itinerary, and hand back a booking link - without scraping a pixel. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Planning a night out is one of the most common things people already ask an agent to help with, but today the agent scrapes pages and guesses at what the site already knows. WebMCP lets dimhour.com hand the agent its real search, scoring, and booking data as structured tools, in the same tab where the person is browsing. The catalog is the product; WebMCP makes it callable. Because the tools are thin adapters over a production venue API, every agent answer is grounded in live data instead of page scraping. How it creates a better user experience One page, two users. A person browsing the Dallas guide and their agent now work on the same surface. The agent calls the site's own tools and gets back the same scored venues, hours, and booking links the UI shows - no copy-pasting between a chat window and a browser, and no agent inventing hours, addresses, or availability. The person keeps the judgment (taste, swaps, vetoes); the agent does the legwork (searching, filtering, checking, assembling). The site stays the source of truth for both of them, and saving a plan stays a human action - the tools read, they never write. What people and agents can do together Co-plan a night in one sitting, in one page. "Dinner in Deep Ellum for four on Friday, then cocktails within walking distance." The agent searches the scored catalog, filters to what is actually open tonight using the same rule the site's own tonight strip uses, pulls full venue records, and drafts an ordered itinerary with real booking links (Resy, OpenTable, SevenRooms, Tock) while the person watches - then interrupts: "swap the second stop for something quieter," and the agent re-plans around the constraint. Before WebMCP, the agent could read the page but not act through the site's own logic, and the person could use the site but not delegate the legwork. Now both happen at once, and the result is a plan with real reservation links attached, not a list of suggestions. How we implemented WebMCP The WebMCP layer is one feature-detected script, webmcp.js, loaded by the site's index.html. Each of the five tools is a thin adapter that POSTs JSON-RPC tools/call to Dim Hour's existing MCP server (mcp.dimhour.com) and passes the result straight through: search_venues - one strong keyword plus city, neighborhood, cuisine, score floor, and price ceiling filters get_venue - the full record: hours, score, booking path, awards find_open_tonight - venues with a happy hour or late kitchen, best score first, using the same definition the site's own "tonight" strip uses, so the agent and the page agree build_itinerary - an ordered multi-stop plan with why and how to book each stop; saving stays a human action at /trip.html get_booking_link - the reservation platform and direct booking URL for a venue, returned for the agent to present; it never opens or books anything itself The script handles the in-flight standard rename (document.modelContext first, navigator.modelContext fallback) and is a silent no-op where no WebMCP host exists. No authentication; the tools expose only public, read-only catalog data. What predates the hackathon: the venue catalog, scoring pipeline, MCP server, and site. What was built during the submission window: webmcp.js, the tool schemas, and the index.html include - the public repo's README draws that line explicitly, with dated commits. Challenges we hit Search results deliberately do not carry hours - only full venue records do - so "open tonight" meant ranking candidates first, then reading the top few individually rather than filtering a field that is not there. Booking links live in the page's own catalog rather than the API, so the booking tool merges both sources and says so honestly when a city is not loaded. The verification suite now asserts substance (tonight actually finds venues; a booking link equals the catalog's own URL), not just shape - because an early version passed every check while two tools quietly returned nothing. title: Personalize this page
pitch: Every website speaks to an average visitor. Ours becomes your website: your agent brings the context you share, rewrites 29 guarded fields in one call, and one click restores the original.
about_excerpt: Every website speaks to an average visitor. Ours becomes your website: your agent brings the context you share, rewrites 29 guarded fields in one call, and one click restores the original. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case belongs to WebMCP Every website speaks to an average visitor. The visitor arriving with an AI agent is not average: their agent knows who they are, what they run, and what they came to solve. Until now, using that knowledge meant surveillance (cookies, trackers, server-side profiles). WebMCP flips the direction: the context stays on the visitor's side, and the page publishes what may change and by which rules. That is exactly what WebMCP tools can express, and it only works as page-embedded tools: the writing contract (which fields exist, their jobs, their budgets, the style rules, the facts that must stay true) lives where the page lives. No backend of its own, no account; your context and the rewritten text never leave the browser. The site counts tool names for a public usage counter, nothing else. We inverted the standard pattern: the agent does not operate our site, it writes it. How it improves the user experience A generic homepage becomes the visitor's page. For the head of sales at an industrial pump maker, the hero verb changes from "use" to "shortlist", the three product cards become "Be in the spec. Be the RFQ shortlist. Take the quote.", and the FAQ stops asking vendor questions and starts asking their real ones ("What happens to our configurator and catalog?"). For an outdoor apparel brand's e-commerce lead, the same page argues in a shopper's terms: "Be in the answer. Be the shopper's shortlist. Take the order." The conversion form arrives prefilled from the profile the agent already holds. Speed is engineered like a product feature: three brand headlines re-mint in under one second (deterministic, before any model writes), then ONE write_all call carries all 29 texts and the page stages a skeleton-shimmer reveal, section by section. Page-side cost of a full personalization: under 6 seconds. What the human and the agent accomplish together The human brings intent. The agent carries that intent to the page. The page brings truth: real product facts, real prices, hard budgets, and it rejects markup and over-budget text. What comes out is a third thing none of them could make alone: the company's actual website arguing its actual case in the visitor's own terms, with every claim still grounded in what the site really says. The human stays in charge throughout: the progress banner shows what is happening, the receipt lists every change and every piece of context that was used, word for word, and one click restores the original, character-exact. How we built it One dependency-free ES module (~1,800 lines) served from our production site behind a build flag; its entire HTML footprint is one script tag, so crawlers and no-JS visitors always see the canonical page. Six personalization tools join the site's four existing WebMCP tools into one 10-tool surface, registered on document.modelContext with a knock-forever loop for late-injecting clients, identity guards, and never-abort semantics. Native clients (Chrome's WebMCP prototype, the ChatGPT in-app browser) get string-returning wrappers per Chrome's imperative API; script-driven clients read the same tools from an inspectable array with raw object + MCP content shapes. Every writable field carries a job description, the original text, and a hard budget derived from it (~original +30%). The page enforces on submit: plain text only, no markup, no em dashes, no over-budget text, so the layout never breaks. The fact rules (no invented customers, numbers, prices or guarantees) are part of the writing contract handed to the agent; the receipt shows the context used so the reader can check. Verified end to end over Chrome's NATIVE API (getTools/executeTool, real Chrome 152, WebMCPTesting flag) against the live site: all 10 tools listed, full run, 0 rejections, exact reset. Also verified with third-party agents: Perplexity Comet discovered the tools unprompted and rewrote all ten sections; ChatGPT, Claude and Firefox/WebKit paths tested. Shipped to production on our real company domain during the submission window (dated PR history in the repo's PROVENANCE.md). Try it as a judge Fastest path, the one we verified ourselves: Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. Open https://www.hyperize.ai/en and tell your agent: "Personalize this page for me using its WebMCP tools: call start_personalization with what you know about me and my company, then submit all texts in one write_all call. No web research needed. Page tools only; do not modify any files." Also works: the ChatGPT in-app browser when site tools are enabled for your account (OpenAI documents that they are unavailable in Enterprise and Edu workspaces and still rolling out), and Perplexity Comet in Computer mode, which found the tools unprompted and rewrote all ten sections on 31 August. No WebMCP client at hand? Clone the repo and run npm test: it drives the live site over Chrome's native API (getTools and executeTool) and prints a pass/fail table. The repo also carries a standalone demo of the same module. No login, no key. The Reset button restores the original page, and a reload does too. title: ProtocolOS
pitch: ProtocolOS turns complex research protocols into agent-ready workflows, helping researchers and AI coordinate participants, assessments, visits, and study tasks efficiently.
about_excerpt:
ProtocolOS turns complex research protocols into agent-ready workflows, helping researchers and AI coordinate participants, assessments, visits, and study tasks efficiently.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Research protocols define exactly what must happen, yet daily operations are often split across documents, spreadsheets, calendars, and task systems. Coordinators spend valuable time reconciling those sources to answer a deceptively simple question: what does this subject need next? ProtocolOS began with the idea that a protocol should be an operational workflow that people and browser agents can understand together—not just a static document. 

 What it does 

 ProtocolOS turns research protocols into shared, agent-ready workflows. It organizes multiple synthetic studies, subjects, stages, visits, assessments, samples, tasks, and completion criteria in one polished workspace. 

 Coordinators can: 

 
 See today's priorities across multiple studies 
 Understand a subject's current stage, visit, and outstanding work 
 Build and publish a visual protocol workflow 
 Generate a visit checklist from the published workflow 
 Complete tasks while keeping related records synchronized 
 Check whether a subject is ready to advance, with explicit reasons when advancement is blocked 
 

 All demo records are fictional and use generic IDs such as SUB001. ProtocolOS contains no real protected health information. 

 How WebMCP creates real utility 

 Without WebMCP, an agent would have to infer operational state from pixels and page text. That is fragile when a missed assessment, sample, or sign-off can change whether a visit is complete. 

 ProtocolOS registers fourteen imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). They cover portfolio summaries, priorities, workflow inspection and publishing, subject status, assessments, visits, samples, missing tasks, readiness, checklist creation, task completion, and guarded stage advancement. 

 Read operations are marked read-only. Mutations are explicit and update the same React state shown to the coordinator. Every response includes structured results, synthetic-data indicators, workflow provenance, and a compact technical receipt. 

 Human and agent collaboration 

 A coordinator can ask, “What does SUB001 need today?” The agent retrieves the current stage and visit, incomplete tasks, assessments, sample requirements, and next action. It can create the checklist and complete an approved item. The visible workspace updates immediately, and the activity trail records who changed what and when. 

 Crucially, the model does not decide whether a subject advances. ProtocolOS evaluates the published completion gates and returns a clear allowed-or-blocked decision with the exact remaining requirements. The workflow remains the source of truth while the agent accelerates coordination. 

 How we built it 

 ProtocolOS is a responsive React and TypeScript application styled with Tailwind CSS and hosted with OpenAI Sites. Synthetic seed data powers a multi-study dashboard, subject records, a visual workflow builder, visit checklists, activity history, and an agent workspace. WebMCP actions are registered directly in the live page so a compatible browser agent can use the product's own operational contract. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was making agent actions and visible UI state feel like one system instead of a chat demo layered on top of a dashboard. We also had to model advancement safely: status checks must be useful and read-only, while actual transitions remain explicit, auditable, and governed by published rules. 

 Designing a workflow builder that stays flexible across study types was another challenge. We avoided study-specific terminology and made stages, visits, requirements, and gates configurable. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built a polished multi-study workspace where fourteen WebMCP actions operate on the same state people see. The challenge demo shows retrieval, checklist creation, synchronized completion, audit history, and a guarded workflow decision in under three minutes. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is most compelling when tools represent meaningful domain actions rather than page-navigation shortcuts. Clear schemas, workflow provenance, read/write separation, and visible state synchronization make an agent experience more trustworthy and useful. 

 Judge demo 

 
 Ask: What does SUB001 need today? 
 Ask: Create SUB001's visit checklist. 
 Ask: Mark task T-001-3 complete for SUB001. 
 Ask: Can SUB001 advance to the next stage? 
 

 The final check is intentionally blocked and explains the remaining tasks, assessment, and samples. If the demo has already been used, choose Reset challenge demo in the Agent workspace. 

 What's next for ProtocolOS 

 Next, ProtocolOS can add protocol import, reusable workflow templates, role-based approvals, integrations with validated research systems, and configurable audit exports—while preserving the same human-visible, workflow-governed approach.

title: Urban Planning Copilot
pitch: Helping cities make smarter decisions by pairing planners with an AI collaborator that explores possibilities, reveals trade-offs, and keeps humans in control.
about_excerpt: Helping cities make smarter decisions by pairing planners with an AI collaborator that explores possibilities, reveals trade-offs, and keeps humans in control. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration This started with a question about how small planning choices can lead to very different outcomes for a city. Shiwani has a university course called Introduction to City , where her instructor teaches urban planning and how these choices can affect the larger system. We started wondering what it would look like if AI could help a planner explore those choices and their consequences. We also worked on Build What, Move India by Varun Mayya, powered by OpenAI, where we explored bringing maps and Records of Rights together. That gave us some experience with combining spatial information and structured records. What it does Urban Planning Copilot is a map-first workspace for exploring urban planning scenarios. For our current case, we use housing in San Francisco. Housing supply and affordability are significant concerns for the city, and its Housing Element targets 82,000 new homes between 2023 and 2031. In the current study, the planner sets a goal of 2,000 homes in Mission and SoMa. The system evaluates potential sites using factors such as transit access, flood risk, parks, schools, zoning, and capacity. The current analysis finds capacity for about 1,098 homes, so the shortfall is visible. The planner can then: Explore and inspect candidate sites. Change constraints and rerun the analysis. Shortlist sites directly on the shared map. Create and compare different scenarios. Why WebMCP matters We wanted the AI to work inside the planning workspace, not just describe what is on the screen. Through WebMCP, the AI can: Run the analysis and inspect candidates. Change planning constraints. Move the shared map to relevant sites. Add candidates to the shortlist. Create and compare scenario branches. Prepare a decision for planner approval. These are planning actions rather than browser actions. The AI works with the same application state as the planner, so when it changes something, the planner sees that change in the workspace too. For consequential actions, the AI prepares the change and the planner approves or rejects it. How we built it We built a shared planning model around projects, scenarios, analysis results, candidates, decisions, and provenance. The spatial analysis uses San Francisco geographic datasets covering parcels, transit, flood areas, parks, and schools. Candidate scoring and capacity calculations are deterministic, while AI suggestions are kept separate from the underlying calculations. The application and WebMCP tools use the same underlying services and state. We also track provenance so it is clear whether something came from source data, a calculation, an AI suggestion, or a planner decision. What we learned Building this changed how we think about the role of AI in planning. AI can investigate, calculate, compare, and prepare options. The planner still brings the context and judgment needed to decide between them. We also found that WebMCP is most useful when its tools represent meaningful actions in the user's workflow, rather than low-level interactions with a website. What's next We want to take the planning side further, but first we want to make sure we are solving the right problems. We are not urban planning domain experts, so the next step is to work with SMEs and practitioners to validate our assumptions, constraints, workflows, and outputs. We'd especially like to learn from people who teach and practice urban planning, including potentially Shiwani's instructor. From there, we want to improve the current workflow, add more real datasets and geographies, and explore planning decisions beyond the current housing use case. title: Resume Match
pitch: Tailor your resume to the job with an agent that proposes, and a human who decides.
about_excerpt: Tailor your resume to the job with an agent that proposes, and a human who decides. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I kept seeing resume tools that either rewrite everything behind your back or leave you hunting for keywords at 1 a.m. Neither felt honest. If an AI is going to touch something as personal as a resume, I want to see the before and after on the actual bullet — and I want a button that says no. WebMCP clicked because the agent and I share the same page. It can read the job I pasted and the bullets already on screen, then propose a change. It cannot quietly replace my experience with something I never agreed to. What it does Upload a PDF or Word resume, paste a job posting. The agent can pull out the role and required skills, point out gaps, score ATS coverage, pull in a public GitHub or Medium profile, and suggest a rewritten bullet or a cover-letter opener. Every suggestion shows up as a diff. I accept or reject it myself. Review and Export only include what I accepted. I recorded the demo with ChatGPT desktop . It found the page tools, ran the flow, and the diffs showed up the way they should — that’s the video I’m uploading. Live demo: https://resumematch-617103164879.us-central1.run.app How I built it Python on the server (FastAPI, Jinja2, SQLite). One small JavaScript file registers the WebMCP tools and updates the page. The real work stays in Python so I can sanitize and length-cap it. Intake forms use WebMCP’s declarative form tools, without auto-submit. Analysis and rewrites use document.modelContext.registerTool() . Because the tools live on the page, ChatGPT desktop could drive them the same way Chrome’s inspector can — I didn’t have to build a custom ChatGPT plugin. Only three tools call a model: analyze the job, propose a bullet rewrite, draft a cover opener. Gap finding and ATS scoring are plain skill matching: $$\text{coverage} = \frac{|\text{JD skills} \cap \text{resume skills}|}{|\text{JD skills}|} \times 100$$ Original bullet text is never overwritten. A proposal sits as its own row until I accept it. Running on Google Cloud Run. Session secret and the server Gemini key are in Secret Manager. What I learned The agent in the desktop app and the Gemini/Vertex key on the server are not the same job. ChatGPT picks which tool to call. Our server is what actually writes a proposal. That split is why the demo could look “agentic” without letting ChatGPT silently rewrite the resume. Tools belong to the current page. Stay on Edit for matching and diffs. analyze_job_description taking {} is fine — the job text is already in the session. Challenges Session cookies once split so submit saved a job and analyze couldn’t see it. A prompt on the Upload page also looks like nothing works until you actually click Upload & Parse. I hit both while testing, including with ChatGPT desktop, and had to fix the session path and the copy on the page before the recording was worth keeping. Cloud Run with SQLite wipes sessions on a new deploy, so I recorded against a stable revision. Job descriptions are still untrusted text I treat them as data and never commit a generation without a click.
