title: AI ACT SHIELD WEBMCP
pitch: AI Act Shield App masks the personal data in your contract without sending to any LLM. WebMCP tools run in your browser page using deterministic checksums. No sensible datas will leave the page.
about_excerpt: AI Act Shield App masks the personal data in your contract without sending to any LLM. WebMCP tools run in your browser page using deterministic checksums. No sensible datas will leave the page. Like Comment Story Updates The agent was never told which tool to use, and reports only the types it received. Left: what the human sees. Right: what leaves the page. external mask_document_in_page {} — the agent called the tool with no arguments, because the app never gives it the document Inspiration Law firms and accountants across the EU are stuck in a small, expensive trap. Generative AI would genuinely help them review a contract — but the contract is full of client data they are not allowed to paste into a cloud model. Under the AI Act and the GDPR that is not a formality; it is their licence to practise. The usual answer is a cloud "anonymization API", which moves the leak one hop away and calls it a solution. I wanted the masking to happen where the document already is: on the lawyer's own machine, in the browser tab, with nothing to trust but code you can read. What it does AI Act Shield detects personal data — tax codes, national IDs, VAT numbers, IBANs, payment cards, names, emails, phone numbers, addresses, company names — and replaces each with a placeholder, so the masked draft can safely go to any AI. When the answer comes back, it puts the real values back where they belong. Detection is deterministic: regular expressions plus real checksums (ISO 13616 for IBANs, Luhn for payment cards, the Spanish DNI/NIE and CIF control characters, the official Italian VAT algorithm). Never an LLM. A model would answer differently on the same document from one run to the next, and sending a document to a model to ask what to hide from that model defeats the purpose. Coverage is Italian, Spanish and English/international. The WebMCP part The app is built on one constraint: the text never leaves the browser. That constraint turns out to be exactly what makes a WebMCP tool trustworthy, because registerTool().execute() runs client-side, in the visitor's own tab. The page registers four tools. The one that carries the argument is mask_document_in_page , and what matters is what it doesn't take: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "mask_document_in_page", description: "Masks the personal data in the document the user has already loaded into this page, without the caller ever receiving the document.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { customTerms: { /* ... */ } } }, execute: async (input) => maskPageDocument(input), }); No text parameter. The person loads the confidential document into the page; the agent calls the tool passing nothing ; the page reads its own content and returns a masked draft plus the types of what it found. The document never enters the agent's context, so it cannot leak one even if it tried. Asked in plain language to mask a contract — without being told which tool to use — ChatGPT's agentic browser produced this row in the page's own log: 1:48:34 PM external mask_document_in_page {} external means the call came from outside the page rather than from its own buttons. {} means there was nothing to pass. That empty object is the whole project. This is also the case for "people and agents using an app together": the UI and the tools share one page-local state, so the person watching the tab sees the masking happen live and can step in — switch a detected entity off, add a custom term — while the agent works. How I built it Vanilla JavaScript. No framework, no dependencies, no build step — you can clone it and open it. 37 tests on node:test , which is built in, so that promise holds for the test suite too. Served as static files from my own nginx, not a platform: the page is the same folder that nginx serves. The detection engine is a port of the one shipping in iaCiao , my platform for local — edge — AI: 32 iApps across health, security and mobility, all built so the model runs on your device and the data stays there. AI Act Shield is the clearest expression of that idea, which is why I brought it here. An app whose entire value is that the sensitive part never leaves your machine turns out to be the natural shape for a WebMCP tool, because that is exactly where execute() runs. Challenges The ecosystem moved under me during the ten days. ChatGPT Atlas was deprecated days before the deadline. The Model Context Tool Inspector extension reports nothing for my page, because it looks for navigator.modelContext while the specification (26 August 2026) exposes ModelContext on document and never mentions navigator. I left that audit check failing rather than shim an API that does not exist — and left the declarative toolname / tooldescription / toolaction checks failing too, since the spec marks that API "entirely a TODO". ChatGPT's Chrome extension looks like it works and doesn't. Asked to mask the document, it produced a fluent, accurate answer — by reading the DOM, without calling a single tool. That is precisely the difference this project is about, and it would have been very easy to film it as a success. Chrome's origin trial has a quirk. It returns inputSchema as a JSON string and rejects a plain-object argument to executeTool() with "Failed to parse input arguments". Nothing in the spec asks for a pre-serialised input, so the code calls the spec-shaped way first and falls back only when that build refuses. My own buttons sabotaged two takes. The "Agent console" had a button labelled CALL MASK_SENSITIVE_DATA() . Asked to "use the page's tools", the agent clicked it — twice. Not a dim agent: the button had named itself after the API, so it was the closest match to the instruction. Renaming it to "Preview the masking response", and adding a line in llms.txt telling agents to call the tool instead, fixed what a better prompt could not. Cloudflare hid three deploys. Assets are served with a four-hour browser cache, so the page kept running the previous build and no hard refresh changed it. I lost two hours because I was verifying with curl --resolve ...:127.0.0.1 , which goes to the origin and bypasses the edge — always showing me the correct file. What I learned The one that mattered: a tool that takes the sensitive data as a parameter cannot protect it. My first version was mask_sensitive_data(text) . It returns only placeholders, never an original value, and I wrote in my notes that "the agent never saw the tax code". That was false, and I did not notice until, halfway through recording, I asked myself whether pasting the contract into the prompt defeated the point of the app. It did — and so, more quietly, did passing it as a tool argument. Whoever calls that tool must already hold the document. There is a real difference between "the response contains no secrets" and "the caller never receives them" , and only the second is a guarantee. mask_document_in_page exists because of that question. The second lesson: instrument your claims. I added a panel that logs every execute() the page receives and marks whether it came from the page's own buttons or from outside. It exists because you cannot otherwise see WebMCP working — the page looks identical either way. That panel is what caught the Chrome extension reading the DOM, and both takes where the agent clicked a button instead of calling a tool. Without it I would have shipped a video of something that wasn't happening. And a third, smaller one: tests find the bugs you just wrote. Four surfaced in a single session, three of them minutes old — including a legal form matching inside an ordinary word, which rewrote the heading "CONSULTANCY AGREEMENT" as "[COMPANY_NAME_1]REEMENT". Honest limits Detection covers Italian, Spanish and English/international formats. A document in another language will still have its IBANs, cards, emails and international phone numbers found, but not its names, addresses or company forms. No PDF or OCR import in this build. Ambiguous candidates — a capitalised pair that may or may not be a person, an amount that usually belongs in the draft — are proposed switched off , and whatever stays readable after masking is listed rather than hidden. An incomplete mask the user trusts is the real failure mode. restore_sensitive_data only works in the tab that masked the document, because the vault is page memory. That is a privacy property, not a missing feature. The guarantee is that the app never hands the document to the caller . It is not that an agent driving a browser is unable to look at the screen. What's next PDF and OCR import, pattern packs beyond the EU, and a tool that lets an agent request a masked excerpt rather than the whole document. Written with Claude (Claude Code), pair-programming style: the specification research, the port of the engine, the Spanish and English coverage and the test suite came out of that collaboration. title: jobContext: The Memory Layer for Your Career, Agent-Ready
pitch: Career searches scatter context across tabs, docs, and tools. With WebMCP, jobContext gives you and your agent one shared memory for every role and next move, directly in your signed-in browser.
about_excerpt: Career searches scatter context across tabs, docs, and tools. With WebMCP, jobContext gives you and your agent one shared memory for every role and next move, directly in your signed-in browser. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The memory layer for your career, with a live Claude MCP call composing a cover letter. Every new AI chat starts from zero. jobContext is the persistent memory. 12 domain tools, 104 actions, one capability layer across desktop, cloud, and mobile. Readiness-aware: Oura sleep, HRV, and recovery on the dashboard to time your outreach. The dashboard is itself an agent surface: every tool is registered in-page over WebMCP. Private by design: same origin only, tenant isolated, open schema, no lock-in. The signed-in cloud dashboard: priorities, pipeline health, and readiness at a glance. Pipeline with AI fitment scoring: a role weighed against the candidate’s real materials. A generated résumé, versioned and linked to its application, previewed in the app. ChatGPT discovers all 12 jobContext tools in-page through document.modelContext, with no connector or second login. Assessment detail: fitment 8/10 with strengths, risks, and evidence weighed against the saved résumé. Provenance gate: every claim traces to source context, with a verifiable pass or fail. Long generations run as async work items, then return with their trust report. A cross-site call to /mcp is answered 401 Unauthorized, so a hostile page cannot ride your session. Inspiration I built jobContext after getting laid off and finding that AI job-search help came with its own tax: every new conversation began cold. I was repeatedly re-explaining my resume, what I had shipped, which companies were already in my pipeline, people I had met, my STAR stories, and the way I write. The context existed, but it was scattered across documents, tabs, and past chats. Copying it into every fresh session was exhausting when I needed that energy for the search itself. I started by building a few small tools to stop re-explaining myself. They grew into jobContext. What I built jobContext is a living career workspace: applications, job search, materials, interviews, people, STAR stories, and the context behind them stay structured and persistent across sessions. It works as a desktop app, hosted dashboard, mobile companion, CLI, and MCP capability layer. It is not another chat that gives advice and forgets the work. The person owns the workspace and stays in the loop; an agent can help move real work forward inside it. For this challenge, I made the signed-in browser workspace agent-ready through WebMCP. A person and an in-browser agent can work from the same live pipeline: understand the search, find or assess a role, create materials, log the work, and leave the result where the person can inspect and use it. No new connector, separate OAuth flow, or blank-slate conversation is required. How I built it jobContext is built with Python, FastMCP, FastAPI, SQLite with a JSON audit trail, and a React dashboard. After authentication, the dashboard asks the live FastMCP server for its tool list and registers the returned names, descriptions, and input schemas directly with document.modelContext. When an in-browser agent invokes a tool, the bridge sends a same-origin JSON-RPC request to the same stateless /mcp endpoint used by other clients. The browser surface is not a second, hand-maintained API. It reflects the running MCP surface, so browser tools cannot quietly drift from the tools the app actually offers. The current surface has 12 consolidated tools and 104 actions behind them. Challenges I ran into More context is not better context. While improving document generation, I discovered that the system had accumulated more context about my writing style than about what I had actually done. That drove a retrieval-first redesign: token budgets, diagnostics, context ceilings, selective retrieval, and a clear separation between stored knowledge and prompt assembly. The lesson was simple: better context beats more context. “No setup” still has to be safe. I wanted the browser agent to work with the signed-in dashboard, not make someone configure yet another connector. But a session cookie is not permission to trust every browser request. The server accepts that session only for same-origin requests to /mcp; a cross-site browser request cannot use it, while deliberate bearer-auth MCP clients still work. A browser tool call is shorter than real document work. In-browser clients can time out before resume or cover-letter generation finishes. I added durable submit-and-poll generation so an agent can start work, return promptly, then retrieve the finished result instead of pretending a long-running job completed. A generated file is not a finished workflow. If a draft lands untracked, it creates another loose end. Generated materials now automatically create or update the relevant pipeline entry. A read-only Generation Trust Report lets the person inspect the claims checked, verdict, correction passes, and durable audit record. Trust has to be architectural. An interview question exposed a gap in my own system: I could observe non-deterministic AI output, but I could not yet prove that a generated claim was grounded. That became a deterministic provenance gate that checks factual claims against the source material on every generation and records the outcome. Prompt instructions alone were not enough. What I learned The useful unit of AI collaboration is not a prettier chat response. It is a shared, current workspace where the human can see what happened and decide what comes next. WebMCP matters because it lets a page describe its live capabilities at runtime. That is fundamentally better than making a person configure a second integration or maintain a browser-only copy of an API. Reducing friction can create more value than adding features. One of the most satisfying product moments was sharing a job from a phone and having the relevant workflow already waiting at the desk. Good agent systems need grounded context, clear permission boundaries, durable work, and inspectable results. Those are product requirements, not cleanup work after the demo. What changed during this challenge The original jobContext project predates this challenge. The WebMCP agent surface and its supporting hardening below were built during the submission period. The core bridge dynamically reflects the live FastMCP tool surface into document.modelContext and calls the signed-in, same-origin MCP endpoint. Agent-driven testing exposed and fixed workspace-aware assessment, validation, and interview-prep round-trip issues. I added provenance reporting, durable submit-and-poll generation for short browser timeouts, workflow instructions for in-browser agents, and automatic pipeline tracking for generated materials. WebMCP implementation synopsis The WebMCP work began by turning the existing hosted dashboard into an agent surface without creating a second browser-only tool API. The React app probes for document.modelContext, with the older navigator.modelContext alias retained as a compatibility fallback. After the user is authenticated, the bridge calls the live FastMCP server's tools/list endpoint, takes the returned tool names, descriptions, and input schemas, and registers those definitions with modelContext.registerTool(). When the browser agent invokes a registered tool, the bridge forwards the call as JSON-RPC over the same-origin, stateless /mcp endpoint already used by other MCP clients. That architecture means the WebMCP surface is generated from the server's real capability layer. There is no separately maintained list of browser tools to drift out of date. At submission time, the live surface exposes 12 consolidated domain tools with 104 actions. New server-side actions can appear in WebMCP automatically through tools/list rather than requiring a second implementation. The bridge also preserves the signed-in experience without turning the session cookie into ambient authority for arbitrary websites. Same-origin browser calls to /mcp may use the existing jobContext session. Cross-site requests are denied session-cookie authority using Sec-Fetch-Site, with Origin and Host checks as a fallback. Bearer-authenticated MCP clients and non-browser clients remain supported. This was built specifically so WebMCP could feel like part of the signed-in application while still enforcing an origin boundary around side-effecting tools. Browser agents also exposed operational gaps that were easy to miss in ordinary chat or direct MCP use. Long-running resume and cover-letter generation can outlive a browser tool-call window, so jobContext gained a durable submit-and-poll control plane. The agent can submit generation work, receive a work-item identifier promptly, and later poll for completion rather than holding the browser call open. Remote LLM clients were then given finite request timeouts and stale-run reporting so

title: Galleon
pitch: Galleon lets Codex pay publishers for original content, delivering valuable answers while funding writers to produce more knowledge.
about_excerpt: Galleon lets Codex pay publishers for original content, delivering valuable answers while funding writers to produce more knowledge. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Publishers earn through subscriptions and advertising. Agents do not look at ads, and they often need one authoritative source rather than a full subscription. A publisher's work can become more useful to agents while generating less revenue for the people who created it. Galleon asks a simple question: what if a webpage could quote an exact price to an agent, let the person approve it, and return the licensed source with its canonical citation? What it does Galleon gives an AI agent an authenticated wallet with human-controlled spending limits. A participating publisher exposes two WebMCP tools. inspect_source returns free metadata, provenance, the exact price, access rights, and a signed offer. unlock_source redeems a short-lived entitlement and returns the full article as formatted Markdown with its canonical citation. Payment authority never enters the publisher page. After the person approves the exact source, price, and rights, the agent calls purchase_offer through the user's local Galleon wallet MCP. The wallet validates the offer, enforces spending policy, records the purchase, and returns an entitlement scoped to that source and publisher. The complete flow is intentionally small: const offer = await inspect_source({}); await human.approve({ source: offer.source.title, price: offer.offer.display_price, rights: offer.offer.rights, }); const purchase = await purchase_offer({ offer_token: offer.offer.offer_token, expected_amount_minor: offer.offer.amount_minor, expected_currency: offer.offer.currency, idempotency_key: crypto.randomUUID(), }); const article = await unlock_source({ entitlement_token: purchase.entitlement.token, }); return { markdown: article.source.markdown, citation: article.source.citation, }; The current prototype uses test credits. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets the commercial terms travel with the source. The agent discovers the offer on the page instead of scraping a paywall or sending the user through a separate checkout. We pair WebMCP with a traditional MCP because they represent different trust boundaries. WebMCP belongs to the publisher page and exposes page-scoped source tools. The wallet MCP belongs to the user and holds identity, balance, policy, and purchase authority. Together, they let a person and an agent buy one authoritative source without exposing payment credentials or moving the article into an intermediary catalog. We believe the end-state of Galleon is one where the human browsing experience remains the same as it has historically been and ad-supported, while agents are metered for their consumption. How we built it We built and deployed Galleon on floo , which helped us ship a multi-service application with Codex and allocate necessary resources such as our postgres database. Codex was our primary agentic development tool. We used Codex to implement the TypeScript application, inspect the repository, test the real browser journey, exercise the WebMCP tools, review trust boundaries, diagnose deployment failures, and iterate on the product experience. The system has three parts: A consumer application for accounts, test-credit wallets, spending policies, and purchases. An authenticated wallet MCP that validates offers, records retry-safe ledger transactions in PostgreSQL, and issues short-lived entitlements. An independently hosted publisher that registers inspect_source and unlock_source through document.modelContext.registerTool(). Offers and entitlements are signed and bound to the content, publisher origin, and browser session. The publisher receives only the entitlement. It never receives the user's wallet credential. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was the economics of very small purchases. Traditional credit-card checkout is poorly suited to charging a few cents whenever an agent needs one source. We built a test-credit wallet and balanced ledger to prove the interaction before connecting production financial infrastructure. The second challenge was separating trust correctly. The publisher needs proof of purchase but must never receive the wallet credential. The wallet must pay the correct publisher but must never trust unsigned claims from page JavaScript. This led us to connect page-scoped WebMCP tools and the authenticated wallet MCP with signed, short-lived capabilities. Live testing also exposed a cross-service signing-key mismatch. Separate service containers generated separate keys, so the wallet correctly rejected the publisher's offer. We moved the key into shared secret-backed configuration and added tests for the multi-service boundary. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a coherent product experience, not only a tool demo. A user can create an account, fund a test wallet, connect Codex, inspect a paid source, approve the exact terms, purchase it, and unlock it on the publisher's own website. The publisher retains its content and canonical URL. The user retains payment authority. The agent receives the evidence and citation it needs. We think that this idea of building a consumer-grade wallet and payments infrastructure could really benefit publishers who need a way to transform their businesses for the AI era. What we learned WebMCP and MCP are complementary. WebMCP provides contextual tools controlled by the publisher. MCP provides durable authority controlled by the user. We also learned that agent payments are a capability and trust problem before they are a checkout problem. Origin binding, session binding, explicit approval, retry safety, and narrow entitlements make the experience understandable and safe. What's next for Galleon Our next step is focused: connect Galleon to real financial infrastructure and work directly with publishers to help them earn from agent demand. The prototype uses test credits today. The goal is real settlement that supports the people producing the knowledge agents depend on. title: StudyTree
pitch: Play a learning game with an AI that can talk but can't cheat. A human and a voice agent alternate turns growing a knowledge tree, and the agent moves only through WebMCP tool calls.
about_excerpt: Play a learning game with an AI that can talk but can't cheat. A human and a voice agent alternate turns growing a knowledge tree, and the agent moves only through WebMCP tool calls. Like Comment Story Updates GamePlay chatgpt image gen inspiration Inspiration I'm a lifelong learner, and I've always loved the idea of studying new topics with tech. Over the last few years I've tried just about every way there is to learn with AI. The seed for this project goes back further than the challenge. Years ago I bought the domain studytree.ai (I'm a bit of a domain freak) and it's been rattling around in my head ever since. The original concept was a way to organize your ChatGPT history: a folder system with interconnected nodes so you could go back and actually study what you'd learned in conversation. The problem was keeping that data in sync, so I could never make it seamless. (err proprietary systems) So I pivoted toward a pure studying tool, but I never quite knew what it wanted to be. I even tried wiring in backend MCP servers to prototype it. It wasn't until WebMCP came out that I saw the real unlock: the agent could live inside the page and act through tools the page exposes, no backend required. That's what turned a vague study tool into a game you play with an AI. I mean I had experimented with somewhat of a complex node system here https://app.studytree.ai but I never was truly satisfied. What it does StudyTree is a turn-based learning game on a shared canvas. A human and an AI agent take turns building a knowledge tree around a single learning question. The human clicks and types. The agent can only change the board by calling registered tools. Voice is the agent's controller. Node types: 🌱 Root (the learning question) · 💡 Concept · 📚 Resource · ⚡ Skill · ❓ Gap Moves: Plant, Branch, Prune, Mark Gap, Mark Clear, and a human-only Undo of the agent's last move. Rules: 10 moves total, alternating turns. Win with 5+ nodes and zero gaps remaining when the moves run out. Lose if gaps are still open. The game works through two agent surfaces, and both go through the same six tools: WebMCP an in-browser agent (like ChatGPT's built-in browser) calls tools registered on document.modelContext . ElevenLabs voice an on-canvas voice panel connects to a public ElevenLabs agent that invokes the same moves as client tools. get_board is read-only and free; the other five are the legal moves. Tool arguments accept a node's label as well as its id, so a voice agent can say "branch from First Principles" instead of spelling out n3 . How I built it The build was almost entirely agent-driven, in stages: Voice dump. I started by talking the idea out loud with a Grok voice bot and let it spit the concept back to me. Cloud agent scaffold. That spec went into a Cursor Cloud agent, which spun up the first version. I pulled it down and tested it on a local port inside the Codex browser. Refinement. I brought in Claude Opus 5 to refine the architecture and tighten the tool layer. Redesign. When Claude 5.1 dropped yesterday, I had it re-evaluate the whole design. I pulled visual references from Cosmos for inspiration and had it pick apart the game mechanics. That's where it evolved from "a tree you build" into a real turn-based pairing between human and agent. Stack: Vite · React 19 · TypeScript · React Flow (canvas) · Zustand (state) Architecture: there is exactly one implementation of each move, in the Zustand store. Three entry points reach it: human buttons ──┐ WebMCP tools ──┼──→ applyMove() ──→ store action ──→ React re-render voice tools ──┘ Neither agent surface can touch the DOM or skip a rule, because both call the identical store actions the human's buttons call. Adding a move means adding it once in moves.ts , and both surfaces pick it up. WebMCP registration is feature-detected, so nothing breaks in browsers without it, and the ElevenLabs SDK is code-split so the board is interactive before the voice stack loads. Challenges I ran into Getting the agent to take its turn on its own. Right now the agent moves when you prompt it. I want true back-and-forth: I make a move, and the agent immediately responds without me nudging it. I don't think I've solved this yet. My current thinking is a polling or event loop that watches get_board and triggers the agent when the turn flips. Keeping the agent honest. The agent needed real agency without being able to cheat. Routing every move through the same applyMove dispatcher the human uses, and giving the human an undo, was how I solved that. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Two completely different agent surfaces (WebMCP and ElevenLabs voice) driving one shared rule set, with zero duplicated game logic. No API keys, no backend, fully static deploy. The whole thing runs in the browser. A concept I've been circling for years finally has a shape I can actually play. What I learned WebMCP is far more powerful than I expected. Exposing a handful of well-defined tools on the page is enough to turn a static app into something an agent can genuinely collaborate in. The Codex browser is going to change how people use the internet. Once the general public starts adopting agent-driven browsers, the interactions are going to get profound. Voice-first, agent-first workflows (talk the idea out, let cloud agents scaffold it, iterate with frontier models) are a real way to build now, not a gimmick. What's next for StudyTree Autonomous turn-taking. Finish the polling/event system so the agent moves the instant the human does. Real back-and-forth, no prompting. Fold it into StudyTree. Finished trees persist as study maps, resource nodes become live links, and the 10-move game becomes the on-ramp to a longer learning session. This is the studytree.ai vision I've been sitting on, finally with a front door. Classroom mode. Make this fun for younger students: a whole class builds one tree together with the agent as a co-player, taking turns to plant concepts, spot gaps, and fill them. The game format already has the ingredients (a shared board, clear turns, a win condition) to turn "what do we know about this topic?" into something kids actually want to play. Built With 11labs react react-flow vercel vite zustand Try it out study-tree-web-mcp-alpha.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I build end to end. Renewed a old idea with many Agents -> and fell in love with webmcp. Anders Kitson Like Share this project: Updates Anders Kitson started this project — Sep 03, 2026 03:58 PM EDT

title: PantryOS
pitch: AI powered kitchen manager using WebMCP to recommend food to use, find recipes, track ingredients, and build smarter grocery lists.
about_excerpt: AI powered kitchen manager using WebMCP to recommend food to use, find recipes, track ingredients, and build smarter grocery lists. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Dashboard and AI activity Saved recipe Kitchen inventory Recipe matching Grocery planning Inspiration I do a ton of home cooking and managing the food in the fridge, can be a real hassle from what Ingredients I have to if they are expired or not. Inventory, recipes, and grocery lists usually live in separate places, leaving me having to compare dates, quantities, and missing ingredients manually. PantryOS explores a different model: Where I already implement AI for planning meals and recipes and managing leftover ingredients it instead homogenizes the information so an agent can access all of it at once. What it does PantryOS tracks ingredients across the fridge, freezer, and pantry, including quantities and expiry dates. It prioritizes food that should be used soon, finds suitable recipes, scales serving quantities, converts units, and can add missing ingredients to the grocery list. Instead of navigating several screens or finding recipes or copying information down and adding it to boxes of text manually the AI agent can automate this for you navigate fill out grab info from and expedite all this busy work so you can get back to your daily life. Here's an example of a use case Find a recipe for four people that uses the ingredients going bad, then add anything else I need to my shopping list. PantryOS turns that request into actual management actions keeping the interface and stored kitchen state up to date as you work or cook. Why WebMCP PantryOS is not a chatbot taped together alongside an application to manage your kitchen. Its features are exposed using structured WebMCP tools. The agent can inspect inventory, evaluate expiry dates, save and retrieve recipes, update quantities, and plan groceries without you having to feed it information about your kitchen and the recipes you have every time. What you end up with is a superior user experience, people can talk to agent in everyday language while PantryOS handles the multi-step coordination between inventory, recipes, serving sizes, and groceries. This also allows for further and more complex syncing of your information later on, the easy of use of the MCP allows for later hosted version of this demo to enable access by your AI agent wherever you are on the go. Human-agent collaboration The agent can prep and perform useful kitchen actions, but the person remains in control. Destructive actions like deleting recipes or throwing out food require confirmation to make sure the Agent doesn't run haywire and delete your grandmother long lost recipe. The activity panel records recent agent assistance, making it clear what is happening and what changed. How we built it PantryOS is a client-only React and TypeScript application deployed using Cloudflare Workers Static Assets. Zustand persists inventory, recipes, and groceries in browser localStorage . Its WebMCP tools register through document.modelContext . Every tool input is validated with Zod and described using a matching closed JSON Schema. Tool callbacks read current application state when they execute and call the same domain actions used by the interface. Automated tests cover tool contracts, persistence, malformed inputs, quantity conversion, grocery deduplication, cancellation, stale state, and confirmation races. What we learned The best agent tools don't feel like a background script or an entirely separate app. They work best when they can work with what you already have and you can see clearly their application. WebMCP made this feel like a more native interaction that just a automations or AI agent that is just added to a kitchen management app. Its quick simple to use and setup easy to for the AI to work with and access the correct information and allows me to use my already exiting workflow and models to do my tasks. What's next Future versions could add opt-in household collaboration and import integrations. I would like to have it persist across different browsers so you can access the info on the go. Inspiration Every tool an agent can call on the web was written by a developer, months earlier, in a schema fixed before anyone knew which question would be asked. That is the ceiling on the agentic web, and it is not a performance ceiling: the number of things an agent can do on a page is capped by how much a product team could anticipate. The obvious way through it — let the model do whatever it likes on the page — gives up the one thing the page is for. The page is where the rules live: which field is an identifier, who may see it, what a write costs. Warrant is the other way through. The person who does the work mints the tool. The page keeps the veto. She is an HR operations coordinator. On the first of every month she opens the same payroll screen, sets one period and one overtime cut-off, and reads off the eighteen people over the line. Three years, and nobody ever shipped her a button for it. Ask an agent instead and the answer comes back as eighteen real names and two national identifiers, in a chat log that syncs to somebody else's laptop — the page had a policy about those fields and the answer left without it. So: she demonstrates the report once . The page turns it into a typed tool any agent can call — name, parameters, defaults, limits, none of which were in anybody's source code. And the page, not the model, decides what that tool may return. A field marked pii is not discouraged from appearing in a result; there is no code path that puts it there. Six months later somebody reclassifies a field and the tool takes itself off the surface, whether or not anyone remembers it exists. What it is, in one session Live at warrant-gray.vercel.app , in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , or ChatGPT's in-app browser. No account, no backend. The workbench. Eight controls, 1,680 rows , seven tools its author wrote. The surface on the right is read from document.modelContext.getTools() , not the page's own bookkeeping. An agent drives her screen. run_query sets the controls in front of her and the table follows. What stays rare is who decides the shape . All 116 were read one at a time, without knowing which row was this project: in the great majority a developer decides the shape in code or config, and the rest divide between a model writing it, an imported OpenAPI or marketplace document, and a shape compiled out of the page's own DOM. In 3 the person doing their own job decides it. That number was 1 in an earlier draft and it was wrong; a reader found Understudy , the selecting regex could not see it, and widening the net surfaced XACT FOUNDRY as well. Both are named, with the argument against our own claim, in webmcp-evaluator/authorship.md . How far it goes The tail this reaches cannot be shipped by hand, and here that is arithmetic rather than rhetoric. The eight controls on one workbench express 1,572,480 distinct questions — 13 × 7 × 4 × 4 × 6 × 6 × 6 × 5, every factor a dropdown you can count. A generic query tool reaches all of them, and this page ships one, so the gap is not expressiveness. It is that none of those questions is a named capability: nothing tells a model which one this team asks every month, that its period must follow the calendar rather than freeze on the month somebody demonstrated, what its threshold means, or which fields may never come back. Those are facts about one team's work, not about the data — which is exactly why the author cannot ship them and the person doing the work can. The mechanism is not about payroll. title: CROSSTALK
pitch: You see the bomb. Your agent has the manual, scanner, and tools. It can’t see or hear your screen. Neither of you can defuse it alone. The game is the conversation.
about_excerpt: You see the bomb. Your agent has the manual, scanner, and tools. It can’t see or hear your screen. Neither of you can defuse it alone. The game is the conversation. Like Comment Story Updates GIF demo mission 3 debrief You see the bomb. Your AI agent holds the manual—as WebMCP tools. Neither of you can defuse it alone. Inspiration Most AI experiences revolve around a chat box: the human asks, the agent answers, and one side usually has all the important context. We wanted to explore something more physical, cooperative, and playful. CROSSTALK began with a simple question: What if WebMCP was not merely an integration layer, but a core game mechanic? We drew inspiration from cooperative bomb-defusal games, escape rooms, radio communication, and the tension of working with someone who knows things you cannot see. In CROSSTALK, the human and AI agent are deliberately given different abilities. The human can see colors, symbols, gauges, displays, and flashing signals. The agent has the operating manual, machine-readable data, and control tools—but cannot perceive the device itself. Success comes from communication, not automation. What it does CROSSTALK is a cooperative browser game in which the second player is an AI agent. The human player is presented with a physical-looking device containing modules such as: A wire bay with colored wires A keypad covered in unfamiliar glyphs A regulator with an analog gauge An echo module with changing labels and displays A signal transmitter producing short and long beeps The AI agent receives a changing set of WebMCP tools. These let it consult the manual, scan machine-readable identifiers, inspect recorded history, adjust controls, and review completed sessions. However, the tools intentionally do not reveal information that only the human should perceive. The resulting loop is: Describe → Look up → Decide → Confirm → Act For example, the agent may know exactly how to decode a signal frequency but must ask the human what rhythm they hear or see. The human may know where the gauge needle is, while only the agent can operate the regulator. Neither participant has enough information or control to finish alone. CROSSTALK contains three escalating missions: HANDSHAKE introduces communication through the wire bay. CROSSED WIRES combines wires, glyphs, and regulator controls. SILENT FREQUENCY tests the full partnership with keypad, echo, signal, and wire modules. Every agent action is shown in the in-game TEAM RADIO , so the human can see what the agent inspected or changed. Mistakes cause strikes, while successful coordination produces a detailed debrief and training record. How we built it CROSSTALK is a client-side TypeScript application built with Vite and the WebMCP API. We treated the WebMCP tool schema as a sensory boundary . Each tool defines not only what the agent can do, but also what it is allowed to know. Tool descriptions explicitly explain missing sensory information and direct the agent to ask the human instead of guessing. The game currently exposes 11 imperative tools and one declarative form tool. These include manual lookups, device inspection, RFID scanning, regulator controls, echo-history retrieval, transmitter tuning, and post-mission review. The toolset changes dynamically throughout a mission. When a module becomes active, its relevant tools appear. When that module is solved, those tools are removed using scoped AbortController lifecycles and a toolchange event is emitted. Read-only sensors and irreversible actuators are also distinguished through tool annotations. To prevent puzzle logic and documentation from contradicting each other, the operating manual and the actual module behavior share the same underlying rule data. We built the interface as a physical workbench rather than a conventional web dashboard. Mission case files, taped instructions, a clipped briefing docket, radio receipts, paper textures, switches, lamps, and a ring-binder manual make the experience feel like handcrafted field equipment. Audio is synthesized with WebAudio, while the visual assets and textures are original, code-native work. Everything runs without accounts, analytics, or a game server. The local operator dossier records only relevant game events—not the player’s conversation—and remains on the device. Reliability is covered by Vitest and Playwright, including: 27 automated tests Deterministic zero-strike runs through all three missions Native WebMCP testing in Chromium Firefox and WebKit compatibility checks Accessibility and interaction checks Responsive layouts at desktop, mobile, and 320-pixel widths Reduced-motion, keyboard, and forced-color support Production deployment verification Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was creating information asymmetry that felt fair. If the agent received too much state, the human became unnecessary. If the agent received too little, the interaction became frustrating. We had to decide carefully which facts belonged to human perception, which belonged to machine-readable sensors, and which actions should require explicit confirmation. Dynamic tool registration created another challenge. Mission resets, completed modules, and stale browser sessions could otherwise leave the agent with tools that should no longer exist. We built lifecycle management around each tool and added tests for repeated missions and state transitions. We also spent significant time making the interface feel authored rather than generated. Early versions resembled a collection of polished panels, but not a believable game. Moving toward a cohesive physical workbench—with imperfections, paper layers, hardware controls, and mission-specific case files—gave CROSSTALK a much stronger identity. Human playtesting caught an especially useful issue in the final mission: the signal module’s beeps could be heard, but its visual feedback was too subtle to notice. Automated logic tests passed because the signal state was technically correct, yet the experience was still unclear. We redesigned it with a large synchronized VISUAL BEEP lamp and a reacting speaker grille, then added rendered-state regression coverage so the problem could not silently return. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud that the AI agent is not simply a hint system or chatbot attached to the side of the game. It is a genuine second player with unique knowledge and controls. Other accomplishments include: Making WebMCP itself part of the game design Creating puzzles that neither participant can solve independently Dynamically changing the agent’s capabilities as the device changes Keeping every agent action visible and understandable to the human Building evidence-bounded coaching without recording conversations Creating an original, tactile visual identity without external game assets Supporting desktop and small mobile layouts without sacrificing clarity Completing deterministic, zero-strike automated runs of every mission Shipping the complete experience as a private, static, client-side application Most importantly, CROSSTALK is fun to play. The tension does not come from pretending the AI is human. It comes from learning how to communicate effectively with an intelligence that perceives and controls a different part of the world. What we learned We learned that tool descriptions are part API documentation, part user interface, and part game design. A small ambiguity in a description can change how the agent behaves just as dramatically as changing the puzzle itself. We also learned that clear limitations make an agent feel more trustworthy. Explicitly telling the agent what it cannot see produces better cooperation than giving it vague access to everything. Dynamic capabilities are more understandable than one enormous permanent toolset. When tools appear only when relevant, the agent receives a clearer picture of the current situation and the player can more easily understand its role. Finally, automated correctness is not the same as playability. State-level tests told us that the signal light worked; a person playing the game told us that it could not actually be noticed. Combining deterministic testing with real human play sessions made the experience considerably stronger. What's next for CROSSTALK Next, we want to expand CROSSTALK with additional missions built around new asymmetric senses and controls: spatial descriptions, timed synchronization, memory, visual pattern comparison, and situations where the human and agent must negotiate uncertainty rather than search for one fixed answer. We would also like to add: More adaptive training drills based on previous mission evidence Optional difficulty and accessibility profiles Additional manual rule packs and randomized mission variants Richer local debriefs and replayable team-performance timelines New physical module designs and environmental storytelling Better support for comparing how different agents communicate and recover from

title: Once Upon
pitch: A living manuscript where every discovery changes what AI can do.
about_excerpt: A living manuscript where every discovery changes what AI can do. Like Comment Story Updates Notes (Clues) Inspector for Debugging Manuscript Inspiration Interactive fiction is most exciting when players can try anything, but its most memorable mysteries still depend on deliberate reveals and consequences. Players should not have to choose between a rigid action menu and an AI story that can improvise past the clues that make discovery matter. We wanted each discovery in the story to become a new capability for the agent. WebMCP made that relationship explicit and inspectable. What it does Once Upon is a living manuscript played through natural-language actions. Each player action becomes the next chapter on the page, while authored discoveries open new ways to interact with the story. The first release centers on one complete authored mystery, The Last Manuscript . It begins in a correction room with a handleless door. Finding a pencil, following a memory, and reading a hidden manuscript do more than change the prose: each discovery gives the agent a new WebMCP action through the page. There are no character sheets, dice, fixed choices, or turn limits. Why it matters Most websites present a fixed interface and leave agents to guess how to operate it. Purely generated stories have the opposite problem: they can respond to anything, but they struggle to protect a carefully timed mystery. Once Upon uses WebMCP to connect free-form play with authored causality. The human supplies intent and makes every meaningful choice. The agent turns those choices into a responsive narrative. The page protects secrets, commits consequences, and reveals new structured verbs when the story earns them. None of the three participants can create the complete experience alone. This turns agent capability into a visible narrative mechanic rather than a hidden automation layer. The result is an agent-native experience that would be difficult to build reliably through UI guessing, DOM scraping, or an unconstrained model prompt. How it works The running product does not call a hosted model or require a specific provider. It works with whichever WebMCP-capable agent is already accompanying the player, so there is no app-owned model API key or provider lock-in. Before every turn, the agent reads the page's structured story state. It then uses a currently allowed action and commits one to three short paragraphs back to the manuscript. The page types the chapter at reading speed, and the agent leaves the prose on the page instead of repeating it in chat. Three stable core tools coordinate the story. Story-object tools are registered only after authored prerequisites are satisfied, remain registered until used, and retire after their one-shot interaction. Using an object changes the page before the next chapter is written; that commit must reference the same effect and every fact it revealed. The page — not the model — owns session state, revision checks, authored discoveries, sealed facts, interaction rules, and completion order. Every mutation checks the active session and revision, while operation IDs make same-page retries idempotent. The agent remains free to improvise characters and consequences without inventing executable tools or revealing protected facts early. Gameplay state remains in the current page and is not uploaded during play. After finishing the story, the player may explicitly create an anonymous, unlisted, read-only manuscript link. Only that completed reader copy is stored as story content, and it expires after 30 days. How we built it Codex was the primary coding agent throughout the project. It helped inspect and refactor the repository, shape the WebMCP protocol, implement the narrative state machine and interface, turn runtime edge cases into validation rules, add regression tests, and prepare the deployment. Claude Code was also used as a supporting coding tool during development. Architecture Once Upon is a TypeScript application built with React 19 and Vinext, deployed on ChatGPT Sites through a Cloudflare Workers-compatible runtime. The in-memory story engine owns narrative state and validation; the WebMCP bridge derives the live tool surface from that state; and Cloudflare D1 stores only completed manuscripts that a player explicitly chooses to share. Testing No account, API key, or credentials are required. Playing requires ChatGPT's in-app browser with an agent attached, or Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Open the public demo in a supported browser with an agent attached. Ask: “Play The Last Manuscript with me through this page. I look around the room before answering the speaker.” Verify that the player's move appears on the sheet and that the committed chapter is typed at reading speed instead of repeated in chat. Continue choosing actions. When a story object becomes available, explicitly ask the agent to use it and verify that the page changes before the next chapter is written. Enable Settings → Tool inspector to inspect the active tools and the prerequisites, registration, invocation, and retirement lifecycle. Choose Start over or reload to confirm that a fresh manuscript begins at the prologue. Follow the Pencil → Memory → Last Manuscript progression. After completion, choose Create a link to open the anonymous, read-only manuscript reader; the link expires after 30 days. The repository passes strict TypeScript checks, linting, the Drizzle schema check, 90 unit tests, a production build, and 22 Playwright end-to-end tests. Challenges and accomplishments The hardest part was keeping free-form narration and authored causality in sync. The player can attempt anything, but an agent still has to recover cleanly from an interrupted turn, avoid revealing a secret early, and finish the exact page change caused by a story object. We turned stale sessions, duplicate operations, interrupted turns, premature discoveries, and early completion into explicit validation rules and regression tests. The finished experience keeps the player's action, the agent's prose, and the page's evolving capabilities synchronized and inspectable from the prologue through the final passage. What's next More stories can be added through the same declarative experience definitions. Next, we want manuscripts to persist across visits. We also plan to expand agent compatibility testing from the evaluation scenarios already documented in the repository. title: DataSweep Pro — agent-human data cleaning on WebMCP
pitch: An AI agent and a person clean the same spreadsheet through the same 15 WebMCP tools. Every change is previewed on real tables, approved by a human, attributed, and reversible.
about_excerpt: An AI agent and a person clean the same spreadsheet through the same 15 WebMCP tools. Every change is previewed on real tables, approved by a human, attributed, and reversible. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every "AI cleans your data" demo we'd seen had the same shape: a chat box, a spinner, and a table that changed. You never saw what the model was about to do, you couldn't check its arithmetic, and if it was wrong you started over. WebMCP changes what's possible there. If a page can publish real tools on document.modelContext , an agent doesn't need to guess at your UI — it calls the same functions your buttons call. That reframes the problem. The interesting question stops being "can a model clean a spreadsheet" and becomes "what has to be true before you'd let one write to your data?" Our answer: it has to show you what it measured, ask before it writes, record who did it, and let you undo it. So we built the execution environment for that, rather than another chat wrapper. What it does DataSweep Pro is a data cleaning studio where an agent and a person work on the same messy spreadsheet through the same 15 WebMCP tools . Load a CSV. Eight analyzers run concurrently and find what's actually wrong — mixed date formats, duplicates, currency strings that won't sum, whitespace that breaks joins, outliers, and rows the parser silently dropped. Each finding carries the measurement behind it and a suggested fix. An agent can do the same thing through the same tools. The load-bearing property: There is no separate "agent path" that could behave differently from the buttons. Everything runs locally. Your file is parsed and queried by DuckDB compiled to WebAssembly, in the tab. External communication — a model API, a desktop MCP client, a GitHub pull request — is opt-in and separately gated. How we built it Four layers, each testable without the one above it. Arrows point one way only: the domain layer knows nothing about tools, and the engine knows nothing about MCP. The WebMCP surface. 15 tools registered via @mcp-b/global . Each is one ToolDefinition — name, description, JSON Schema, annotations, execute — and that single object serves three consumers: WebMCP registration, the in-app Tool Inspector, and the agent loop. That's what guarantees the schema a reviewer inspects is the schema an agent is offered. Bridgeable to Claude Desktop with @mcp-b/webmcp-local-relay . The approval gate. A mutating tool called without a confirmation_token runs the transformation against scratch tables, measures exactly what changed, drops the scratch tables, and returns a token. Your data hasn't moved. The token is bound to a fingerprint of the exact arguments, single-use, and expiring — so an agent can't preview something harmless and reuse the token for something else. Enforced once in middleware, not per tool. A mutating tool declared without a preview() throws at construction rather than silently skipping the gate. Prompt injection. A spreadsheet cell is attacker-controlled text. Cell content leaves every tool inside a fence carrying a per-call random nonce, so injected text can't forge the closing tag and escape into the instruction region. Pattern detection also runs, but it's treated as advisory — the structural defence is what holds for payloads no rule matches. Testing. 380 tests. The integration and security-eval suites run real DuckDB-Wasm through its Node bindings, not a mock, because the interesting bugs live in the SQL. title: TALK FAST
pitch: Your blind spot has a voice. One human, one AI agent, one manual — through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Your blind spot has a voice. One human, one AI agent, one manual — through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates What it is TALK FAST is an asymmetric co-op arcade game for one human operator and one AI agent reader. The human sees a physical 3D console and presses every control. The agent agrees not to inspect the screen and instead holds the manual through WebMCP tools registered by the page. Neither can win alone: ten minutes, three strikes, five acts. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Most agent demos have the agent do the task for you. TALK FAST uses the WebMCP boundary as the wall between two players. Information asymmetry—the central game mechanic—runs through the API surface. The agent receives structured, typed access to only the information a reader should have: procedures, charts, codebooks, the clock, and the operator’s text channel. Each act registers its own scoped tools with an AbortSignal and removes them when it ends, so the agent’s live tool list becomes part of the game state. Honest caveat: the page cannot technically prevent an agent from looking at the screen. The tools make fair play the obvious typed path, and the client-captured interaction record makes the intended collaboration inspectable. How it creates a better experience Without WebMCP, the reader would have to scrape a DOM it is not supposed to see, while the operator would have to paste manual pages into chat. With WebMCP, the agent can call narrow tools, reason over the correct manual, ask for clarification, and place one decisive instruction on the operator’s teleprompter. Consequential actions stay visibly bounded. Every normal control press belongs to the human; the sealed override is marked consequential and requires confirmation; and one act gives the reader exactly one physical action of its own. Strikes are attributed to the reader or operator, making communication failures legible. The result is both a game and a compact practice arena for human-agent delegation: describe state precisely, ask useful questions, verify instructions, and keep consequential actions explicit. It is not presented as validated training; the mechanics simply make those collaboration habits immediate and measurable. What humans and agents can now do together TALK FAST creates a task neither participant can finish alone. The human has eyes and hands but no manual. The agent has the manual but no sanctioned access to the visual answer and almost no control over the console. Winning requires a fast, precise, two-way conversation. A completed run can be signed into a chronological public Operations Log. The server independently replays the input log against the same seeded engine before storing its score, while the replay page preserves the client-captured WebMCP interaction record. Reader identity and native-WebMCP status remain explicitly self-reported, so this is evidence of a collaboration rather than a model benchmark. How WebMCP is implemented The bridge in src/lib/webmcp.ts feature-detects document.modelContext , registers every tool natively with an AbortController per scope, and tracks registration promises and failures for an on-screen Evidence panel. It passes execute(input, { signal }) through so reader_wait_for_operator is genuinely cancellable, listens for tool lifecycle events, and dispatches the in-page console through the browser’s own getTools() / executeTool() path when available. Global tools cover briefing, status, manual search, teleprompter output, the operator channel, log signing, and replay history. Act-scoped tools cover glyph lookup, chart queries, and the reader’s timed key action. The same tool objects are mirrored into an explicitly labelled simulator so the game remains testable in browsers without native WebMCP; the UI never disguises that fallback as native execution. The application uses Next.js App Router, TypeScript, React, three.js / React Three Fiber, Drizzle ORM, and PostgreSQL. The 3D operations room responds to live tool traffic, strikes, time pressure, and act changes. Runs use server-issued sessions, one-time submission, deterministic replay, and server-computed scoring. title: PairAlgo.ai — WebMCP Algorithm & Interview Workspace
pitch: An AI-native algorithm practice space where browser agents pair-coach you via WebMCP—offering Socratic hints, instant Web Worker test execution, and deterministic spaced repetition.
about_excerpt:
An AI-native algorithm practice space where browser agents pair-coach you via WebMCP—offering Socratic hints, instant Web Worker test execution, and deterministic spaced repetition.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 PairAlgo.ai — WebMCP Algorithm & Interview Workspace 

 

 Inspiration 

 When practicing coding interview problems, asking an LLM for help usually fails in two ways: 

 
 Hallucination : The model claims broken code "looks correct" because it cannot actually execute the code or evaluate edge cases. 
 Solution Dumping : You ask for a subtle nudge, and it immediately dumps the full optimal solution, spoiling the problem. 
 

 Most browser AI agents attempt to interact with web apps by taking screenshots and scraping the DOM. This is slow, fragile, token-heavy, and lacks structured execution context. 

 With WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) , the web app exposes typed execution tools ( run_tests , get_hint , get_recommendation ) and pushes live state ( clientState ) directly to the agent. Code executes in an isolated in-browser Web Worker, giving the agent deterministic test results so it can act as a reliable, zero-hallucination pair programming coach. 

 

 What It Does 

 PairAlgo.ai is an in-browser algorithm workspace built for WebMCP. It allows browser agents (ChatGPT in-app browser, Chrome with WebMCP enabled) to inspect editor state, execute code deterministically, and provide progressive hints. 

 1. Ambient State Synchronization ( setClientState ) 

 The app continuously syncs session telemetry to the agent via document.modelContext.setClientState() (with navigator.tools fallback): 

 
 Active problem ID, difficulty, and target time 
 Test pass count (e.g., 3/5 passing ) 
 Hints revealed count (Levels 1–3) 
 Current interview readiness score and streak 
 

 The agent knows what the user is working on and whether tests pass without repetitive prompt questions. 

 2. Six Typed WebMCP Tools 

 The app registers 6 typed tools via standard document.modelContext.registerTool() and navigator.tools.register() : 

 
 get_recommendation : Returns the optimal next problem based on category skill gaps, interview frequency weights, and SM-2 review schedules. 
 start_problem : Loads the problem starter code into Monaco and resets the timer. 
 run_tests : Executes editor code in an isolated Web Worker sandbox and returns structured pass/fail JSON diffs, timing, and console logs. 
 get_hint : Returns 3 tiers of hints (Level 1: Intuition → Level 2: Data Structure → Level 3: Implementation Detail) so the agent guides without spoiling. 
 submit_solution : Validates the full test suite, logs the attempt in IndexedDB, and updates SM-2 repetition schedules. 
 get_skill_profile : Returns the user's readiness score, streak, and per-category breakdown. 
 

 3. Deterministic Scoring Engine 

 Readiness is calculated purely from IndexedDB attempt logs without AI guesswork:
 Readiness = 0.40 × PatternStrength + 0.25 × Retention + 0.20 × Speed + 0.15 × Independence 

 

 How It Works in Practice 

 
 Recommendation : The user asks what to study. The agent calls get_recommendation({ set: 'core-75' }) , which identifies an unpracticed high-weight category (e.g., Graphs) and returns course-schedule . 
 Context Setup : The agent calls start_problem({ problemId: 'course-schedule' }) , loading the starter code into Monaco. 
 Execution & Coaching : The user writes a BFS cycle detection solution and asks why it fails. The agent calls run_tests() , inspects the failing assertion, and calls get_hint({ level: 2 }) to guide the user on in-degrees without revealing the solution. 
 Submission : Once all tests pass, the agent calls submit_solution() , updating the user's progress and SM-2 review dates in IndexedDB. 
 

 

 How We Built It 

 
 Frontend & Editor : Vite, TypeScript, and @monaco-editor/loader with Ctrl+S / Cmd+S instant testing. 
 Web Worker Sandbox : Runs untrusted code inside an isolated Web Worker using new Function() with a 2,500ms timeout guard to prevent infinite loops. 
 Data Structure Serialization : Custom BFS serializers and deserializers ( arrayToList , listToArray , arrayToTree , treeToArray ) with cycle detection, allowing complex ListNode and TreeNode structures to pass seamlessly across worker boundaries. 
 Storage : IndexedDB (via idb ) for offline persistence of 150 challenges, attempt histories, notes, and SM-2 review intervals. 
 WebMCP Evals : Built an automated eval suite ( evals/webmcp-evals.json and tests/evals.test.ts ) to verify tool-calling accuracy across 6 core intents (100% pass rate across all 10 test suites). 
 Demo Mode : ?demo=true pre-populates IndexedDB with 52 completed problems, an 83% readiness score, and active practice history for rapid evaluation. 
 

 

 Challenges We Ran Into 

 
 Complex Data Structure Serialization Across Worker Boundaries :
Coding interview problems frequently involve linked lists ( ListNode ) and binary trees ( TreeNode ), which lose class prototypes and can cause circular reference crashes during standard postMessage transfers. We had to build custom BFS serializers ( arrayToTree , treeToArray , arrayToList , listToArray ) with cycle-detection guards so complex data structures could pass between Monaco, the Web Worker sandbox, and assertion runners cleanly. 
 Sandboxing Untrusted Code Without Freezing the Agent :
Allowing users to run arbitrary algorithm code in-browser creates a severe risk of infinite loops ( while (true) ) freezing the browser tab and hanging the agent. We designed an execution harness inside an isolated Web Worker with a hard 2,500ms timeout guard that forcibly terminates the worker and spins up a fresh instance if a solution times out. 
 Designing Anti-Spoiling Tool Contracts :
If a tool returns too little information, the LLM hallucinates why tests failed. If it returns too much, the model immediately writes the optimal code and ruins the practice session. We had to carefully architect tool schemas ( run_tests , get_hint ) to return granular assertion diffs (Expected vs. Actual) without implementation details, alongside strict 3-tiered hints, grounding the model so it can act as a Socratic coach rather than a solution dumper. 
 

 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Deterministic Sandbox : Actual in-browser code execution—zero hallucinated test passes. 
 Sub-10ms Feedback : Tests run locally with zero network round-trips. 
 150 Real Problems : Complete bank of 150 algorithm challenges across 18 patterns with verified test cases and 3-level hints. 
 100% Client-Side : No backend servers, zero database costs, works fully offline. 
 

 

 What's Next for PairAlgo.ai 

 
 Multi-Language Sandboxes : In-browser Python (Pyodide) and Go (WASM) execution. 
 Visual Traversal Debugger : Interactive step-through animation for graph/tree traversals wired to WebMCP inspection tools. 
 Timed Mock Interviews : Agent-conducted 45-minute timed sessions with follow-up complexity questions.

title: AI Boardroom
pitch: One browser AI. Six specialist perspectives. You decide.
about_excerpt: One browser AI. Six specialist perspectives. You decide. Like Comment Story Updates One COO and 6 Ai Assistant Agents Inspiration Founders often need to make consequential decisions with incomplete evidence, changing constraints and too many disconnected conversations. AI Boardroom puts a founder and a browser assistant in one shared decision room where specialist perspectives, evidence and trade-offs remain visible. What it does AI Boardroom gives one browser AI six specialist perspectives: Product, Evidence, Commercial, Operations, Technology and Chair. WebMCP lets the assistant read the live brief, request named roles, post evidence-linked contributions, respond when constraints change, and retrieve the exact decision record. The central interaction is deliberately human-controlled. A fictional launch budget changes from R20,000 to R8,000; the previous recommendation becomes stale, the assistant reads the new revision, and a new recommendation can be prepared without rewriting the earlier record. The founder reviews alternatives and reservations, then approves, rejects or requests revision in the visible page form. This is stateful collaboration rather than a detached chatbot transcript. The app does not run six independent AI workers or call a model API. One browser assistant adopts the roles and the human retains the final decision. How we built it The app is built with the OpenAI Sites React and TypeScript scaffold, Vinext and D1. Native document.modelContext.registerTool exposes seven WebMCP tools: start_session, get_boardroom_context, update_agenda, request_perspective, add_contribution, prepare_recommendation and get_decision_record. UI actions and WebMCP tools share the same API and persistence logic. Mutation inputs use expectedRevision for optimistic concurrency and operationId for safe retries. Evidence is stored with the relevant contribution and rendered as untrusted text. The visible review channel is a workflow boundary, not proof of human identity. Challenges The design challenge was making an AI council useful without pretending that six hidden agents or automatic consensus exist. We made the roles explicit, preserved disagreement, invalidated recommendations when the brief changed, and kept approval out of the WebMCP tool surface. A second challenge was handling uncertain browser or network outcomes without duplicating or overwriting decisions. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when the agent can operate on the same visible, stateful interface as the human. Structured tools make the collaboration legible, while revision checks, evidence snapshots and a human review stop make the limits legible too. What's next Production use would require stronger identity and access controls, consent design, privacy and retention rules, abuse and rate-limit controls, independent security review, and integrations governed by explicit human approval. Disclosure All briefs, budgets, evidence and decisions in this project are fictional. The app does not make purchases, send messages, or change external systems. Browser-generated council text is created at runtime and is not preseeded consensus.
