title: KineticFlow: AI Motion Design Studio
pitch: An agent native motion design workspace bridging visual timeline editing with WebMCP driven key-framing, SVG orchestration, and real-time animation.
about_excerpt: An agent native motion design workspace bridging visual timeline editing with WebMCP driven key-framing, SVG orchestration, and real-time animation. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Motion design tools are powerful, but even small animation changes often require repetitive timeline editing, precise layer targeting, and multiple export steps. Browser agents usually struggle with these tools because they must guess what the user selected and interact through fragile screen coordinates. I built KineticFlow to explore a better model: the designer points to what they mean, while the AI agent handles the structured motion work. WebMCP makes this possible by giving agents direct, typed access to the application’s canvas and timeline state. Live app: kinetic-flow.netlify.app Source code: github.com/SamyakJ05/KineticFlow Demo video: Watch on YouTube What it does KineticFlow is a browser-native vector motion design studio where humans and AI agents work on the same canvas. A designer can select a layer and ask an agent to: Inspect the complete scene and current human selection Add rectangles, circles, hearts, stars, and sparkles Refine a layer’s position, size, color, rotation, scale, or opacity Generate multi-track animation keyframes Apply easing curves and spring physics Load polished motion presets Play, pause, or seek the live preview Export the animation as CSS, animated SVG, or Lottie JSON Every operation appears in a live Tool Stream with its inputs, structured result, status, and execution time. Designers can continue editing manually, drag objects, adjust properties and keyframes, or undo an agent’s changes. When WebMCP is unavailable, an in-page co-pilot and manual tool tester use the same underlying handlers, making the complete experience accessible in standard browsers. How I built it KineticFlow is built with: React TypeScript Vite Zustand Tailwind CSS SVG Netlify The WebMCP integration registers seven imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool includes: A focused name and human-readable title A natural-language description A strict JSON Schema inputSchema Input validation Structured return values Cancellation-signal support Read-only annotations where appropriate The main architectural component is a shared Zustand editor store. The canvas, timeline, property controls, in-page co-pilot, and browser agent all read and update the same state. The getCanvasScene tool returns more than a scene snapshot. It also provides: The layer selected by the human The current playhead position Playback status Loop state This enables natural handoffs such as: Make this coral, add a spring pulse, and play it. The user does not need to find or provide an internal layer ID. A requestAnimationFrame loop drives the live preview, while a custom interpolation engine evaluates position, scale, rotation, opacity, width, and height tracks. The exporter compiles the shared scene into reusable CSS and HTML, standalone animated SVG, or Lottie JSON. The application is deployed on Netlify with SPA routing, security headers, asset caching, and an explicit tools=(self) permissions policy. Challenges I ran into WebMCP is an emerging specification, so one major challenge was keeping the implementation aligned with the latest API. Earlier experiments used navigator.modelContext and a parameters field, while the current specification uses document.modelContext and inputSchema . I migrated the primary implementation while retaining a compatibility path for earlier experimental builds. Another challenge was designing tools that were useful to an agent without removing control from the designer. Small atomic tools were precise, but agents also needed enough context to understand the user’s intent. Returning the current human selection alongside the scene created a much more natural collaboration model. I also had to ensure that tool responses reflected the updated state rather than a stale snapshot. Playback and animation handlers now read the store again after mutations before returning structured results. Finally, animation exports required translating the same internal motion model into three different formats while preserving timing, transforms, opacity, and layer geometry. Accomplishments that I’m proud of Built a complete motion-design product rather than only a technical proof of concept Implemented seven structured WebMCP tools Created a shared-context workflow between human selection and agent action Added multi-track keyframes, easing curves, and spring-motion interpolation Made agent operations visible through a real-time execution stream Produced CSS, animated SVG, and Lottie exports Added a fallback co-pilot and manual tester powered by the same handlers Created automated smoke tests that register and execute all seven tools Deployed the application publicly with WebMCP-compatible permissions What I learned I learned that agent-native applications work best when agents receive semantic actions and meaningful application state—not just access to buttons and screen coordinates. WebMCP is especially valuable for creative software because human intent is often communicated through selection. A designer clicking a layer is already providing useful context. Exposing that selection to the agent allows short, natural instructions to become precise structured operations. I also learned that tool descriptions, schemas, validation, and return values are part of the product experience. Well-designed tools make agents more reliable while making the system easier for humans to understand and trust. What’s next for KineticFlow: AI Motion Design Studio Planned improvements include: Agent-generated motion plans that designers can preview before applying Multi-layer selection and batch animation operations Natural-language editing of easing curves and spring parameters SVG import and advanced path manipulation Collaborative history with agent-versus-human change attribution Reusable brand and motion-style systems Additional production exports and framework integrations Declarative WebMCP support as the specification matures The long-term goal is to make KineticFlow a creative workspace where humans provide taste, direction, and final judgment while agents handle repetitive, structured animation work. pitch: A local-first WebMCP workspace where agents and people inspect, transform, validate, and clear one-off file work together.
about_excerpt: A local-first WebMCP workspace where agents and people inspect, transform, validate, and clear one-off file work together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration One-off file requests are often tiny: update a name in a brief, remove comments, create a PDF packet, and send it. For an agent, that can still mean selecting libraries, installing packages, writing glue code, and checking intermediate artifacts in the user's environment. What it does Agent File Workbench is a local-first browser workspace for documents, PDFs, data, text, images, presentations, and media. People drop files into one visible workspace; agents use typed WebMCP tools against the same files, versions, previews, and validation results. When the deliverable is downloaded, the task workspace can be cleared in one action. Why WebMCP WebMCP gives the agent a stable, typed file surface instead of forcing it to infer a UI or assemble a new task-specific toolchain. The workbench exposes eight tools: workspace_file, inspect_file, extract_content, patch_document, format_document, convert_file, validate_file, and render_preview. Format-specific operations are discovered from the file at hand, so an agent can move from inspection to an auditable result through a shared browser state. Human + agent workflow The demo follows a last-minute client packet request. The agent lists the workspace, inspects the brief, patches a scoped section, removes comments, converts the brief to PDF, appends an approval page, validates the two-page packet, and opens the preview. The user sees each version and the final validation in the same workspace. The finished PDF is kept; task files, versions, and history are then cleared. How we built it The application is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, IndexedDB, and browser-native file APIs. Its WebMCP registration connects the typed tool interface to the same workspace store used by the UI, keeping human and agent operations synchronized. Document adapters provide inspect, extraction, editing, conversion, validation, and preview paths for the supported formats. Challenges Keeping one typed contract useful across DOCX, PDF, spreadsheets, and media required clear boundaries between inspection, mutation, preview, and validation. We also had to surface compatibility limits honestly, especially for Word-specific layout and PDF text extraction. What we learned The strongest WebMCP experience treats a website as a reusable task runtime: the page provides the capabilities, the agent performs structured file work, and the person keeps a visible, verifiable result. about_excerpt: An agent-ready surplus-food rescue control room with explainable safety, role-scoped WebMCP, and human-approved handoffs. Like Comment Story Updates Completion view: four-stop route, 92 servings rescued, safety score, and verified handoff receipts. Proof view: the fresh-browser agent trace, role boundaries, and human dispatch checkpoint. Safety view: seven adversarial scenarios refused with evidence, safe alternatives, and no live-state mutation. FoodLoop FoodLoop is an agent-ready surplus-food rescue control room for moving good food before it expires. The problem Food rescue fails in the coordination gap. Donors know what is available, recipients know what they can safely use, and an operator must reconcile food category, dietary requirements, quantity, timing, vehicle capacity, pickup-before-delivery dependencies, and chain of custody. A generic chat box can suggest a match, but it should not silently dispatch a vehicle or claim a delivery happened. The solution FoodLoop gives browser agents a focused operations surface and gives the human operator one shared, inspectable control room. The agent can read current supply and community need, find compatible matches, reserve reviewable allocations, draft a dependency-safe route, independently audit timing and capacity, explain why a match won, model route delays, run sandboxed safety checks, request dispatch review, and stage delivery receipts. The operator must release the route and verify each final handoff. The guided Springfield simulation uses fictional data to demonstrate two compatible allocations, a four-stop route, 92 servings loaded, 100/100 safety, 22 minutes of minimum slack, a visible dispatch checkpoint, and two verified handoff receipts. Judge evidence The live app includes a dedicated proof surface: A 13-call fresh-browser walkthrough shows the Planner chain, independent Auditor checks, a forbidden Planner dispatch request, and a Dispatcher checkpoint. Seven adversarial safety cases refuse expired food, allergen mismatch, insufficient capacity, late delivery, duplicate handoff, malicious donor notes, and prompt-injected partner content. Each result shows refusal, evidence, a safe alternative, and sandbox-only state protection. Match counterfactuals show score components and the next-best safe alternative. Route counterfactuals show how a 15-minute departure delay changes deadline slack without mutating the plan. A role map makes capabilities explicit: Planner proposes, Auditor inspects, Dispatcher requests approval, Operator approves dispatch, and Recipient verifies the final handoff. The shared tool console, role trace, safety lab, decision queue, route map, impact ledger, and activity trail all reflect the same deterministic state. Published-data benchmark FoodLoop includes a reproducible adapter benchmark on the public FoodGo Test Dataset: 500 published food-rescue orders and 50 volunteer records from the U.S. Department of Transportation / Mobility21 at Carnegie Mellon University. Against a FIFO first-feasible baseline, the deadline-and-distance-aware adapter accepts 94 orders versus 91, reduces modeled route distance from 2,806.98 km to 2,277.92 km, and improves minimum modeled deadline slack from 4.0 to 40.1 minutes. It rejects 23,052 unsafe candidate plans before assignment. The coordination-time number is explicitly a scenario proxy, not a human study; the assumptions, source attribution, and reproduction command are in the public repository's benchmarks directory. Why WebMCP This is structured, stateful work shared between a person and an agent. Agents are good at scanning constraints and assembling a plan; operators are accountable for consequential actions and ambiguous real-world context. WebMCP makes that division legible in the product instead of hiding it behind an opaque assistant. app.js registers thirteen focused tools directly through document.modelContext.registerTool(...). The portable contracts are separated into tool-contracts.js, with bounded JSON Schemas, compact outputs, readOnlyHint on read operations, and untrustedContentHint for partner-entered content. The consequential path is: observe → propose allocation → draft route → audit route → request review → HUMAN APPROVES DISPATCH → stage receipt → HUMAN VERIFIES HANDOFF The agent never impersonates either human approval. How we used AI FoodLoop itself is deterministic and self-contained for the competition. It does not call a hidden model, require an API key, or fabricate a logistics integration. OpenAI Codex/GPT-5 supported implementation, test design, browser replay, and product iteration. The refreshed demo narration uses the creator's private VoiceBank recordings; raw recordings remain private and are excluded from the repository. Testing The repository includes deterministic tests for matching, reservations, routing, audits, adversarial safety, counterfactual reasoning, role capabilities, approval boundaries, handoff validation, metrics, WebMCP contract annotations, and the external-data benchmark. npm test passes 25 tests. npm run verify passes the 13 tool contracts, JavaScript syntax checks, required judge artifacts, the benchmark result, and the compact orientation-response budget. The public GitHub Pages build, the refreshed 2:42 video, and the public video page were independently checked. Links Live app: https://moscraciunxxx.github.io/foodloop-webmcp/ Open-source repository: https://github.com/moscraciunxxx/foodloop-webmcp/ Judge walkthrough: https://github.com/moscraciunxxx/foodloop-webmcp/blob/main/docs/JUDGE_WALKTHROUGH.md Benchmark source record: https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/56260 Demo video: https://youtu.be/07p1pvKEuHI The prototype is self-contained and uses fictional Springfield simulation data for the product demo. It does not send messages, move food, call a fulfillment service, or require API keys. Production integrations would add identity, authorization, durable storage, observability, consent, and partner-specific retention controls while preserving both human approval gates. title: A11yFix
pitch: A11yFix: A WebMCP QA tool that detects WCAG 2.2 barriers, proposes exact ARIA code fixes, and generates automated Playwright tests, always keeping the developer in control.
about_excerpt:
A11yFix: A WebMCP QA tool that detects WCAG 2.2 barriers, proposes exact ARIA code fixes, and generates automated Playwright tests, always keeping the developer in control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Years of advocating for strict WCAG compliance and building specialized testing wrappers revealed a persistent gap in the industry: static analysis tools catch syntax errors, but developers still struggle to implement complex WAI-ARIA patterns accurately. The WebMCP challenge sparked the idea for an active, contextual assistant. Rather than just flagging a missing focus trap or a target size failure, the goal was to build a system that understands the active DOM state and proposes exact, compliant remediations while keeping the developer firmly in control. 

 What it does 

 A11yFix is a Web QA Workbench that acts as an intelligent copilot for accessibility. It audits web pages in real-time against strict WCAG 2.2 Level AA and WAI-ARIA APG standards. When it detects a barrier (like an invalid heading order or insufficient target size), it uses a WebMCP agent to deeply analyze the semantic context. It then proposes specific, compliant code patches and automatically generates a Playwright regression test to verify the fix. Crucially, it operates with strict "human-in-the-loop" execution—no DOM mutation happens without developer approval. 

 How we built it 

 The architecture follows a Spec-Driven Development (SDD) approach. The client interface is a React-based QA Workbench deployed on Vercel that intercepts the active page state and isolates the accessibility tree. The backend is a Node.js WebMCP Server that exposes eight granular tools categorized by permissions (READ, PROPOSE, WRITE) using robust Zod schemas. This setup creates an automated QA loop: the agent audits, proposes patches, and invokes tools to generate automated Playwright regression tests, closing the development cycle seamlessly. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The primary hurdle was context window saturation. Raw DOM structures contain massive amounts of CSS and visual noise that easily confuse LLMs. To solve this, the application parses and purifies the tree before sending it to the model, stripping away everything except pure semantic accessibility data. This extreme DOM reduction was critical to prevent hallucinations and drastically reduce latency. 

 Additionally, we had to guarantee security. Establishing a strict "human-in-the-loop" barrier for the apply_remediation tool required meticulous state management, ensuring the WebMCP agent could never autonomously mutate the live page without explicit developer consent. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are incredibly proud of bridging the gap between theoretical accessibility guidelines and practical developer workflows. Successfully implementing a robust "human-in-the-loop" safeguard within the WebMCP framework ensures that the tool is both powerful and secure. Furthermore, automatically generating ready-to-use Playwright regression tests directly from an AI's remediation proposal transforms a traditionally tedious QA task into a fast, one-click experience. 

 What we learned 

 Integrating the Model Context Protocol within a live browser environment proved that agents are drastically more effective when constrained by strict schemas and pure semantic data. The development process reinforced that AI should not act as a black box that bypasses the developer, but rather as a high-precision instrument that amplifies their ability to ship inclusive, accessible software. 

 What's next for A11yFix 

 The next step is to integrate A11yFix directly into CI/CD pipelines and popular IDEs via a dedicated extension. We also plan to expand the test generation engine to support other frameworks like Vitest and Playwright, building upon our previous research in automated accessibility testing. Ultimately, we want to evolve A11yFix into the definitive open-source standard for autonomous, yet developer-guided, web accessibility remediation.

title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. title: Job Scout: WebMCP Career OS
pitch: A WebMCP-powered career OS for job discovery, fit scoring, resume tailoring, application capture, CRM, and interview tracking—with human approval before any submission.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered career OS for job discovery, fit scoring, resume tailoring, application capture, CRM, and interview tracking—with human approval before any submission.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Job searching is fragmented across job boards, spreadsheets, resumes, recruiter messages, application portals, and interview notes. I originally built Job Scout to solve that problem for myself: find relevant jobs, understand why they fit, and keep the entire application lifecycle in one place. 

 It evolved into something much bigger: a multi-user Career OS designed for both humans and AI agents. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, the goal is to make those workflows agent-accessible without giving an AI uncontrolled authority over a user's career. The system can help discover, analyze, organize, and prepare — but consequential actions such as submitting an application remain behind explicit human approval. 

 What it does 

 Job Scout: WebMCP Career OS brings the job-search lifecycle into one product: 

 
 Job discovery and searchable market browsing 
 Personalized job-fit scoring and explanations 
 Saved, dismissed, applied, and application-stage tracking 
 Resume building, versioning, ATS analysis, and job-specific tailoring 
 Cover-letter generation 
 Reusable application-answer generation 
 Application capture and career CRM workflows 
 Interview-management workflows 
 Anonymous demo access with isolated temporary state 
 Durable multi-user accounts and preserved career history 
 Agent-accessible workflows designed around WebMCP 
 Human confirmation before any application submission 
 

 The underlying philosophy is simple: AI should reduce the mechanical work of a job search without taking control away from the job seeker. 

 How we built it 

 Job Scout uses a split-plane architecture. 

 The job market is represented as an immutable, versioned snapshot rather than repeatedly loading the global job corpus into each user's database. Each user's mutable state — preferences, sessions, saved jobs, applications, resume evidence, and lifecycle history — stays in a much smaller PostgreSQL-backed state plane. 

 The backend is built primarily with Python and FastAPI , with PostgreSQL/asyncpg for durable state. The product includes server-side sessions, role and lifecycle separation, anonymous demo identities, telemetry, health receipts, rate limiting, and account-upgrade paths. 

 The browser experience is built as a responsive product UI with desktop and mobile acceptance testing. Automated tests cover backend contracts, database behavior, cross-user isolation, lifecycle safety, accessibility, keyboard behavior, reduced motion, and end-to-end browser flows. 

 WebMCP provides the bridge between the web application and agent-driven interaction: rather than depending on brittle visual automation, the product is being shaped around explicit, bounded capabilities that an AI agent can understand and invoke. 

 Challenges 

 One of the hardest problems was separating identity, authorization, and lifecycle correctly. 

 Anonymous users need to explore the product without creating an account, but if they later sign in, their saved jobs and application state should survive. At the same time, cleanup of expired demo accounts must never be capable of deleting an account that has become durable. 

 That led to explicit lifecycle classification, atomic demo-to-durable conversion, revocable sessions, race-condition testing, and a strict rule that user IDs are opaque identifiers rather than sources of authorization truth. 

 Another challenge was making agentic behavior useful without making it reckless. Job applications affect real people and real opportunities, so Job Scout intentionally stops short of autonomous submission. The agent can prepare the work; the human remains the final decision-maker. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest lesson was that agent-ready software benefits from the same things that make distributed systems reliable: explicit contracts, narrow capabilities, deterministic state transitions, provenance, and fail-closed boundaries. 

 WebMCP is especially interesting because it creates an opportunity to design web applications that are understandable to both people and agents instead of forcing agents to reverse-engineer interfaces intended only for humans. 

 What's next 

 The remaining work is focused on deeper WebMCP convergence, end-to-end acceptance, additional workflow polish, named-account authentication, and demonstrating the complete career journey: 

 discover → evaluate → save → tailor → prepare → track → interview 

 The end goal is a Career OS where an AI agent can do dramatically more of the busywork while the user keeps control of every consequential career decision.

title: Crown and Cipher
pitch: Infinite, procedural 3d mysteries in Unity 6 WebGL powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Infinite, procedural 3d mysteries in Unity 6 WebGL powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Starting & Game Controls Investigating the site More investigation Driving car to travel around the city A lot of locations Catching the killer Winning Panel Inspiration Every gamer dreams of dynamic worlds where NPCs aren't bound to static, scripted dialogue trees. Modern developers, however, rarely ship production titles powered by real-time LLMs due to a harsh economic reality: server-side inference costs scale linearly with player traffic , which can bankrupt an indie studio overnight. Furthermore, naive real-time agent architectures suffer from the polling trap in which agents repeatedly ping game state to check for changes, rapidly burning token budgets and hitting rate limits just asking "Has anything happened yet?" When the WebMCP specification launched, it presented a chance to flip this paradigm completely. By embedding agent tooling directly into the browser client, the player brings their own compute/agent. The developer only hosts static WebGL assets achieving zero marginal inference cost while empowering an autonomous agent to act as the game's dynamic Dungeon Master. What it does Crown and Cipher is a 3D open-world detective game set in a low-poly city, running natively in Unity 6 WebGL and driven by a WebMCP agent: Procedural Mystery Generation: Each playthrough procedurally selects a new killer, establishes three essential investigation leads, and generates an indirect knowledge network among city residents. Living NPC Roleplay: Suspects are not rigid chatbots; the agent temporarily possesses individual characters, adhering strictly to each NPC's bounded knowledge graph. Zero-Polling Event Loop: Through an asynchronous, promise-based wait tool, the game halts agent execution until the player speaks or interacts, eliminating token waste during exploration and driving. Dynamic Win Validation: The agent validates clues, enforces investigative requirements, and triggers the victory state once the player pieces together the full case. How we built it The project establishes a bidirectional bridge between Unity's native WebGL runtime and the browser's model context interface: Unity Controller ( WebMCPManager.cs ): Manages procedural case assignment, orchestrates the NPC knowledge matrix, dispatches dialogue events, and calls into native JavaScript functions via [DllImport("__Internal")] . Browser Bridge ( WebMCPBridge.jslib ): Registers five core tools ( get_system_context , speak , wait , get_npc_location , and show_winning_panel ) with navigator.modelContext / document.modelContext . When the agent triggers an action, the bridge routes data to Unity via window.unityInstance.SendMessage . The Suspended Promise Loop ( wait tool): Rather than continuously querying game state, the agent invokes wait after each action. The tool holds an open JavaScript Promise for up to $120\text{s}$. When the player submits text through Unity's dialogue UI, EnqueuePlayerMessage() fires from C# and resolves that specific Promise immediately with the interaction payload. Challenges we ran into Event Synchronization in WebGL: Coordinating an asynchronous browser LLM loop with Unity's single-threaded WebGL execution required strict queue management. If a player sends a message while the agent is still executing, messages are staged in an internal queue ( window.mcpMessageQueue ) to prevent dropped events. Controlling Hallucinations & Spoilers: An unrestrained LLM will immediately reveal the killer if pressed. We solved this mathematically by generating an indirect knowledge graph in Unity before the mystery starts, passing strict graph constraints into get_system_context to force NPCs to claim ignorance when asked about unlinked characters. Browser Sandbox Limitations: Embedded browser webviews (such as ChatGPT's in-app browser) often restrict Pointer Lock APIs, making first-person mouse look difficult to control. Documenting these constraints and optimizing for standard desktop browsers ensured smooth playability. Accomplishments that we're proud of Pioneering the wait Tool Architecture: Solving the token-waste problem in agentic gaming with an event-driven, suspended Promise pattern that keeps the agent responsive with minimal token usage. Zero-Cost Generative Gaming: Proving that studios can ship rich, LLM-orchestrated open worlds without maintaining costly GPU clusters. Seamless Unity ↔ WebMCP Integration: Creating a clean, reusable .jslib bridge pattern that other developers can adopt to connect WebGL games to browser models. What we learned Agents Should Wait, Not Poll: Shifting from polling loops to event-driven suspended promises fundamentally reduces latency and token consumption in web-based agent architectures. Client-Side MCP is a Game Changer: Decentralizing AI compute to the user's browser runtime unlocks interactive, generative entertainment models that were previously cost-prohibitive. Structured Tools Beat Pure Prompting: Grounding the story loop in explicit tools ( get_npc_location , speak , show_winning_panel ) provides the guardrails necessary to keep an open-ended narrative coherent. What's next for Crown and Cipher Multimodal Clue Analysis: Allowing agents to visually analyze screenshots of crime scenes and player positioning using vision models. Dynamic Audio & Voice Acting: Integrating local neural TTS models via WebGPU to dynamically voice NPC lines in real time rather than displaying text subtitles alone. Expanded Sandbox Mechanics: Introducing inventory systems, physical evidence gathering, and forensic mini-games exposed as modular WebMCP tools. title: Conspiracy
pitch: A shared mystery corkboard where people and AI agents connect, inspect, and audit evidence together.
about_excerpt: A shared mystery corkboard where people and AI agents connect, inspect, and audit evidence together. Like Comment Story Updates A shared board for human and agent reasoning Visual reasoning spaces work well for people and poorly for agents. A person can glance at a corkboard and understand a suspicious cluster, a directional relationship, or a provisional theory. A browser agent usually sees pixels, coordinates, and brittle labels. Moving the investigation into a chatbot would make it legible to the model, but discard the spatial interface that makes the reasoning useful to the person. Conspiracy gives the person and the agent one living evidence board. People can pin, edit, drag, search, group, connect, discard, restore, and audit clues through a tactile noir interface. Compatible browser agents discover 22 typed WebMCP tools that operate on the same cases, cards, directional strings, semantic regions, trash, viewport, and undo boundary. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP makes the visual workspace understandable as a semantic tool surface instead of a screenshot. Stable evidence IDs, typed directional relationships, strict schemas, provenance, and proposal status let an agent act on what the board means without guessing at screen coordinates. People and agents can now collaborate on the same visible artifact: the person contributes spatial judgment and context, while the agent contributes structured inspection, search, synthesis, and traceable proposals. Every resulting change appears in the interface the person already understands. The mystery is a playful demonstration of a broader pattern that can support research synthesis, incident review, threat modeling, debugging, reporting, and risk analysis. Human judgment remains authoritative Agent-created deductions are deliberately provisional. A proposed string records its direction, relationship type, rationale, confidence, and provenance, then appears visibly on the corkboard for review. The person can inspect why it was suggested, accept it, reject it, or undo it. The resident WIRE detective can inspect, search, audit, and trace the case, then stage a proposed string or semantic group. It cannot edit source evidence, delete clues, accept its own deductions, or manage cases. If hosted inference is unavailable, a deterministic detective keeps the core experience usable. Implementation The React interface and WebMCP tools cross the same WebMCPActions boundary into one canonical local CaseLibrary. Cards, directional threads, semantic regions, freehand strokes, trash, and viewport state are persisted per case in browser local storage. Agent deductions always enter the model as proposed objects. src/webmcp/registerTools.ts defines the shared 22-tool catalog. A stable delegating action facade keeps registered browser tool handles current while React refreshes its handlers. Strict enums, stable IDs, coordinate bounds, color validation, additionalProperties: false, destructive annotations, and untrusted-content hints constrain the surface. WIRE executes seven allowlisted read/proposal operations through that catalog. Its same-origin server route adds request and output caps, rate limiting, timeouts, structured validation, store: false, and pseudonymous safety identifiers. Local attachment bytes, machine paths, and object URLs never enter model requests, exports, or WebMCP results. AI and Codex Codex was the primary build collaborator across implementation, debugging, regression tests, deployment hardening, QA, documentation, and demo editing. Agent-driven QA exposed stale tool handles, overlapping asynchronous registration, duplicate proposals, model prose getting ahead of successful tool calls, deployment-secret formatting, and mobile scrolling problems. Each issue was isolated, fixed, and preserved as a test or QA procedure. Conspiracy also uses the OpenAI Responses API for WIRE. Claude- and Qwen-shaped tool sequences generated from a sanitized public contract were replayed through the registered execution layer to test schema clarity and multi-step flows; these were contract replays, not claims of direct browser integration. The project produced significant learning. I have already begun applying WebMCP patterns to Android Hell and my Drabzin CAD editor, turning the experimental browser API into a professional skill I can bring to future products. Try it Open the live app and choose Open a Case . Confirm WEBMCP BRIDGE LIVE and open the 22-tool workbench. Inspect or search the board, then ask WIRE to propose a useful connection. Review its rationale and use Accept , Reject , or Undo . No account or credentials are required. The sample case and deterministic fallback provide the fastest judge path. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. title: EZI ChemLab
pitch: A 3D chemistry and physics lab where an AI agent runs the experiment. Through WebMCP it mixes reagents, switches modes and writes the lab report, for schools without a safe lab.
about_excerpt: A 3D chemistry and physics lab where an AI agent runs the experiment. Through WebMCP it mixes reagents, switches modes and writes the lab report, for schools without a safe lab. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Many schools in Indonesia teach chemistry without a laboratory that is safe or complete enough for students to run experiments themselves. Teachers describe reactions on a whiteboard, and students memorise colour changes they have never actually seen. The missing piece is not information. It is the instructor standing beside you who pours the reagent, points at the bubbles as they form, and stops you before you make an unsafe combination. We wanted to find out whether an AI agent could take that role, and WebMCP is the first thing that makes it possible. A chatbot can describe a reaction. With WebMCP, it can run one. What it does EZI ChemLab is a 3D chemistry and physics lab that an AI agent drives from inside the browser. The student talks to the agent, and the agent operates the bench. There are three practical modes, mapped to Phases D, E and F of the Indonesian national science curriculum: Acids and bases , with indicator colour change and gas evolution Electrolyte and non-electrolyte solutions , tested with a conductivity lamp Density and buoyancy , the classic egg in fresh water against salt water The agent can switch topics, mix substances, read the current state of the bench, explain each stage, raise an educational safety warning, reset the experiment, and write up the observation report at the end. Reagents are not teleported into the beaker. Each one is measured out into its own graduated cylinder first, or lifted on a spatula if it is a powder, and only then poured in one at a time. The amount_ml the agent asked for is something you can read off the glass rather than take on trust. How we built it Seven tools are registered client side through the browser model context API: switch_experiment_mode , mix_substances , get_lab_state , explain_reaction_step , trigger_safety_alert , reset_experiment and render_lab_report . The frontend is Next.js with React Three Fiber. Every object on the page is built from geometric primitives in code, with no third party assets: the glassware is turned on a lathe from a profile the way real glassware is, and the floor tiles and the room the glass reflects are drawn to a canvas at runtime. Bubbles are capped at 110 instances so the simulation runs on the standard school laptops we are aiming at. The backend is Rust with axum, acting as a proxy so that no API key ever reaches the client. One decision shaped everything else: reaction outcomes come from a static lookup table, never from a language model. The visual result of a reaction is a scientific fact, and a hallucinated colour change would teach a student something false. The model writes prose. The table decides the chemistry. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP specification moved the API from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext in July 2026, and browsers in the field are still split across both locations. Every registration goes through a resolver that checks both, because a page that registers nothing looks exactly like a page that was never built. Refracting glass nearly cost us the experiment. The renderer builds the buffer that transmissive glass reads from opaque objects only, so anything marked transparent inside a beaker is not merely faint, it is absent: the liquid, the bubbles and the electrodes all disappeared behind the very glass that was meant to show them. Worse, our whole browser test suite stayed green while the beaker was empty on screen, because every check ran at 900 pixels and refraction only switches on from 1024 up. We now have a check that runs wide, hides the interface panels so that a text update cannot stand in for a reaction, and insists the contents are actually visible. We also had to design for a judging period that runs for weeks. An API quota running out in mid September would leave the lab looking broken, so step explanations are generated once, reviewed for scientific accuracy, and served as static content. Only the lab report, which depends on what the student actually did, calls a model at run time, and the backend accepts several numbered providers and moves to the next one when a call fails. That is not a claim on paper: in production the first provider currently fails on every request and the second answers, and the report still arrives. Every remaining failure path returns vetted static text with a 200 response rather than an error. Accomplishments that we're proud of Every execute handler returns a structured result containing the visual state, the temperature change and a plain language observation, so the agent narrates what actually happened instead of guessing. Unknown reagent pairs return a structured error listing the valid pairs, which lets the agent correct itself without the student ever noticing. We also built the lab so that it stays usable when WebMCP is not available. A status badge reports what the browser supports, a manual panel calls the exact same handlers rather than mock versions, and the topic buttons in the header run switch_experiment_mode the same way an agent does. The tool layer is genuinely separate from the interface. What we learned Reading matters as much as writing. get_lab_state returns the same view of the bench that the interface shows, so the agent can check what is actually there before it acts rather than assuming its last call succeeded. Together with the structured errors, it is what keeps a long conversation from drifting away from the simulation. We also learned that visible tool call indicators are not decoration. Every call is written to an activity console with the tool name, the outcome, and whether it came from an agent or was run by hand. Watching that line appear at the exact moment the liquid changes colour is what makes the whole thing legible, both to a student and to anyone evaluating it. What's next for EZI ChemLab Reaction rate is the next topic, and it is the one that rewards an agent most. It has four variables to manipulate and two beakers to compare, so the agent stops triggering effects and starts designing an experiment. Thermochemistry follows closely behind, since temperature data already flows through mix_substances . Beyond that: teacher accounts with printable worksheets, offline packaging for schools with limited connectivity, and coverage extending into Phase F electrochemistry. I designed the product and made the calls on how the lab should behave: measuring each reagent before mixing so the amounts are visible, building the room and glassware as 3D geometry rather than using imported assets, and keeping reaction outcomes in a static table so the science cannot be hallucinated. I set up the infrastructure, VPS, domains, Dokploy, and the provider chain behind the lab report, and I tested the whole session in the ChatGPT desktop app. The implementation was written with AI coding agents working to those decisions, and I reviewed and tested what it produced. title: Data Canvas
pitch: A local-first visual analytics workspace where humans and WebMCP-connected AI agents explore shared data and make visible changes in the same live canvas.
about_excerpt: A local-first visual analytics workspace where humans and WebMCP-connected AI agents explore shared data and make visible changes in the same live canvas. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Demo with Bar Chart Demo with Donut Chart Demo with Matrices and Line Chart Inspiration I started Data Canvas with a simple question: what would an analytics app look like if an AI agent worked inside the workspace instead of through a separate chat, API, or UI automation layer? I wanted one thing to stay true throughout the project. If an agent creates a chart, I should see it and keep working with it. If I change a filter, the agent should see that change on its next action. We should not end up with two versions of the analysis. That idea became Data Canvas. What it does Data Canvas is a local-first visual analytics workspace for exploring data in the browser. You can import CSV, TSV, JSON, and NDJSON files, inspect the data, build charts, filter and transform it, create metrics, connect datasets, make selections, add annotations, and undo or redo changes. A WebMCP-connected AI agent works with the same workspace. It can inspect a dataset, analyze it, create or update a visualization, apply filters, highlight data, define metrics, add annotations, and more. Its changes appear directly on the canvas, alongside the work done through the UI. The data and analytical engine run in the browser with DuckDB-Wasm. Data Canvas has no application backend, cloud database, authentication service, or built-in LLM. How I built it The most important architectural decision was to give the UI and WebMCP the same path into the application. Both go through one action dispatcher. A chart created through WebMCP is a normal Data Canvas visualization. A filter created by an agent is the same filter the UI understands. Undo and redo work across actions from either side. DuckDB-Wasm owns the imported rows and runs the analytical queries. Zustand holds workspace state and history. React renders the interface, and ECharts renders the visualizations. The WebMCP layer currently defines 19 semantic tools around real Data Canvas operations. Agents can ask the application to analyze data, create a visualization, apply a filter, define a metric, or connect datasets. They cannot submit arbitrary SQL, JavaScript, DOM selectors, or ECharts configuration. Challenges I ran into The hard part was not registering WebMCP tools. It was making sure I did not build the application twice, once for humans and again for agents. That affected a lot of small decisions. Agent writes carry the workspace revision they observed, so an outdated action cannot overwrite newer human work. Human and agent actions also use the same domain rules instead of maintaining separate implementations. Data access needed the same care. Dumping an entire dataset into every agent call would defeat much of the point of a local-first analytics app. The tools instead expose schemas, statistics, aggregates, bounded previews, and the data needed for a particular analysis. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud of the human-agent equivalence in the application. The codebase tests equivalent operations through the human and WebMCP paths and checks that they produce the same workspace state. Agent-created objects remain normal workspace objects, stale writes are rejected, and undo can reverse changes made by either side. I also like that none of this required adding an AI backend to Data Canvas. The application remains a browser-native analytics tool on its own. WebMCP gives an external agent a structured way to participate in it. What I learned I originally thought a capable agent would need very powerful tools. Building Data Canvas pushed me in the opposite direction. The useful tools turned out to be the ones that match operations the application already understands. create_visualization , apply_filter , or create_metric give the agent enough control to do real work while keeping the result valid, visible, and editable in Data Canvas. For me, that is the interesting part of WebMCP. The agent does not need to learn how to click through the interface when the application can expose what those controls actually mean. What's next for Data Canvas The biggest missing piece is local persistence. The current workspace lives in memory, so a reload starts a new session. Next, I want to persist complete workspaces locally and make them portable between browsers while keeping Data Canvas backend-free. I also want to extend the agent evaluations to longer workflows where a human and an agent repeatedly hand the analysis back and forth. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. pitch: The first marketplace where negotiation is a native web capability. Humans set goals. Agents execute the deal — through standardized WebMCP tools declared directly on the listing page.
about_excerpt:
The first marketplace where negotiation is a native web capability. Humans set goals. Agents execute the deal — through standardized WebMCP tools declared directly on the listing page.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every "AI marketplace" I've seen is just an existing store with a chatbot bolted on. The agent still scrapes DOM elements, blindly clicks buttons, and breaks on every UI update. I kept asking: what would a marketplace look like if AI agents were the primary client from day one? 

 The answer was AgentMarket — and the Chrome WebMCP standard made it finally possible to build it properly. 

 What it does 

 AgentMarket is a peer-to-peer marketplace where the entire negotiation protocol is declared natively on the webpage via navigator.modelContext.registerTool() . Two independent AI agents — a buyer and a seller, in separate browser tabs — can discover listings, initiate offers, counter, accept, and schedule pickup entirely through structured WebMCP tool calls. No scraping. No hidden API. No blind button clicking. 

 The 8 registered protocol tools include: 

 
 search_listings(query, maxPrice, category) 
 get_listing_details(listingId) 
 make_offer(listingId, amount, message) 
 counter_offer(negotiationId, amount, message) 
 accept_offer(negotiationId) 
 reject_offer(negotiationId, reason) 
 propose_pickup(negotiationId, location, time) 
 get_negotiation_history(negotiationId) 
 

 Tools are dynamically gated by role and turn — a buyer cannot accept_offer on their own offer; the tool surface itself enforces business logic. 

 How I built it 

 Built on Next.js 16 with a serverless in-memory store backing the negotiation state. The WebMCP tool registration lives in lib/webmcp-tools.ts , loaded on both the marketplace feed and individual listing pages. Cross-tab negotiation state is synchronized via BroadcastChannel + 1.5s polling — when one agent takes an action, the opposing tab's UI reflects it within seconds without any WebSocket infrastructure. 

 A built-in WebMCP Protocol Inspector drawer lets judges see every tool call, its arguments, and its result in real time as the negotiation unfolds. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 
 Turn-based enforcement at the tool registration layer was non-trivial. Dynamically re-registering tools on each state change (to gate accept_offer by whose turn it is) required careful AbortController management to avoid stale tool references. 
 Cross-tab state sync without WebSockets — I had to combine BroadcastChannel (for instant same-origin signals) with polling as a fallback to handle cases where tabs open in different contexts. 
 Role isolation — the buyer and seller tool surfaces needed to be distinct subsets without two separate codebases. The exposedTo scoping in the WebMCP spec guided the security boundary design. 
 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 The thing I'm most proud of is the "impossible before" story actually being true . Before WebMCP, an AI agent on a marketplace had two bad options: find a private API (rare) or scrape HTML (fragile). AgentMarket makes the negotiation protocol a first-class, machine-readable capability of the webpage itself — the same way <form> made submitting data a first-class web primitive in 1993. 

 The live two-agent negotiation demo — two tabs, two roles, watch them go from listing to closed deal in under 90 seconds — is something that genuinely did not exist before this standard. 

 What I learned 

 
 The WebMCP registerTool surface is deceptively powerful as a business logic boundary , not just an AI interface layer. 
 Serverless stateful apps are perfectly viable for hackathon-scale demos when the state model is simple and the sync strategy is explicit. 
 Writing for agents first and humans second produces a dramatically cleaner API surface — it forces you to make implicit business rules explicit and machine-verifiable. 
 

 What's next for AgentMarket 

 
 Persistent storage (Redis / Vercel KV) to survive cold starts and support real multi-user sessions. 
 Cross-origin tool scoping — enabling embedded listing widgets on third-party sites that still invoke AgentMarket's negotiation tools via exposedTo whitelisting. 
 Autonomous agent integration — wiring up an actual LLM agent loop so buyers/sellers can set a budget goal and let the agent negotiate on autopilot while the human watches the audit log. 
 Reputation & escrow tools — extending the protocol with rate_transaction and initiate_escrow tools, making trust and payment first-class WebMCP capabilities too.

title: SharableWorlds
pitch: An agent that builds with you, not for you.
about_excerpt: An agent that builds with you, not for you. Like 1 Comment Story Updates SharableWorlds A 3D miniature studio in the browser, where you and an agent build on the same canvas. What inspired me I was tired of the usual AI 3D demo: you type a prompt, a pile of objects appears, and you’re left wondering if it actually understood what you asked for. There’s no real way to work with the scene. You just watch it happen. WebMCP clicked for me because the page can be what the agent uses, not some API off to the side. Tools live on the site. A person can still be there, placing pieces, locking lots, arguing with the result. I wanted that to feel what we were accustomed to. A grid. A bunch of assets. You say "a harbor," or you drop a boat yourself, and the agent has to work in that same language. How I built it Everything runs in the browser. Next.js as a static export, React, Three.js for the isometric view, Zustand for the world. It deploys on a Cloudflare Worker. No login. Nothing on a server that "is" the scene. When the page loads it registers tools on document.modelContext . If something changes the world, it goes through one of those tools. Surprise Me button, share, the kit assets, and a connected agent all hit the same functions. Three.js only reads the state, the agent never talks to the renderer. I made the agent go through and follow a sequence instead of dumping pieces: get_occupancy → plan_scene → compose_scene → populate_zones → create_environment → inspect → validate_scene → repair_scene It thinks in lots ( C4 ), zones ( picnic ), and things like "east of the grill." validate_scene scores the result on six dimensions. Done means the score is high enough, not that a bunch of calls returned in an ok state. The assets are Kenney , CC0. Roughly 1,800 pieces in 22 packs. What I learned An agent can call place_piece 47 times and still not build a picnic. I had been treating a successful tool call as progress. It is not. I ended up scoring the scene and handing back repairs, otherwise it would stop early and look finished. Coordinates were a dead end. "Put this in the picnic zone, facing the grill" is something a model can actually use. (12.4, 0, -3.1) is not. If the agent can knock over what you just placed, you are not collaborating. That is why locks on human placed pieces and "build on this" matter as much as the fancy compose step. WebMCP being the only write path was annoying at first and then useful. I also needed to see what it was doing. The Details panel, the trace, the percentage all dove into what was happening behind the scenes. Otherwise it still feels like a black box, just a prettier one. Challenges I faced The first version technically used WebMCP and still sprayed pieces. My own runner was looping place_piece so the cursor had something to do. The model got a paragraph of instructions instead of a real sequence. Validation was so loose a picnic with no table could score 100. So I split it up. plan_scene does not mutate anything. Layout and objects are compose_scene and populate_zones . Twenty rules, each with a { tool, args, why } if it fails. repair_scene runs those. build_scene is the whole loop for hosts that will not steer. extend_scene is there because "add a harbor" should not delete the village. Then the small stuff started breaking the feeling of it. The cursor spawned under the kit and jumped when the camera moved. An empty board still looked like leftover scenery. You could not rotate the view. Share links replay a seed, which I wanted, until a leftover test URL made it look like a default world had kept rendering. Most of those bugs were the same issue: the person and the agent are looking at one stage. If that stage is lying, the whole thing falls apart. Getting registerTool working was the easy part. The work was making the tools a language two sides can share, and knowing when the harbor is actually a harbor.
