title: Bridge to Agentia
pitch: Bridging the Web and AI Agents through Native Tools, APIs, UI
about_excerpt: Bridging the Web and AI Agents through Native Tools, APIs, UI Like Comment Story Updates arch1 Native-WebMCP-without-auth-tool-expose Native-Webmcp-login-tool-expose-emptycart API-Adapter-without-login-expose API-Adapter-login-expose UIAutomation-Adapter-login-tool-expose UIAutomation-Adapter-without-auth-tool-expose Bridge to Agentia — Project Overview & Narrative Inspiration The web was built primarily for humans: we view a page, interpret its visual layout, click buttons, fill forms, and complete workflows. AI agents, however, require something fundamentally different—they need discoverable, structured, and actionable capabilities . WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) provides a compelling foundation for solving this problem by allowing web applications to expose their capabilities directly as machine-readable tools that AI agents can discover and execute within the browser security boundary. This prompted an essential architectural question: What happens when a website does not natively support WebMCP? That question inspired Bridge to Agentia . What I Built Bridge to Agentia explores three complementary architectural paradigms for bridging AI agents with web applications: Native WebMCP — The web application directly exposes its capabilities as schema-validated WebMCP tools registered in the browser context via document.modelContext . API Adapter — An external proxy adapter translates an existing website REST API into agent-accessible WebMCP tools via a serverless edge worker (Cloudflare Worker). UI / Automation Adapter — An external adapter translates agent intent directly into DOM interactions and automation steps over the existing user interface. The objective is not to replace existing web applications, but to construct a robust, unified bridge between agent intent and underlying web capabilities . For example, the same user prompt: “Find an indigo denim jacket under $150 and add it to my bag.” can be executed through any of the three underlying integration mechanisms: AI Agent Intent │ ├── Native WebMCP ─────────► In-Browser Tool Registry (34 Tools) │ ├── API Adapter ───────────► Serverless Edge Proxy ──► Storefront API │ └── UI Adapter ────────────► Headless Automation ─────► Storefront DOM To demonstrate this in practice, we built an in-website AI Stylist featuring both text and voice interaction , allowing shoppers to converse naturally while the agent discovers and orchestrates available WebMCP tools in real time. Human Shopper │ ├── Natural Language Chat ───┐ │ │ └── Real-Time Voice Mic ─────┤ ▼ AI Agent ▼ WebMCP Tool Registry ▼ Storefront Capabilities This architecture enables consistent, semantic agent interactions regardless of the underlying execution layer. How I Built It Bridge to Agentia is architected around a declarative, tool-based interaction lifecycle: Discovery : The agent inspects available tools for the current session state via document.modelContext.getTools() . Schema Comprehension : The agent parses typed JSON Schemas defining required fields, types, enums, and numerical constraints. Intent Resolution & Selection : The LLM resolves user requests into appropriate tool calls and structured arguments. Security & Privacy Gating : Inputs are checked for prompt injection patterns; sensitive operations require user confirmation; credentials never enter model context. Execution & State Mutation : The tool executes against the same-origin API, updates application state, and dispatches UI synchronization events. Result Sanitization & Synthesis : Tool results are scrubbed of PII before return to the model for conversational summarization. User │ (Chat / Voice) ▼ AI Agent Controller │ ├── 1. Sanitize Prompt & Check Delimiters ([USER_MESSAGE]) ├── 2. Discover Available Tools (State-Gated) ├── 3. Resolve Tool & Parameters (Gemini Function Calling) ├── 4. Request User Confirmation (if Destructive / Transactional) ▼ WebMCP Registry Execution │ ├── Validate Input Schema (Types, Enums, Integer Bounds) ├── Invoke Same-Origin Commerce API ├── Update Application State (Auth / Cart / Wishlist) ▼ Response Sanitization & Privacy Boundary │ ├── Scrub PII (Mask Emails, Redact Street Addresses & Phones) ├── Neutralize Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool Payloads ├── Record Execution to Append-Only Audit Log (/api/audit) ▼ Conversational Natural-Language / Voice Audio Response State-Aware Capability Exposure Tool availability dynamically reflects session state: Guest (Logged Out) : 18 public tools active (catalog search, fashion filters, size guides, comparison matrices, shipping rates, auth status). Authenticated, Cart Empty : 33 tools active (cart operations, wishlist management, address updates, order history). Checkout is gated ( 33/34 ). Authenticated, Cart Populated : All 34 tools active, unlocking create_order ( 34/34 ). End-to-End Security & Privacy Guardrails To prevent data exfiltration and credential theft: Auth Isolation : login and register tools are omitted from LLM tool declarations; authentication occurs strictly through browser UI. PII Scrubbing : Contact numbers and home addresses are replaced with semantic tokens (e.g., [Saved Address #1] ), and emails are recursively masked. Prompt Injection Defense : Inputs and tool payloads are wrapped in boundary markers, with automated detection for instruction overrides, role spoofing, and delimiter escapes. Human-in-the-Loop Confirmation : Destructive tools ( create_order , cancel_order , clear_cart , logout , update_shipping_address , remove_from_cart ) pause execution for explicit user confirmation. Persistent Audit Trail : Execution durations, parameters, and threat signatures are logged in memory and flushed to server-side append-only JSONL files. What I Learned Building Bridge to Agentia demonstrated that making a web application agent-accessible requires far more than exposing raw endpoints. Key learnings include: Separation of Interface and Implementation : The semantic tool interface presented to an agent can remain identical whether backed by native browser APIs, edge API adapters, or DOM automation. Designing for LLM Tool Consumption : Writing descriptive tool documentation, strict parameter schemas, and clear error contracts directly dictates model planning accuracy. State-Aware Tool Gating : Dynamically updating available tools based on session state dramatically reduces model hallucinations and invalid function calls. Failure Modes and Resilient Error Contracts : Tools must return structured, machine-actionable error payloads ( code , retryable , userActionRequired ) so agents can self-correct when encounters occur (out of stock, invalid coupons, unauthenticated states). The Necessity of LLM Security Boundaries : Unchecked agent access risks prompt injection and privacy violations. Defensive prompt guards, PII scrubbers, and confirmation gates are essential for trustworthy agentic commerce. Challenges Bridging the Paradigm Gap : Native WebMCP provides optimal latency and security, but requires website-level implementation. API adaptation avoids visual dependency but requires backend schema knowledge. UI automation requires no backend access but introduces brittle DOM coupling. Balancing these trade-offs across edge runtimes was a primary architectural challenge. Dynamic State Synchronization : Ensuring that an action performed by an AI agent (such as adding an item to the cart or logging in) immediately synchronizes React UI context, cart counts, and native tool availability without causing stale closures or infinite re-renders. Full-Duplex Voice Control : Implementing natural speech recognition and Text-to-Speech playback while providing instantaneous cancellation (mute toggles, sound wave stop controls, and drawer close events) to prevent background audio runaway during asynchronous multi-turn tool loops. Rigorous Failure Handling : Constructing deterministic tests to validate that the system fails safely and predictably across wrong argument types, negative integers, execution order errors, out-of-stock items, and network interruptions. Why Bridge to Agentia? Bridge to Agentia envisions a web where humans and AI agents interact with applications through a common, capability-oriented interface . Instead of asking: “Does this website support WebMCP?” we explore the broader, forward-looking question: “How can any web capability become discoverable, secure, and actionable for an AI agent?” By unifying native browser WebMCP , edge API adaptation , and DOM-level automation with comprehensive security guardrails, Bridge to Agentia provides a practical blueprint for the agentic web. Different architectures, same destination: making web capabilities discoverable and actionable by AI agents. title: forhub
pitch: Talk to Forhub over WebMCP, add your own guidance pack, and build style-consistent tools in a WYSIWYG workbench — each tool ships with a light backend, MCP and WebMCP built in.
about_excerpt:
Talk to Forhub over WebMCP, add your own guidance pack, and build style-consistent tools in a WYSIWYG workbench — each tool ships with a light backend, MCP and WebMCP built in.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Small everyday tools often take too much effort to build and deploy. I created forhub to simplify that process, keep privacy and control in focus, and explore how MCP and WebMCP can help AI agents support our daily lives. 

 What it does 

 forhub brings small apps into one browser workspace, with code editing, interactive previews, project management, and data storage. Compatible AI agents can help build and interact with these tools through scoped MCP and WebMCP interfaces. 

 How we built it 

 Built with TypeScript, React, and CodeMirror on Cloudflare Workers, using D1, R2, and Durable Objects for storage and application state. OpenSpec guided development, with automated browser, runtime, and security tests. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Initial deployment still requires too much technical knowledge. Making infrastructure setup approachable for ordinary users—while keeping private data protected and agent permissions clear—is a key challenge. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 forhub makes personal ideas feel achievable, from agent-assisted recipe management to easier mind-map drafting. Spending less effort on setup gives me more freedom to experiment and make everyday life a little better. 

 What we learned 

 I estimate the foundation is about 90% complete, but turning it into an intuitive product takes substantial work. This competition taught me how much UI and UX matter: powerful capabilities need clear, comfortable interactions. 

 What's next for forhub 

 Simplify the interface and deployment process, develop reusable community guidance, evaluate how reliably models follow it, and make Demo development faster and easier.

title: GymDeck
pitch: A gym webapp that lets ChatGPT build, adapt, and improve your workouts as you use it.
about_excerpt: A gym webapp that lets ChatGPT build, adapt, and improve your workouts as you use it. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When I started looking into going to the gym, getting a workout plan was easy. ChatGPT could make one in seconds. The problem was actually using it: the routine stayed in the chat, my workout logs lived somewhere else, and ChatGPT had no way to know what I completed or how much weight I used. I built GymDeck to connect those steps. ChatGPT can create the plan directly inside the workout tracker, while GymDeck records what actually happens in the gym. That history gives the agent enough context to recommend what should change next. And the best part of all, it's free! Training should still be a routine. The agent is most useful when it helps improve that routine over time or adapt it when something changes. For example, when equipment is unavailable, time is running short, or the user wants to have a change of scenery. ## What GymDeck does GymDeck is a mobile-first workout tracker designed for human-agent collaboration through WebMCP. A user can: Create and edit a multi-day workout plan Load a saved training day as today’s workout Track sets, reps, weight, effort, notes, rest time, and cardio Replace or reorder exercises during a workout Preserve completed work when a workout changes Review training history, volume, consistency, and personal records Receive clear progression recommendations based on previous performance Accept, edit, ignore, or apply those recommendations to the saved plan Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can read and update the same workout state shown in the interface. It can create a plan, add or replace unavailable exercises, shorten a workout, log sets, review history, recommend a new weight, and apply that change directly to the next session. Every human and agent change is visible in GymDeck’s activity history and recent changes can be undone. ## How I built it GymDeck is built with React and TypeScript and hosted as a browser-based application without a built-in application server. The app exposes 23 tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() . These tools are separated into focused read and write actions, including: Reading the athlete profile, current workout, saved plan, and exercise history Creating or editing training plans Adding, replacing, or reordering exercises Logging and correcting completed sets Adding timed cardio Reviewing progress Generating progression recommendations Applying accepted recommendations to the saved weekly plan The normal interface and WebMCP tools call the same underlying state functions. This keeps the visible workout, history, recommendations, and agent actions synchronized. All important data is stored locally in the browser using versioned persistence. GymDeck works after a refresh and supports JSON import and export, demo data, and a fresh-workspace option. It does not require authentication, an external database, an OpenAI API key, or a chatbot embedded inside the app. ## Challenges I faced The biggest challenge was designing tools that an agent could use reliably. The first versions were too ambiguous. An agent might update only today’s workout when the user meant to change the saved plan, or interpret creating a first plan as replacing existing data. I separated these actions into clearer tools for first-time plan creation, explicit plan replacement, editing saved days, and loading a plan day into today’s workout. Another challenge was keeping history accurate across both human and agent actions. Correcting a completed set now updates its persisted history entry, repeated logging does not accidentally reopen a set, and replacing an exercise preserves work that was already completed. Progression also needed to be more than a generic message. GymDeck now compares recorded performance with the saved prescription, explains why it recommends increasing, maintaining, or reducing a weight, and can apply the accepted change back to every matching exercise in the plan. Finally, WebMCP support depends on the browser hosting the site. GymDeck’s manual workout interface works on mobile, but the complete agent workflow currently requires a WebMCP-capable desktop browser such as ChatGPT’s in-app browser. ## What I learned I learned that WebMCP is not about placing a chatbot inside a website. The important part is giving an external agent a clear and dependable interface to the product’s real state. Tool names, schemas, descriptions, safety boundaries, and return messages matter as much as the visual interface. Small, focused tools were much more reliable than broad actions that tried to handle every possible request. I also learned that a useful agent experience needs visible results. When ChatGPT changes a workout, the user should immediately see what changed, understand why it changed, and remain able to edit or undo it. GymDeck demonstrates how an agent can move beyond giving workout advice and directly help maintain a training routine that improves with the user. It is also licensed under the MIT license for all to use and develop. title: Merge-Queue
pitch: Merge Queue gives AI agents a branch instead of giving them the last word. Humans and agents can edit the same live application simultaneously, then safely merge their work without silent overwrites.
about_excerpt: Merge Queue gives AI agents a branch instead of giving them the last word. Humans and agents can edit the same live application simultaneously, then safely merge their work without silent overwrites. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most agent demos quietly assume the human stops touching the application while the agent works. That assumption will not survive the real world. A person might reassign an urgent task while an agent reorganizes the project board. A store manager might correct inventory while an agent prepares a merchandising update. Both actions can be reasonable, yet the application normally accepts whichever write arrives last and silently erases the other participant’s intent. Software teams solved a similar problem for source code with branches and three-way merges. We wanted to explore what that collaboration model could look like for everyday web applications. That became Merge Queue: humans keep working, agents get a branch. What it does Merge Queue is a local-first project board where a person and an AI agent can edit the same workspace concurrently without overwriting each other. When the agent begins a task, Merge Queue snapshots the current workspace and creates an isolated agent branch. The agent can stage multiple structured changes—moving tasks, assigning owners, changing priorities, updating deadlines, or archiving stale work—without mutating the live board. Meanwhile, the human continues working normally. When the agent finishes, Merge Queue performs a semantic three-way merge between: Base: the workspace when the agent started Human: the current live workspace Agent: the agent’s proposed workspace For every changed field, the merge engine determines whether: Only the human changed it, so the human value is preserved. Only the agent changed it, so the proposal can merge safely. Both selected the same value, so the duplicate change is collapsed. Both selected different values, so the decision returns to the human. Compatible work is merged automatically. Genuine disagreements appear as focused conflict cards showing the original value, the human’s choice, the agent’s proposal, and the consequence of each decision. The agent can request a merge review, but it cannot approve its own work. There is intentionally no agent-accessible commit tool. The final merge is committed through the visible human interface as one atomic revision. How we built it Merge Queue is a dependency-free web application built with JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. It runs entirely in the browser, persists versioned state locally, and requires no API key or backend service. The application is organized around a shared deterministic command layer. Human interface actions and WebMCP tool calls invoke the same underlying operations, which prevents the agent from using a hidden automation path with different behavior from the visible application. We implemented WebMCP using imperative tools registered on the top-level page with document.modelContext.registerTool . The tool surface allows an agent to: Read the live workspace and its revision Open an isolated agent branch Stage bounded task updates Stage new tasks Inspect the branch diff Generate a semantic merge preview Read unresolved conflicts Request visible human review Check the branch status Abort an uncommitted branch Revert the latest completed merge Each tool uses a narrow JSON Schema, validates its inputs again inside the domain layer, clearly describes its side effects, and returns enough structured information for the agent to verify the result and select the correct next action. Agent proposals are visually distinguished from live state. A moved task can appear as a proposed destination while its original live card remains intact. An activity timeline interleaves human actions, agent proposals, and system merge events so the collaboration remains understandable throughout the workflow. Merge previews are bound to a specific workspace revision. If the human changes the board after a preview is generated, that preview becomes stale and cannot be committed. The merge must be recalculated against the latest human state. Commits are atomic and idempotent. Repeated commit attempts cannot apply the same branch twice. The previous workspace snapshot is retained so an approved merge can be reverted as a new revision without deleting history. We also built a deterministic walkthrough that consistently produces safe changes, duplicate choices, and three meaningful conflicts. This makes the concurrency problem—and the value of the merge—visible in under ninety seconds. Challenges we faced Defining what a “conflict” means outside source code Text files have lines. Application state has meaning. Moving a task and changing its owner are independent operations that should usually merge. Moving the same task into two different workflow stages is a real conflict. Archiving a task while the other participant edits it also requires special handling. We had to model these cases semantically instead of treating every modified object as one large conflict. Preserving live human work The most important invariant was that an agent proposal must never mutate the human workspace before approval. We maintained separate base, human, and agent snapshots and forced every staged operation through the isolated branch. We added tests for independent edits, overlapping edits, creation, archival, stale previews, repeated commits, aborts, and reverts. Designing human control without approval fatigue Confirming every agent action would technically keep the human in control, but it would make the product painful to use. We moved approval from the individual-action level to the merge level. The agent can prepare a substantial body of work, while the human reviews only the places where their intentions actually differ. Making the agent understand what happened A correct interface is not enough if the agent receives an ambiguous result. Every tool response includes the current revision, branch status, affected records, and valid next step. The agent can distinguish between “staged,” “waiting for human resolution,” “ready for approval,” “merged,” and “aborted” without guessing from the page. Remaining useful without WebMCP The complete human interface and deterministic walkthrough work in ordinary browsers. When WebMCP is available, the agent discovers the structured tools and participates directly. When it is unavailable, the project remains a functional demonstration of the merge model rather than displaying a broken screen. What we learned The most important lesson was that safe agent collaboration is not only about restricting what an agent can do. It is also about defining how agent intent coexists with human intent. Audit logs explain what happened after the fact. Approval dialogs interrupt actions before they happen. Merge Queue explores a third primitive: allow both participants to work, calculate where their intentions are compatible, and return only the irreducible decisions to the person. We also learned that tool results are part of the user experience. A useful WebMCP tool needs more than a successful return value—it should explain what changed, what remained untouched, what state the workflow is now in, and what the agent should do next. Most importantly, WebMCP feels strongest when it enables a collaboration model that ordinary browser automation cannot reproduce reliably. Merge Queue is not simply a faster way for an agent to click task-board buttons. It gives the agent a typed, versioned role inside the application. What we are proud of Agent proposals never mutate live state before approval. Human work can continue while the agent stages a multi-step plan. Compatible changes merge automatically. Genuine conflicts remain human decisions. Stale previews cannot commit. Commits are atomic and idempotent. Completed merges remain recoverable. Human actions and WebMCP calls share the same application logic. The complete experience runs locally without an API key or backend. What’s next Merge Queue’s engine is intentionally domain-independent. The same protocol could power a wedding seating planner where a couple moves family members while an agent balances tables, or a merchant catalog where a store manager protects prices while an agent prepares a collection update. Future versions could add multiple agent branches, collaborative network persistence, configurable application schemas, dependency-aware conflict explanations, and a reusable withMergeQueue() library for adding branch-and-merge semantics to existing WebMCP applications. Our broader goal is to make concurrent human-agent editing a standard capability of the agentic web. Humans keep working. Agents get a branch. Intent gets merged. title: StreamBot | Agent Edition
pitch: A streamer dashboard with a built-in AI teammate: it proposes themed setups, teaches the UI with guided tours, and edits vertical clips you approve everything
about_excerpt: A streamer dashboard with a built-in AI teammate: it proposes themed setups, teaches the UI with guided tours, and edits vertical clips you approve everything Like Comment Story Updates Home Clipit Studio Custom Command Chat Alert Overlay Builder StreamBot — Agent Edition Project Story Inspiration Streamers run a one-person production studio. Before they ever go live, they may have to manage chat commands, alerts, timed promotions, overlays, clipping highlights for TikTok, and countless other pieces of production across a dozen different tabs. Meanwhile, AI agents are still largely stuck outside the product. They screen-scrape interfaces, guess which buttons to click, and operate without a real understanding of the application's state. We wanted to change that. StreamBot is a real streamer dashboard already in production use. The WebMCP Challenge gave us the missing piece: instead of bolting an AI chatbot onto the side of the product, we gave the agent a first-class seat inside the application . The agent uses the same tools as the streamer, operates against the same state, and leaves the same audit trail. That led to the question driving this project: What does setup feel like when a streamer and their AI agent share one workspace, while the human remains in control of anything that matters? What It Does Three experiences define StreamBot Agent Edition. 1. Propose, Don't Just Do The agent isn't simply given unrestricted control. A streamer can say: "Set up my horror night." Instead of immediately changing their dashboard, the agent creates a complete themed proposal: !scary and !brave commands 👻 Follow alerts Timed promotional messages A JUMPSCARE channel-point reward A follower goal bar Other relevant stream configuration The entire setup appears as a review card . The streamer can inspect the proposal, remove anything they don't want, and then hit Approve . Only after approval does the agent execute the changes. Proposal → Review → Approval → Execution It's collaboration with a veto, rather than blind automation. 2. Guides That Teach on the Live UI Agents shouldn't teach users from outdated screenshots or hallucinated interfaces. If a streamer asks: "How do chat alerts work?" The agent first uses discover_targets to inspect the actual DOM and identify the elements currently available on the page. It then uses compose_tour to build a spotlight walkthrough directly against those discovered elements. The result is a guide that operates on the real product, in its current state . No stale screenshots. No guessed buttons. No hallucinated UI. The agent discovers the interface first, then teaches from reality. 3. Skilled Hands, Not Chat The agent isn't limited to answering questions. Inside StreamBot's ClipIt editor, it can stage vertical social edits directly against the mounted editor state. That includes: Vertical layouts Facecam resizing Caption placement Real transcribed captions Designer-created caption presets Editor configuration The agent isn't pretending to edit a clip through text. It's operating the actual editor. How We Built It with WebMCP Route-Scoped Tool Suites Each StreamBot dashboard route registers the tools relevant to the feature currently being viewed. Examples include: Commands Alerts Timed Messages Rewards Canvas ClipIt This is implemented through src/webmcp/suites.ts . The agent only sees tools that are valid for the current context and available to its seat. The Agent Uses the Same API as the UI We didn't create a separate "AI version" of StreamBot's functionality. Every agent tool calls the same endpoints used by the human interface . That means the resulting state is identical regardless of who performed the action. For example: Agent creates !scary → the command immediately appears in the streamer's command list. There is no synchronization layer or second source of truth. Agent actions and human actions operate on the same application state. Tool executions are also written to the account's audit log, just like actions performed by other members of the team. A Bridge into Live Editors For ClipIt, we needed the agent to interact with a mounted editor rather than a traditional API. We built mountClipItEditorCommands , which connects the WebMCP suite directly to the ClipIt store. The bridge dispatches real reducer actions and waits for state convergence before reporting success. That distinction matters. We don't report success because an action was dispatched. We report success when the editor has actually reached the requested state. Human-in-the-Loop Primitives Human approval is built into the tool architecture itself. propose_stream_setup opens a PrepProposalCard and blocks execution until the streamer makes a decision. Our guide tools work similarly: they compose tours from curated block types that can only be placed on targets discovered from the current page. The agent therefore has useful autonomy without having unlimited authority. Permissions The agent is treated as a real seat within StreamBot. Its permissions are governed through: Settings → Your Team Tool suites are only registered in areas where the agent has permission to operate. Challenges 1. Timeouts That Lied Our first ClipIt bridge used pixel changes as proof that an operation had succeeded. That seemed reasonable until we encountered a simple case: A facecam was already in the requested position. The operation succeeded, but because the pixels didn't change, the bridge waited 12 seconds and eventually reported a timeout. We rewrote the system around state convergence instead. A no-op move is now considered a successful operation if the editor is already in the requested state. We also added fail-fast validation using valid-ID lists. 2. Making the Demo Deterministic Transcription and streaming are inherently live, variable, and slow. A two-minute demo can't wait around for production systems to finish processing. We built a simulated backend using: An in-browser API shim A simulated stream engine Deterministic application state This gives us a world that behaves like the real product without depending on unpredictable external timing. For captions, we went further. The demo pipeline uses real ASR transcripts generated with the same model and segmentation approach as production , then bakes those transcripts into the demo environment. The result is deterministic while still containing genuine transcribed speech , rather than lorem ipsum pretending to be captions. 3. Spotlight Honesty Our earliest tours referenced UI elements that didn't actually exist on the current page. That exposed a fundamental problem with agent-generated walkthroughs: The agent was assuming what the interface looked like. We turned the fix into a core design principle: Discover before you teach. Every walkthrough begins with discover_targets . The tour is then composed against what actually exists. What We Learned The biggest lesson was simple: Agents Don't Need More Autonomy. They Need Better Seats. Once the agent shared the human's: Tools Application state Permissions Audit trail Context the interaction fundamentally changed. It stopped feeling like: "Prompt and pray." And started feeling like genuine teamwork: Proposal → Review → Approval → Execution The guardrails aren't friction. Scoped tool suites, approval cards, permission boundaries, and discover-before-teach aren't there to make the agent weaker. They're what make the agent trustworthy enough to delegate to . That's the direction we believe the agent-native web should move toward: AI agents shouldn't sit outside applications, guessing how to use them. They should have a real seat inside the product with the right tools, the right context, and a human who stays in control. title: Gates of Galloo
pitch: A voice-directed voxel world where people and AI reshape the same live scene through WebMCP, from bridges and domino chains to characters, weather, and contextual commerce.
about_excerpt: A voice-directed voxel world where people and AI reshape the same live scene through WebMCP, from bridges and domino chains to characters, weather, and contextual commerce. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration In the HBO show Silicon Valley, Dinesh turns on a microphone inside a game and mentions pizza. The game immediately fills itself with Domino's advertising. It is funny because the world appears to be listening and rewriting itself around the conversation. Gates of Galloo asks a more useful version of that question: what if speaking to a game did not merely open a chatbot or trigger an advertisement? What if the AI could understand the actual world, change it with you, and let you interrupt whenever its taste became questionable? What it does Gates of Galloo is a voice-directed voxel world shared by a person and an AI character named Nika. The player can walk around the island and speak at the level of intention: "Build a bridge in front of me." "Create a domino path from the chapel to the harbor, but leave it standing." "Extend the island with a mix of grass, stone, and water." "I am hungry." "That is too much. Undo it." Nika reads the current state of the island and turns the request into visible actions. Terrain grows, objects arrive, characters move, weather changes, dominoes fall, and contextual storefronts can become part of the scene. These changes happen over time, so the player can watch, interrupt, redirect, or reverse the result. The commerce interactions are no-charge previews. They demonstrate how a product, delivery, or storefront could enter a game as a playable event rather than as a detached banner. Why WebMCP matters The useful context is already inside the page: terrain, buildings, player position and facing, selected regions, actors, shops, domino runs, camera state, and recent changes. Ordinary computer control would force an agent to infer all of that from pixels and simulate mouse clicks. WebMCP lets the website expose the world directly through meaningful actions. Gates of Galloo registers six page tools: inspect_world list_assets place_asset erase_at paint_path undo_last_action The agent works with island objects and validated grid coordinates instead of screen positions. The available vocabulary is intentionally defined by the game, while the model remains free to decide what to create with it. This makes WebMCP part of the creative medium. The person and agent can see and change the same evolving artifact without repeatedly describing what is already on screen. How it creates a better experience The conversation stays inside the activity. The player does not have to export a screenshot, explain the map to a separate assistant, wait for generated code, and reload the result. Instead, an idea becomes visible inside the current world. If the interpretation is wrong, the player can correct it while it is happening. References such as "here," "in front of me," or "beside the bridge" work because the agent receives the live player and scene state. The result feels closer to improvising with another participant than issuing commands to a detached chatbot. How we built it The project began with the open-source Mykonos Island Voxels game by Ibrahim Boona. During the submission period, we transformed it into Gates of Galloo. The browser adapts the live game controller into WebMCP tool definitions and registers them through document.modelContext.registerTool() . For voice interaction, OpenAI Realtime handles the live conversation and transcription. It has one high-level function called direct_world . That function sends the player's original request, together with a semantic snapshot of the island, to a server-side director built with the OpenAI Responses API. The director produces a structured sequence of terrain, object, actor, camera, commerce, and domino operations. The browser validates that plan and performs it incrementally. The production interaction is model-directed rather than selected through keyword rules or canned responses. We also added an embodied isometric player, pathfinding, bridge traversal, camera follow, open-ended terrain growth, mixed-terrain paths, live transcripts, interruption, conflict-aware undo, actors, weather, chain reactions, and contextual storefront scenes. Challenges and lessons The hardest problem was giving the model enough live context to make those actions feel intentional. We had to solve placement validation, connected terrain painting, object footprints, isometric occlusion, bridge traversal, camera framing, world expansion, interruption, and undo without allowing one half-finished plan to corrupt the next. We also learned that the design of the tool vocabulary changes the personality of the agent. A model with raw DOM access behaves like an operator. A model given verbs such as inspect, place, paint, stage, and undo can behave more like a collaborator. Gates of Galloo is one playful example, but the same pattern can extend to design software, educational simulations, music tools, filmmaking environments, and any website where the human and agent should remain inside the work together.  Inspiration 

 First and foremost, I have been experimenting with AI. One of my main goals was to see how much work I could realistically get done with AI assistance. I pitched the idea, tested the website, reviewed changes, and repeatedly stripped away unnecessary bloat. 

 I decided to build a meal planner because eating well and staying consistent can be difficult, whether you are trying to gain weight, lose weight, or simply eat better. Automating parts of meal planning can make that process much easier to maintain. 

 What it does 

 Meal Planner allows users to plan breakfast, lunch, and dinner in advance. Meals are linked to recipes, while recipes can also be stored independently for later use. 

 Users can keep track of pantry inventory, calculate what ingredients they still need, and generate a shopping list based on their planned meals. 

 All of these core functions are also exposed to an AI agent through WebMCP. An agent can read recipes, inspect pantry inventory, plan multiple meals, update stock, calculate shopping requirements, and help research prices or promotions based on a location the user explicitly provides. 

 The application also supports importing and exporting meal data between devices. 

 How we built it 

 The application was largely vibe-coded. I pitched the meal-planning concept and used ChatGPT to help implement it. 

 My role was defining the product, testing the implementation, making architectural decisions, reviewing changes, and removing features that made the application more complicated without making it more useful. 

 The final application is deliberately simple: HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, browser localStorage, and WebMCP. It runs as a static site with no required backend or database. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Our original project idea was significantly more ambitious. Because of time constraints and implementation complexity, we abandoned it and focused on building something smaller that worked well. 

 Another challenge was designing the application so that the same functionality could be used by both humans and AI agents without building two separate systems. 

 The final application runs entirely as a static site. User data is stored locally in the browser, and no third-party API is required for the core functionality. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The entire application was built in one day. 

 Despite the short development time, it includes recipe storage, meal planning, pantry management, shopping-list generation, import/export, and 20 WebMCP tools that expose the application to AI agents. 

 What we learned 

 Vibe-coding works, but only if you understand what you are trying to build. 

 AI can produce a large amount of implementation very quickly, but a human still needs to define the goal, make architectural decisions, test the result, identify unnecessary complexity, and decide what should actually ship. 

 For this project, having a human in the loop was indispensable. 

 What's next for Meal Planner 

 With more time and resources, I would expand the agent integration, improve local price and promotion discovery, add better cross-device synchronization, and continue improving the meal-planning workflow. 

 The core idea would remain the same: let the website manage structured meal data while an AI agent handles the repetitive planning and orchestration.

title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: ChangeFrame
pitch: A shared construction decision room where humans set constraints and retain approval authority while WebMCP agents explore solutions, simulate impact, and prepare the resulting change.
about_excerpt: A shared construction decision room where humans set constraints and retain approval authority while WebMCP agents explore solutions, simulate impact, and prepare the resulting change. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Construction teams already have strong systems for drawings, issues, schedules, budgets, and change orders. But one part of the workflow still depends heavily on people manually connecting all of that context: deciding what to do when something changes. A field conflict is rarely just a drawing problem. A decision may affect constructability, cost, schedule, contracts, and downstream approvals at the same time. That made construction change decisions a strong fit for WebMCP. Instead of building another chatbot beside a project-management interface, we wanted to explore a different interaction model: what if the construction workspace itself could become understandable and actionable to a browser agent? That became ChangeFrame — a shared construction decision room where humans contribute field knowledge and retain authority, while agents investigate alternatives, react to live constraints, simulate impact, and prepare downstream artifacts. What it does ChangeFrame lets a construction project manager and a browser agent resolve a field coordination issue together inside the same live workspace. The demo starts with a synthetic construction scenario at Riverside Office Tower where HVAC duct D22 conflicts with structural beam B14. The agent can inspect the current issue through WebMCP and propose multiple resolution strategies with estimates, assumptions, risks, and route geometry. The project manager can then add information that the agent did not previously know. For example, the human can draw a blocked region directly on the construction plan to indicate that a proposed duct route cannot pass through an electrical riser. The agent can immediately discover that new constraint through WebMCP and revise the affected solution without the human having to describe the geometry again in chat. From there, ChangeFrame supports the rest of the decision workflow: the agent proposes and revises resolution alternatives the human compares, rejects, and selects options the agent simulates cost and schedule impact the agent can propose mitigation for schedule impact the agent prepares the decision for review the human retains the only approval path after approval, the agent can draft the resulting change order The key idea is that the human and agent operate on the same versioned application state . The agent is not clicking around the interface or working from a copied snapshot of the project. ChangeFrame exposes structured construction capabilities directly through WebMCP, and every agent action updates the same Decision Room that the project manager is reviewing. We also built an Agent Flight Recorder that makes the collaboration visible by showing human actions, agent tool calls, state versions, and changes in available capabilities. How we built it ChangeFrame is a frontend-only application built with: React TypeScript Vite Zustand Tailwind CSS shadcn/ui SVG-based construction-plan rendering The application is organized around a central domain state machine. The human interface and the WebMCP tool executors both call the same domain actions. This was important because we did not want separate “agent state” and “UI state” that could drift apart. WebMCP integration is implemented with: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) ChangeFrame exposes typed, domain-level capabilities rather than low-level UI actions. Examples include: The browser agent works against the same live decision state the project manager sees. It does not scrape cards or guess through the DOM. Tools appear only when their action is valid: Tool Purpose get_decision_context Read the complete live context and current alternatives get_user_constraints Read human-authored field constraints configure_decision_context Structure an arbitrary user project brief into the workspace evaluate_resolution_options Submit 2–5 original alternatives with assumptions and confidence revise_resolution_option Submit a complete route revision that is geometry-checked simulate_project_impact Add an optional agent mitigation; ChangeFrame calculates the totals prepare_change_decision Prepare the selected result for human review draft_change_order Draft an artifact only after human approval There is deliberately no tool for selecting, rejecting, or approving an alternative. The collaboration loop The user keeps the visible starter project or describes a different project issue to the browser agent. For a different brief, the agent calls configure_decision_context with the facts, relationships, and plan geometry it has. The agent reads the current state and authors original alternatives. The human reviews the rationale and assumptions and draws a field constraint. Any intersecting route is marked needs_revision automatically. The agent reads that new constraint and submits a revised route. ChangeFrame rejects the revision if the route still intersects the constraint. The human selects an eligible alternative. The agent may propose an evidence-backed mitigation; ChangeFrame performs the arithmetic. The agent prepares the decision, the human approves it, and only then can a draft change order be created. Every mutation carries expectedStateVersion . Stale calls fail without side effects. Agent inputs and capability changes are recorded in the Agent Flight Recorder. The available tool set changes depending on the current decision phase. For example, the agent cannot draft a change order before a human has approved the decision because that tool is not available yet. Selection, rejection, and final approval are deliberately reserved for the human interface and are never exposed as agent capabilities. We also added optimistic concurrency using a versioned application state. Mutation tools receive an expected state version, and stale calls fail without modifying the project. This protects the workflow from retries or agent actions based on outdated context. The MVP does not depend on a backend or its own LLM service. The browser agent supplies the reasoning, while ChangeFrame supplies the live domain state, structured tools, deterministic calculations, and visible workspace. Why WebMCP? ChangeFrame is a strong fit for WebMCP because construction decisions depend on live, structured application state . The agent needs to understand more than what is visible in a screenshot. It needs semantic access to things such as: the active construction issue the current drawing and affected elements human-drawn field constraints resolution alternatives the option selected by the project manager cost and schedule impact the current decision phase whether human approval has occurred the latest application state version Without WebMCP, the project manager would have to repeatedly copy this information into a conversation, or an agent would have to infer application state by reading the DOM, interpreting screenshots, and clicking through the interface. ChangeFrame instead exposes explicit construction capabilities through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) This lets the browser agent work directly with the same state that powers the human interface. The result is not simply faster browser automation. It enables a different collaboration model. What people and agents can now do together The project manager contributes the information that requires human judgment and real-world context. For example, while reviewing a proposed duct reroute, the project manager can draw a blocked region directly onto the construction plan because they know that area contains an electrical riser. The agent does not need the user to describe that region again in chat. It can discover the new constraint through WebMCP, understand its geometry and applicability, revise the proposed route, recalculate the impact, and update the same Decision Room the project manager is already viewing. The collaboration continues throughout the workflow: The agent investigates the issue using structured project context. The agent proposes multiple resolution strategies and materializes them in the workspace. The human adds field knowledge directly through the visual interface. The agent discovers that new state and revises its solution. The human compares and selects the preferred direction. The agent simulates cost and schedule consequences and prepares the decision. The human explicitly approves the outcome. Only after approval does the agent gain the capability to draft the change order. This division of responsibility is intentional. The agent handles work where scale and computation help: retrieving context exploring alternatives revising solutions comparing trade-offs calculating impact preparing structured artifacts The human retains work that requires judgment or authority: providing field context rejecting unsuitable alternatives

title: MOTH FORGE: QUAMPUTE
pitch: A human-governed creative workbench where WebMCP agents carry evidence, consequence, and continuity—without taking identity, cost, deletion, or publication away from the creator.
about_excerpt: A human-governed creative workbench where WebMCP agents carry evidence, consequence, and continuity—without taking identity, cost, deletion, or publication away from the creator. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI-assisted creative tools collapse two different kinds of work into one chat box. The person is expected to provide identity, taste, boundaries, and every supporting detail, while the model is allowed to improvise over missing evidence. That is convenient, but it is not dependable collaboration. MOTH FORGE: QUAMPUTE began with a different relationship: people and agents should remain differentiated. The creator owns premise, identity, consent, locks, and consequential gates. The agent should do the exhausting work of reading, routing, checking, deriving, preserving provenance, and carrying decisions through a visible workflow. WebMCP made that relationship implementable on the open web. Instead of guessing at a UI, an agent can receive declared tools with explicit inputs, side effects, and boundaries—while the person sees and controls the same workbench. What it does QUAMPUTE turns a creative spark into an evidence-routed Review and honest Export package through six visible stages: Spark — the person supplies the premise and build shape. Sources — evidence is attached with an authority role such as canon, reference, inspiration, or format-only. Locks — creator-owned truths and player boundaries are preserved with revision-safe writes. Quampute — the system frames the evidence, performs the allowed synthesis, and stops before any unapproved paid action. Review — conclusions remain separated as confirmed, derived, adapted, reserved, or not applicable. Export — structured JSON and readable Markdown preserve provenance and QA state without falsely claiming compilation, installation, runtime testing, or publication. The public challenge build includes a deterministic, no-cost museum-registrar example. It contains a synthetic 29-tab, 607-question authority pack so judges can inspect the complete workflow without exposing private creator material or triggering a model charge. Why WebMCP is essential The app registers 13 WebMCP tools covering studio inspection, project discovery, visible premise staging, project creation, exact project reopening, text-source attachment, revision-safe creator-lock updates, Review inspection, creator-answer staging, stage navigation, safe demo preparation, and Export-link retrieval. This is not a second API hidden behind the website. The WebMCP tools coordinate the same visible state the human is reviewing. A staged answer appears in the on-page form before it is saved. Navigation keeps the human and agent on the same stage. Read-only tools expose provenance, blockers, completion state, and human-only gates. Mutating tools disclose their effects, including when restoration can replace saved demo state. That makes the experience materially better than either UI automation or a chat-only assistant: the agent does not guess from pixels; the person does not surrender authorship; side effects are declared; state is version-pinned; evidence and inference stay distinct; reserved decisions return to the person; Export does not overclaim completion. How we built it TypeScript application using the Next.js-compatible Vinext runtime WebMCP tool registration bound to the visible workbench OpenAI Sites deployment Cloudflare D1-compatible SQLite persistence with Drizzle migrations R2-compatible source storage and cleanup receipts Optimistic revision checks, claim tokens, renewable leases, quota-safe writes, and durable deletion ledgers A fresh, single-root public release containing only allowlisted application code and a generated synthetic authority pack Independent exact-commit privacy, migration, build, concurrency, save/reopen, semantic-routing, and production QA Challenges The hardest problem was not adding tools. It was making tool behavior honest under failure and concurrency. We repaired identity migration so a visible creator question survives save and reopen under the same stable ID. We made deterministic demo repair advance revision atomically so it cannot race a paid claim against a stale source snapshot. We made provider cleanup receipts durable even when a terminal result races a human abandonment action. We also refused to label routed evidence as support when the cited source did not actually establish the displayed claim. The public release introduced a second challenge: proving absence. The release is generated into a fresh directory and fresh one-commit history through a closed allowlist. It contains synthetic tab titles, prompts, identifiers, and examples; it does not contain the private Forge corpus, private character canon, checkpoints, local paths, credentials, or earlier repository history. Accomplishments Exactly 13 useful WebMCP tools operating on one shared human-agent workbench A deterministic no-cost judge path with no API key and no paid model call 29 synthetic authority tabs and 607 unique, normalization-safe question routes Stable creator-answer save and reopen behavior Honest completion-state and provenance-preserving Export Human-only gates for cost, deletion, uncertain cleanup, and publication One-root public Git history with no hidden prior objects Reproducible frozen offline install, typecheck, lint, migrations, focused regressions, and full production builds Signed-in production QA with zero browser errors and successful Worker outcomes What we learned Agent-native design is not about maximizing agent permission. It is about giving the agent the strongest precise capability that preserves the person's role. WebMCP works best when tools expose meaning, state, and side effects—not just button equivalents. “Inspect the Review candidate and its unresolved creator questions” is more useful than “click the Review tab.” “Stage this answer visibly but do not save it” creates collaboration. A correct tool contract can become part of the product's trust model. Try it Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Ask: “Inspect this Forge and open the completed no-cost example.” Ask the agent to inspect the Review and explain the difference between confirmed, derived, and reserved results. Ask it to stage an answer to the one reserved question. The answer appears visibly and remains unsaved until the person chooses the Save control. Ask for the Export links and inspect the honest completion state. No API key is configured. The public judge flow makes no paid model call. Links Live app: https://moth-forge-quampute-webmcp.mothling.chatgpt.site Source repository: https://github.com/shortlaughs0-sudo/moth-forge-quampute-webmcp Demo video: https://youtu.be/fN3CZCaUe6A What's next After the challenge, the submitted version will remain frozen during judging. Future work belongs on a separate branch or fork: broader source adapters, additional export destinations, and more domain-specific Forge packs—all while preserving the same human-authority and evidence-custody model. title: Haggle
pitch: Your agent haggles with the seller's agent so you don't have to Price, pickup and terms get negotiated agent to agent, the site enforces the limits you set and nothing closes until both people say yes
about_excerpt: Your agent haggles with the seller's agent so you don't have to Price, pickup and terms get negotiated agent to agent, the site enforces the limits you set and nothing closes until both people say yes Like Comment Story Updates Main Web MCP Tools Inspiration Every time I try to buy or sell something on a marketplace it's the same thing. I message, they answer three hours later, I'm at work, they're at dinner, someone forgets, and a $150 bike takes a week of messages and then nothing happens. The negotiation is not the hard part. The hard part is that two busy people have to be online at the same time to close something simple. So I wanted to try this: you bring your own agent, it talks to the seller's agent, and you get out of the loop. You come back only to say yes or no. And then the obvious problem. If my agent is negotiating for me, how do I make sure I don't end up buying something it picked because "it fit"? That's why the mandate and the double approval exist. They're not extras, they're what makes the first part safe. What it does Haggle is a bike marketplace where the agents do the back-and-forth and you only show up to decide. You bring whatever agent you use (I tested with the ChatGPT desktop browser). The page gives it WebMCP tools to search listings, set your limits, make and counter offers, wait for the seller to answer, and check where things are. It doesn't click around or scrape anything. On the other side, the seller sets up an agent in Seller Studio: how it negotiates, a floor price, some rules. Your agent can't read any of that. They negotiate everything, not just the price. When to meet, where (public place), and what's included, like a lock. Before you send your agent, you give it a mandate: max price, when you're free, public pickup only, what has to come with the bike. That's saved on the server and enforced there. If your agent tries to accept $195 and your max is $180, the site says no, and you see it in the timeline as "Blocked by your mandate, not by your agent." When they reach something, you see each term next to what you asked for. You approve, or you decline and leave a note for your agent, and it keeps going. The seller sees the same screen against their own limits, and those numbers never leave the server. Nothing closes until both people approve. How I built it Next.js and TypeScript on Vercel, Postgres with Drizzle. Tools are registered with document.modelContext, with a fallback to navigator.modelContext. The tools change depending on where the negotiation is: read-only ones are always there, the action ones only appear when that action actually makes sense. The seller's agent runs in the background, so I added a read-only wait_for_seller_response tool. Otherwise the agent had to guess when to check again, and it usually didn't. Tools have readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint. All the checks (budget, mandate, seller limits, valid pickup options) run on the server. Whatever the seller's agent writes comes back marked as untrusted. There's a panel called Agent Lens that shows you what tools your agent can see on each screen. If your browser doesn't support WebMCP yet, it still shows you the list. Challenges I ran into The main one was giving the agent room to negotiate without losing control of it. I tried doing it with prompts first. It didn't work. Moving the limits into the site fixed it. Then keeping everything consistent with the seller running in the background, tools appearing and disappearing, and private info on both sides. It's easy to end up in a state where nobody knows whose turn it is. And the small one that turned out to matter: at first, declining ended the negotiation. Now declining is a message to your agent. Accomplishments I'm proud of Two agents with opposite interests, private information on both sides, limits the site enforces, and two separate human approvals. All of it through tools the page exposes. I'm mostly happy with how the site ended up being the referee, not just a place where agents click things. What I learned Exposing tools is the easy part. The real decision is what the agent must never be able to do. Once that lived on the server I could stop babysitting the prompt. Also, "no" has to be information for the agent, not a stop button. And the state of the deal should decide what tools exist, not the prompt. What's next for Haggle Sellers bringing their own agent, with Haggle staying in the middle as the referee. Delegation levels, from "ask me everything" to "close it if it fits." And going past bikes to anything two people sell to each other. Bikes today. Any local deal tomorrow. Note for judges Seller Studio is a labeled persona simulator so you can play both sides in one session. It's not authentication. pitch: Can an AI agent actually use your website? AgentReady runs real agents through your raw UI and your WebMCP tools, scores the site 0-100, and publishes the gap. Measured: UI 0/3 vs WebMCP 3/3.
about_excerpt: Can an AI agent actually use your website? AgentReady runs real agents through your raw UI and your WebMCP tools, scores the site 0-100, and publishes the gap. Measured: UI 0/3 vs WebMCP 3/3. Like Comment Story Updates Benchmark Run Log Live Agent Traffic Scorecard Human Agent Cowriting Agent Ready Inspiration Everyone in the agent era repeats the same claim — "AI agents struggle to use websites" — and nobody measures it. Site owners have zero visibility into whether an agent can actually finish a checkout on their site, and WebMCP adopters have no way to prove the investment worked. We stopped arguing and built the measuring instrument. What it does AgentReady is the readiness benchmark for the agent-native web. It runs real AI agents against real task flows on a site twice — once through the raw UI, once through the site's WebMCP tools — and scores the site 0–100 from success rate, tool surface, and steps-to-complete, with a failure taxonomy (auth walls, popups, navigation loops, timeouts) explaining every miss. The benchmark's own dashboard is agent-native: 8 WebMCP tools let your agent query scores, compare sites, and co-write a readiness report with you in a shared on-page editor — it drafts, you edit by hand, and it reads your edits back through a tool before revising. Its queue_live_audit tool triggers a real serverless audit — headless browser, LLM agent, results into the database — that your agent then reads back. A demo store with 5 more tools (one cart shared between human and agent) is the reference implementation, and every tool call on the deployment streams to a live analytics view. Measured result on our own store: raw UI 0/3 (all timed out at 15 steps), WebMCP 3/3 in ~4 steps. How we built it Entirely on Cloudflare: the app runs on vinext (the Vite-based Next.js reimplementation) on Workers, D1 stores telemetry and audit results, Queues orchestrates audit jobs, Browser Run provides headless Chrome at the edge, and Workers AI (Llama 3.3 70B) is the audit agent. A small shim ( lib/webmcp.ts ) registers WebMCP tools via document.modelContext with a navigator fallback, instruments every execution for the live analytics view, and mirrors tools onto a page registry so headless auditors can drive the exact same tool functions. A local Playwright runner audits external sites with confidence intervals; a queue-consumer Worker runs the serverless audits. The demo video was produced by a multi-agent pipeline too: strategy, script, Playwright screen-capture of the live site, Kyutai pocket-tts narration, Veo b-roll, and a Remotion composition. Challenges we ran into vinext is explicitly experimental — our first deploys shipped an assets-only Worker (no server code) until we discovered the config needed an explicit main: "vinext/server/fetch-handler" . UI-mode audit runs take 12+ minutes, which blew past queue consumer wall-clocks when we batched runs into one message — the fix was one message per run. Workers AI sometimes returns parsed JSON objects where we expected strings, which silently killed our first serverless audits. Browser launch failures burned queue retries without recording anything until we made every failure write a result row. And securing an intentionally unauthenticated API (judges' agents must call it) meant same-origin audit restriction, a daily run budget, and payload caps instead of auth. Accomplishments that we're proud of The headline number is measured, not claimed: same site, same task, same agent — 0/3 through the UI, 3/3 through WebMCP. The bidirectional co-writing loop ( draft_readiness_report → human edits → get_report_draft reads them back) treats the page as a two-way channel between human and agent, not a tool facade. The benchmark audits its own demo store with one tool call, on camera, in production. And we kept the methodology honest: sample rows are clearly badged as synthetic, the real runs are labeled with their n, and the whole thing is MIT-licensed and reproducible. What we learned Agent-readiness is measurable, and the gap is bigger than the discourse suggests — our agent burned 15 steps and still failed on a UI it could clear in 4 steps with tools. A tool surface beats heroic UI parsing every time, and the score gap is the business case in one number. Architecturally: mirroring tools onto a page registry made the site testable by any headless browser, serverless constraints (queue wall-clocks, browser session limits) should shape job design from day one, and honest small-n data presented plainly is more credible than inflated claims. What's next for Agent Ready Audit real production sites (with permission) to grow the index into an industry readiness leaderboard. An embeddable "agent-ready score" badge and a CI check so a site's score updates on every deploy. Richer task suites beyond add-to-cart — search, auth flows, form completion, multi-step journeys. Durable Object browser-session pooling to parallelize serverless audits. And opening the instrumentation SDK so any site gets /live -style agent analytics by wrapping registerTool in one line.
