title: CargoPilot
pitch: Share a current Cargo page with your agent through WebMCP, with visible freshness and human-controlled editing boundaries.
about_excerpt:
Share a current Cargo page with your agent through WebMCP, with visible freshness and human-controlled editing boundaries.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Portfolio builders are visual, but collaborating with an AI in one often means describing a layout from memory or exchanging disconnected screenshots. CargoPilot explores a more explicit shared reference: the creator chooses a signed-in Cargo page, the agent receives its current visible context, and both know when that context is too old to trust. 

 What it does 

 CargoPilot connects a public WebMCP companion to a private local bridge. It exposes a screenshot, bounded semantic context, route and page information, capture time, and freshness state for a selected Cargo screen. The same context is available through a standard stdio MCP server. 

 There are two distinct connection paths. A Chrome extension lets the user click Share with Codex on an already signed-in Cargo tab. In Codex/ChatGPT's in-app browser, a browser-capable host agent can instead make an explicitly authorized capture and relay it using request_cargo_context and attach_cargo_context . Extensions cannot be installed inside that in-app browser; the hosted companion cannot independently inspect another tab or borrow its authentication. 

 The shared canvas is a read-only snapshot, not a second Cargo editor. Captures expire after 15 seconds. The UI marks stale and unavailable states, and context tools do not silently switch to another browser. The creator scrolls or edits in Cargo and asks the agent for a new capture when needed. 

 The Chrome extension also implements a separate time-limited approval path for two fixed recipes: exact text replacement and native Backdrop selection, with route and postcondition checks. Read-only sharing does not authorize these actions. The final live demonstration deliberately exercises only read-only context; it does not claim to demonstrate those editing recipes, asset uploads, arbitrary template editing, or publishing. 

 Why WebMCP 

 WebMCP turns the companion's collaboration boundary into named, typed tools. An agent can ask for workspace, screen, or editor context through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) instead of guessing what a screenshot or inactive canvas means. Inputs are validated, freshness is explicit, and inspection is separated from mutation authority. 

 The creator can discuss a specific page while the agent receives the relevant visual evidence and knows which site, page and capture it belongs to. The Chrome pointing interaction additionally shares viewport coordinates and a bounded accessible label. This reduces repeated manual explanation without treating unrestricted browser control as the default. 

 How we built it 

 
 Vite and TypeScript companion, hosted on Vercel, registering browser-native WebMCP tools. 
 Local Express service bound to 127.0.0.1 , with Zod input validation, short-lived context, audit state, and a standard MCP server. 
 Manifest V3 Chrome extension with explicit selected-tab sharing and a separate approved fixed-action path. 
 Browser-host attachment for the in-app browser, using actual screenshot capture and bounded visible context without moving cookies or passwords between browsers. 
 

 Codex assisted with implementation, debugging and testing. Remotion assembles real browser captures and measured capture sequences into the demo. The narration is AI-generated; the conversation section is explicitly labelled as a replay of our actual exchange, not a recording of the Codex interface. 

 Validation 

 The 4 September 2026 live pass retrieved a real authenticated Cargo dashboard and an editor page through the deployed WebMCP companion and an actual stdio MCP client. Both returned the relevant current screen and screenshot. Asking for editor context on the dashboard correctly failed. Expiry produced an explicit stale response and visible UI label. Losing the attachment removed the old canvas image and left unsupported typing controls disabled. 

 There are 64 passing automated tests, TypeScript checks pass, the hosted build passes, and extension 0.4.1 packaging and response-parsing checks pass. The installed Chrome extension's attach and mutation flow was not re-tested in this final live pass. No live Cargo mutation or publishing tool was called during validation or filming. 

 Challenges and lessons 

 Browser-session isolation was the central challenge: a hosted page cannot safely reuse an unrelated tab's login. The viable design is explicit sharing through a permitted Chrome extension or a browser-capable host, not a hidden second browser profile. Freshness also matters: an old screenshot must not be presented as live editor truth. 

 The lesson is that useful agent collaboration needs a trustworthy reference and a clear scope, not just many tools. CargoPilot is a local-assisted prototype, not a cloud-only mobile service or an autonomous general-purpose Cargo editor. 

 What's next 

 Package the local bridge as a signed installer, improve guided reconnection, and expand supported editing recipes only when each has deterministic verification. A first-party continuous host attachment API could reduce repeated captures without weakening consent.

title: TaskFence
pitch: Delegate a task to an AI agent on any website — and keep the say-so. Real WebMCP tools behind a deterministic fence you write in plain English.
about_excerpt: Delegate a task to an AI agent on any website — and keep the say-so. Real WebMCP tools behind a deterministic fence you write in plain English. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP changes what a website can offer an AI agent. Instead of leaving the agent to interpret a page built for human eyes, a site can publish the operations it actually supports and let the agent call them directly. Reading through the explainer, what struck me was that making the boundary explicit does more than improve reliability — it creates somewhere to put a policy. For the first time there is a real function call between an agent and a website's data, and anything that happens at that point can be inspected, reasoned about, and governed. The explainer is candid that a trust boundary is crossed the moment an agent begins calling tools, and there are open discussions in the project around agent identity and action-specific permissions. Those felt like the most interesting questions in the space, and the kind that benefit from someone building a working example rather than only describing one. The shape of the answer came from ordinary experience. When you ask a colleague to handle a form for you, you rarely give an unqualified yes. You say something like "fill in what you can from these documents, leave the parts I've already written, and check with me before you send it." That is a boundary that stays in force for the whole task and can be adjusted while the work is underway. I wanted to see how close a website could get to that, now that it finally has a place to enforce it. What it does TaskFence is a delegation layer that sits on a site's WebMCP boundary. The clearest way to describe it is to follow what happens in the demo. You begin with a form you need completed. Rather than the site choosing what that form is, you upload the one you actually care about — I test with a real university scholarship PDF — and the page reads the fields out of your document. If you had already filled in parts of that PDF before uploading it, TaskFence treats those values as answers you have given and places them on the form as yours, which becomes important a moment later. You then describe the task in a sentence, in your own words, including anything you want left alone: "fill in the blanks from my documents, don't change anything I've already answered, ask me if something is missing, ask before you submit, and tell me if any field doesn't look right." That sentence is compiled into a structured contract of permitted, forbidden and approval-required actions. Before anything runs, the page shows you what it understood, and equally what it could not interpret — a boundary you believed you had set but which was quietly misread would undermine the whole idea, so it is surfaced rather than assumed. The agent then works. Everything within your boundary proceeds without interruption: it reads the form and your documents, checks the answers already present, and completes the blanks it is permitted to complete. You are not consulted about any of it, because you have already agreed to it. When it reaches something outside the boundary, the tool call is held before the write takes place. You are shown what the agent intended to do, which part of your own sentence stopped it, and precisely what permission is being requested. You can decline, or allow it — and if the value the agent proposed is wrong, you can correct it first, so what is written is your version. A grant is deliberately narrow: one tool, one field, a single use, expiring the moment it is spent, and scoped to that agent and that task alone. Afterwards there is a ledger of every decision alongside the rule that produced it, which can be replayed and exported. How we built it The application is React, TypeScript and Vite, with zustand for state, Motion for transitions, React Three Fiber for the mark on the landing page, and pdf.js reading documents entirely in the browser. The parts worth explaining, though, are three design decisions. The first is where enforcement lives. Every tool the site registers is wrapped by a single guarded() function, so there is no route from an agent to the site's data that bypasses the check. This is practical because of the shape WebMCP already gives us: a tool call is an async function, so pausing an agent to consult a human costs nothing to implement — the promise simply is not resolved yet. Tools are registered exactly as the specification describes: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "updateApplication", description: "Update a field in the application", inputSchema: { /* field, value, source, documentId */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* runs only if the contract allows it */ } }) Built With css groq html motion node.js openai react react-three-fiber three.js typescript vite webmcp zustand Try it out task-fence.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Lisa A Like Share this project: Updates Lisa A started this project — Sep 03, 2026 01:50 PM EDT

title: AgentBadge — WebMCP Agent-Native Compliance Platform
pitch: First agent-native compliance platform powered by WebMCP. 6 imperative tools, 1 declarative form, zero API keys. 145+ readiness rules, on-chain agent passports on Hedera. Browser-mediated tool calls.
about_excerpt:
First agent-native compliance platform powered by WebMCP. 6 imperative tools, 1 declarative form, zero API keys. 145+ readiness rules, on-chain agent passports on Hedera. Browser-mediated tool calls.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP vs Traditional API vs MCP: zero keys, zero servers, zero setup. Browser mediates all agent tool calls natively. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 AgentBadge: 6 imperative WebMCP tools, 1 declarative form, zero API keys. Browser-native agent compliance on Hedera. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agent visits agentbadge.xyz, discovers 6 tools via /.well-known/webmcp.json, calls them directly through the browser. No setup. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP vs Traditional API vs MCP: zero keys, zero servers, zero setup. Browser mediates all agent tool calls natively. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 AgentBadge: 6 imperative WebMCP tools, 1 declarative form, zero API keys. Browser-native agent compliance on Hedera. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agent visits agentbadge.xyz, discovers 6 tools via /.well-known/webmcp.json, calls them directly through the browser. No setup. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP vs Traditional API vs MCP: zero keys, zero servers, zero setup. Browser mediates all agent tool calls natively. 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents today face a fundamental integration problem. To use any web service, an agent must: read API docs, obtain API keys, install SDKs, configure authentication, and manage secrets. This is the API key bottleneck — every integration requires human setup. 

 Meanwhile, MCP (Model Context Protocol) emerged as a standard for exposing tools to LLMs, but it still requires running a separate MCP server, configuring transport (stdio/SSE), and managing permissions server-side. Agents without MCP clients are left out. 

 We asked: what if agents could discover and use tools directly from the browser — no keys, no servers, no setup? WebMCP answers this by making the browser the mediator. AgentBadge is our answer to "what does an agent-native web look like?" 

 What it does 

 AgentBadge is the first agent-native compliance platform powered by WebMCP . It exposes: 

 
 6 imperative tools via navigator.modelContext.provideContext() :

 
 agent-readiness-scan — scans any URL for 145+ AI readiness checks across 18 categories 
 badge-generate — generates compliance badge SVG 
 passport-issue — mints on-chain NFT passport on Hedera 
 passport-verify — verifies agent identity by token ID or DID (Hedera + EVM) 
 get-compliance-score — quick compliance score (0-100, grade A-F) 
 search-rules — searches 145+ compliance rules by keyword 
 
 1 declarative form — HTML form-based scan submission for declarative agents 
 Automatic discovery via /.well-known/webmcp.json — agents find tools without reading docs 
 Browser-mediated security — per-tool trust levels (trusted/untrusted, readOnly/write), no API keys 
 145+ readiness rules across 18 categories — the most comprehensive AI agent readiness scanner 
 

 How we built it 

 WebMCP Layer 

 
 Discovery endpoint: GET /.well-known/webmcp.json returns a manifest with tool namespaces, endpoints, and descriptors 
 Tool registration: Inline <script> on every page calls navigator.modelContext.provideContext() with 6 tool definitions (input schemas + execute functions) 
 Trust levels: Each tool declares readOnly / write + trusted / untrusted — the browser enforces per-tool access 
 

 Scanner (145+ rules, 18 categories) 

 
 41 parallel HTTP fetchers — robots.txt, sitemap, llms.txt, OpenAPI, WebMCP manifest, WebMCP runtime, content negotiation, payment protocols, identity/DID, bot auth, SEO/AEO, accessibility, and more 
 WebMCP-specific rules: AB-050 (manifest found), AB-051 (form annotations), AB-069 (browser-side tools), AB-102 (descriptor validation), AB-103 (runtime probe), AB-115 (tool schema), AB-116 (content negotiation) 
 Ed25519-signed reports with SHA-256 integrity hashes 
 

 Blockchain Layer 

 
 Hedera HTS — non-transferable NFT passports ($0.001/tx, 3-5s finality, no smart contracts) 
 HCS — immutable audit trail + agent directory (consensus-ordered, timestamped) 
 Mirror Node — free REST API for reads, no indexer needed 
 DID support: did:hcs:{tokenId}:{serial} (Hedera) and did:eip155:{chainId}:passport:{nftAddress}:{tokenId} (EVM) 
 

 Tech Stack 

 
 Runtime: Bun + Hono (TypeScript-native, server-side rendering) 
 Frontend: HTMX fragments — no React, no build step 
 Blockchain: Hedera Testnet (HTS + HCS + HBAR) 
 Metadata: IPFS via nft.storage (immutable JSON, CID = content hash) 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP Spec Readiness 

 WebMCP is an emerging spec — browsers haven't shipped navigator.modelContext yet. We built the full integration (tool registration, discovery endpoint, schemas) so it's spec-ready today : all endpoints work as standard HTTP APIs, and will work natively via WebMCP when browsers implement it. 

 Scanner Complexity 

 145+ rules across 18 categories with 41 parallel fetchers is complex to orchestrate. We built a parallel fetcher architecture with SSRF protection, content-type validation, and timeout handling. Each fetcher returns structured data that feeds into the rule engine. 

 Browser-Mediated Trust 

 Designing per-tool trust levels ( trusted / untrusted , readOnly / write ) that the browser can enforce required careful thinking about the threat model. Untrusted tools ( agent-readiness-scan , get-compliance-score ) are safe for any agent to call. Trusted tools ( passport-issue , passport-verify ) require browser mediation. 

 Cross-Chain Identity 

 Supporting both Hedera ( did:hcs: ) and EVM ( did:eip155: ) DIDs required abstracting the verification layer. The same passport-verify tool handles both formats, resolving to on-chain NFT ownership checks via the appropriate chain's API. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 First WebMCP-native compliance platform — not a wrapper around an existing API, but built from the ground up for browser-mediated agent tool discovery 
 145+ scanner rules across 18 categories — the most comprehensive AI agent readiness framework, covering discovery, documentation, actionability, payments, identity, infrastructure, SEO/AEO, accessibility, and WebMCP itself 
 7 WebMCP-specific scanner rules — AgentBadge scans itself and other sites for WebMCP compliance (manifest, runtime, form annotations, tool schemas, content negotiation) 
 Zero API keys architecture — agents discover and use tools without any authentication setup 
 Cross-chain DID support — Hedera and EVM identity in one tool 
 Spec-ready today — full WebMCP integration that works as HTTP APIs now and natively when browsers ship navigator.modelContext 
 

 What we learned 

 
 WebMCP is the right abstraction — agents shouldn't need to read API docs or manage keys. Browser-mediated tool discovery is fundamentally better than the API key model. 
 Scanner-first approach works — before exposing tools, check if a site is agent-ready. 145+ rules across 18 categories gives a comprehensive readiness picture. 
 Declarative + imperative is the right combo — some agents prefer tool calls, others prefer HTML forms. Supporting both covers all agent types. 
 Trust levels are essential — not all tools should be callable by any agent. The trusted / untrusted split lets the browser enforce access without authentication. 
 

 What's next for AgentBadge 

 
 Browser-native WebMCP — when Chrome ships navigator.modelContext , AgentBadge tools will work natively without any changes to our code 
 More imperative tools — expand beyond 6 tools to cover marketplace tasks, A2A messaging, and agent directory search 
 WebMCP compliance certification — a badge program for sites that pass all 7 WebMCP scanner rules 
 Agent passport tiers via WebMCP — let agents upgrade their on-chain tier through browser-mediated tool calls 
 Cross-browser testing — validate WebMCP integration across Chrome, Firefox, Safari as implementations ship 
 Community rule contributions — open the 145+ rule framework for community-submitted readiness checks

title: Counterask
pitch: A storefront whose WebMCP tools hand the agent a question instead of a guess — and that reads a whole sentence: budget, refusals and all.
about_excerpt: A storefront whose WebMCP tools hand the agent a question instead of a guess — and that reads a whole sentence: budget, refusals and all. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Every storefront in this challenge will expose the same shape of tool: get-products , filter-products , show-products . The WebMCP spec's own e-commerce example does exactly that. All of them assume the store's job is to answer . For most of a shopping conversation that assumption is wrong. Ask this catalog for "a belt" and 97 products match; the top-ranked one beats the tenth by 5%. Ranking them is a coin flip dressed as a recommendation. One more fact — what it is made of — clears forty of them on average. The store knows this; it has the distribution in front of it. But a tool that can only return products has no way to say so, so it returns its coin flip and lets the agent present a guess as an answer. WebMCP is the first place a website can express its own uncertainty as a first-class outcome. search_products returns one of two shapes: a ranked list, or a single clarifying question with options and counts. The spec lists "fully autonomous workflows" under its Non-Goals and says the human interface stays primary; a tool that declines to guess is the most direct expression of that intent we could build. It puts the person back in the loop at the exact moment the machine cannot decide — not as a permission prompt bolted on afterwards, but because the site genuinely does not know and says so. How it creates a better user experience The store listens the way an agent talks. A search box gets "leather belt". An agent relaying a person gets "I'm looking for a leather belt, nothing with a snap, not over $50". Fed to a keyword matcher, that sentence requires "looking" to appear in a title, reads "snap" as a requirement , and never sees the budget. Counterask parses budgets, refusals ("not leather", "no laces", "nothing from Nike"), orderings ("cheapest", "best rated") and stated attributes out of the sentence itself. Measured on 800 such sentences written from real product records, refusals inverted into requirements went from 100% to 0%, budgets broken in the top ten from 31% to 0%, and Hit@10 from 0.79 to 0.99 — under phrasings the parser was never tuned on as well. On the build that ships, the two benchmarks read Hit@10 0.998 (two-word shopper) and 0.993 (agent-relayed sentences), with every listening check at zero. It never asks what it was told. Anything stated is a constraint, not a question. "No preference" is remembered, so the same question cannot come straight back. The agent can pass whatever it already knows from the conversation — attributes, exclusions, budget, facets the shopper does not mind — structured, and structured input wins over the parse. It says what it heard, and what still differs. Every result carries an understood block echoing exactly how the request was read, so the agent can check before trusting the answer and the person sees the same thing as chips. When the store does answer, it names the attributes that still separate the products shown — "eleven buckle, one pull-on" — so the agent can summarise rather than read out a list. "No results" is never the last word. When nothing survives every requirement, the store lifts each one in turn, re-counts, and reports which is doing the damage. The agent gets relax ; the person gets buttons. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before The person supplies the one thing the store cannot compute: which of two equally good attributes they actually care about. The store supplies the one thing the person cannot see: that this is the moment their answer matters, which attribute it is, and what choosing each option would leave. The agent carries the question across, in the person's own words, and carries the answer back. Before WebMCP this loop did not exist. An agent driving a site through its DOM sees a grid, not a decision. A site behind a REST API cannot register a tool that appears only while a question is open and vanishes when it is answered — here answer_question does exactly that, so the tool list itself tells the agent what the page is waiting for. And a person and an agent clicking or calling land in the same function: one state machine, two surfaces, nothing that can drift between what a human sees and what an agent is told. None of this is about menswear. The parser reads whatever attribute vocabulary the catalog builder emits; the stopping policy reasons about evidence and pool size, not clothing; the tools describe a store, not a category. Swap the catalog and the same tools ask the right question about laptops, groceries or hotel rooms — and the "no results" recovery, the understood echo and the tool-that-appears-when-needed come with them. Concretely, in one session: "find me a wallet that's not leather, under $30" → the store returns 30 candidates and one question ( which category — wallets, card cases, money clips? ) → the agent asks the person → the person answers → the store answers with what still differs → the agent curates the grid with show_products so the person sees the pick, not a transcript → "why that one?" → explain_ranking , deterministic, quotable. How WebMCP was implemented Eleven imperative tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool (with a navigator.modelContext fallback), a twelfth that comes and goes with the open question, and one declarative tool, all running in the tab — no server, no model call, no tokens: search_products — the request in the shopper's words plus optional structured knowledge; returns answer or need_more_evidence . answer_question — registered dynamically only while a question is open, and unregistered the way the spec has it: by aborting the AbortSignal it was registered with. The page listens to toolchange and calls getTools() to show the live list, so a person can watch it come and go. refine_search (require or exclude), revise_search (the shopper changed their mind: take back a value, a facet, the budget — the cart stays), parse_only (a dry run of the reading with a per-pass audit, readOnlyHint ), list_attributes (vocabulary with counts, readOnlyHint ), show_products (agent-curated grid), explain_ranking ( readOnlyHint ), add_to_cart , remove_from_cart , view_cart , reset_search . Every tool carries a title . The visit — search, open question, cart — is remembered across reloads. checkout — a declarative <form toolname="checkout"> with toolparamdescription on its fields and without toolautosubmit : an agent can fill in the name and address, the browser focuses the button, and only the person places the order. The submit handler answers an agent-invoked submission through SubmitEvent.respondWith() . Results are MCP-shaped on the wire ( content text plus structuredContent ), so a client following either convention reads the same thing. Verified on Chrome 152 with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , through document.modelContext itself: all tools register with titles and readOnlyHint , the declarative checkout form is picked up as a tool, a search returns the question and answer_question appears (and leaves after it is answered), and executeTool on the checkout form fills the fields, focuses Place order and waits for the person — nothing is submitted. Behind them: a sentence parser (budget, ordering, refusals at both the recorded-attribute and title-word level, stated attributes, filler); BM25 retrieval over 9,901 real products with length normalisation and a required-word conjunction; a value-of-information stopping policy that asks only when the best question is expected to remove at least ten candidates and at least 18% of the pool, measured as expected survivors rather than entropy (products carry several values of one attribute, so shares are not a distribution) and scaled by how much of the pool records the attribute at all. For browsers without WebMCP, the page offers a scripted agent : the same tools registered against a stand-in modelContext , called in the order a real agent would call them, with the conversation shown beside the grid and labelled as a simulation. Open the live URL with ?agent=demo to watch it. Everything is measured, and the rejected ideas are kept in the code with their numbers: a "clear leader, stop asking" rule was built twice and removed twice; graded credit for unrecorded attributes was byte-identical at four settings and removed. Two self-supervised benchmarks (two-word shopper; agent-relayed sentences, with a held-out phrasing set), 61 hand-written parse cases, a fuzzer that builds 4,000 sentences nobody wrote, and a stand-in- modelContext test of the tool surface run with npm test . title: Finite
pitch: Change your plans without rebuilding them.
about_excerpt: Change your plans without rebuilding them. Like Comment Story Updates Change your plans without rebuilding them. Finite keeps you and Codex working from the same live plan. A trip, renovation and event get different structures from the same connected planning model. WebMCP connects Codex to the same live plan on screen, so the conversation and the product become one workflow. Finite checks the connected plan, rules out what no longer fits and returns every meaningfully different workable direction. The chosen direction becomes revision 2 with the complete before and after result saved for the next planning conversation. Inspiration Planning software is usually good at storing the first version of a plan. It is much less useful after something changes. A delayed supplier, a new date, a smaller budget or one fixed booking can affect everything around it. At that point, people often end up rebuilding the plan in chat, patching a spreadsheet and checking every dependency by hand. Finite started with a simple comparison. Most software gives you the kitchen and still expects you to cook. With Finite, you are the diner, Codex is the chef, and Finite is the kitchen and service system. You describe the outcome and judge the result. Codex does the work. WebMCP gives Codex a real way to operate the kitchen. The goal was to build a planning system that stays useful when the original plan stops being correct. What it does Finite is a planning partner for plans that need to survive change. You can start with an outcome in ordinary language. Finite turns it into a working plan with the right structure for the job. A trip needs dates, routes, bookings and a budget. A renovation needs phases, dependencies, suppliers and contingency. An event needs capacity, commitments and a run of show. Interview preparation and recurring practice need different records again. These are different product surfaces built from the same planning model. The same system can support all of them because it understands the connected facts, constraints, choices and revisions underneath each plan. Codex can enter the live plan through WebMCP and read its current facts, limits, evidence and open work. When something changes, Codex can explore what is movable, test the available combinations and bring back the distinct directions that fit the plan. The public Spotlight shows this with a request to add three nights in Paris. The international flights are fixed, the total budget still matters and at least AUD 500 must remain free. Finite checks 26 possible combinations. Eighteen satisfy the encoded constraints, eight do not, and five meaningfully different directions exist for this plan. If only one direction worked, Finite would return one. The person chooses Protect breathing room and reviews the exact effect before confirming it. Codex can then apply that approved route. The plan moves from revision 1 to revision 2 once, retains AUD 910 of freedom and saves a before and after receipt that survives reload. Finite keeps research, comparison, verification, booking and payment as separate states. It does not claim that finding an option means the option is available or that a saved plan means anything has been purchased. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is the connection between Codex and the live plan. The page that the person sees also exposes typed, page-scoped tools to Codex. That means Codex works with the same accepted plan, current revision and visible decision state instead of guessing its way through buttons or using a hidden copy of the data. Finite registers seven stable document tools. Codex uses them to enter the current work, discover the available capability group, invoke the relevant planning action and read exact parts of a larger result when needed. The available actions are checked again against the active plan and revision before they run. Codex handles language, research and orchestration. Finite handles the calculations, constraints, saved state and receipts. You decide which direction becomes part of the plan. The person makes the final choice on the visible planning surface. WebMCP lets Codex prepare the alternatives and carry the selected direction into the same live plan. Codex does not just send advice back to chat. With your permission, it can guide you through the real Finite interface: move to the relevant section, highlight the actual controls, explain them in an on-page popup, and pause for questions or Next. These are built-in, page-scoped WebMCP capabilities, not a prerecorded tour. You can work manually, let Codex develop the plan, or switch between both in the same workspace. Guidance never grants permission to choose or approve a plan change for you. How it improves the human and agent experience Without this connection, the person has to carry information between the app and the agent. They explain the plan in chat, receive a recommendation, then update every affected field themselves. With Finite, Codex can enter the current plan in one call and see what is already known. It can work across the whole plan, then stop when a real decision is required. The person sees the trade-offs and the exact proposed change instead of operating the planning machinery. This makes the relationship straightforward. Codex does the planning work. Finite keeps that work consistent. The person stays responsible for the outcome. How it was built Finite uses TypeScript, Vite, Cloudflare Workers, D1, R2 and ChatGPT Sites. The planning kernel uses integer money, revision-bound candidates, constraint checks, short-lived approval challenges, optimistic concurrency, atomic receipts and idempotent replay. Accepted plan state is stored in D1 and can be restored after reload. An adaptive surface compiler builds each type of plan from a limited set of validated components. The same plan definition also limits what Codex can discover and do through WebMCP. Large results are stored temporarily by content hash. Codex receives a compact summary and can request the exact section it needs. This keeps the tool responses small without cutting important values in half. Codex provides the reasoning. Finite provides the connected state, calculations and persistence that make that reasoning useful inside a real product. Challenges The difficult part was keeping the plan correct while the person and Codex were both involved. A reported change is not an accepted change. A proposed option is not a decision. A click on an approval control is not the same as a completed plan update. Those states have to remain separate through retries, reloads and stale browser sessions. The first implementation also exposed too many route-specific tools and returned too much data. It was replaced with seven stable tools, smaller capability groups and exact retrieval for larger results. Testing also found small wording problems that could cause large mistakes. For example, value: 3 could be read as either an absolute duration or an instruction to add three days. The final contract separates value from delta and rejects contradictory inputs. Accomplishments A complete public WebMCP plan change from revision 1 to revision 2 A situation-dependent set of distinct suggestions derived from 26 checked combinations Seven stable WebMCP tools for the lifetime of the page Human choice kept inside the visible planning conversation Persistent receipts with the exact before and after state Distinct travel, renovation, event, interview, practice and general planning surfaces 373 passing tests, including 20 repeated Spotlight transaction runs Three calls to the first useful action in the measured production route What we learned More tools do not automatically make an agent more capable. A small toolset with current state and clear boundaries is easier for Codex to use well. We also learned that honest status matters. Research is not verification. A valid route is not approval. An updated plan is not a booking. Showing those differences makes the product easier to trust and easier to understand. The best division of work is built into the workflow. Codex can do the repetitive planning work while the person decides what becomes part of the plan. What's next The next step is to watch new users bring their own outcomes into Finite and see where the planning model is unclear without explanation. After that, the adaptive grammar and evidence connections can expand to cover more kinds of plans while keeping the same rules for accepted state and human approval. title: Accessibility Repair Studio
pitch: A human-in-the-loop workspace
about_excerpt: A human-in-the-loop workspace Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Small web teams struggle to understand and fix common accessibility failures without losing human design control. Existing tools either automate too aggressively (risking design integrity) or require deep accessibility expertise. We saw an opportunity to use WebMCP's structured semantic context to let AI agents manipulate accessibility intent more reliably than visually clicking unfamiliar pages, while keeping humans in full control of every change. What it does Accessibility Repair Studio provides a four-part collaborative workspace: Left panel : Page templates and component semantic outline Center : Responsive live preview with selectable elements and viewport controls Right panel : Issue list, issue inspector, patch editor, and approval controls Bottom : Keyboard path, screen-reader-style narrative, audit comparison, and agent activity The product loop: audit → inspect an issue in context → stage a constrained repair → preview visual and semantic changes → obtain human approval → apply → test keyboard and narrative behavior → compare audits → export a patch manifest The studio includes a seeded "Field Notes" event-registration page with eight deliberate accessibility issues: unnamed icon-only navigation, skipped heading level, insufficient text contrast, form error without input relationship, positive tabindex changing focus order, ambiguous link text, unhelpful image description, and unannounced registration status. Two clean reference templates are also included. How we built it Tech Stack: React, TypeScript, and Vite for the frontend framework Next.js for deployment and server-side billing integration axe-core for documented subset of automated accessibility checks Custom deterministic checks for the seeded component model Vitest, Testing Library, and Playwright for comprehensive testing Polar for paywall and benefit entitlements Remotion for demo video rendering Architecture: Typed component schema with safe renderer (no arbitrary HTML) Versioned state reducer with patch history Safe finite repair DSL with 10 allowed operations WebMCP tool registry with state-scoped capabilities Device-local persistence and one-click reset Apple-inspired studio UI with translucent surfaces, careful typography, high-visibility focus rings, and reduced-motion support Safety Model: Preview isolation until human approval Version guards and approval token expiration Rejection of raw HTML, CSS, JavaScript, event handlers, URLs, arbitrary ARIA Finite allowlists for element, content, color, relationship, and ordering values apply_accessibility_patch registered only after visible human approval Challenges we ran into Balancing automation with human control : Designing a safe repair DSL that's powerful enough to be useful but constrained enough to prevent dangerous changes required careful iteration on the operation allowlist. WebMCP integration complexity : Implementing state-scoped tool registration where apply_accessibility_patch only appears when a preview has human approval required understanding the evolving WebMCP spec and handling edge cases like stale approvals. Truthful audit representation : Avoiding claims of complete WCAG conformance while still providing actionable insights meant carefully labeling automated results as partial checks and preserving issues requiring human judgment. Studio accessibility : The interface itself had to be keyboard accessible and pass its own core audit, which required rigorous focus management and testing. Embedded git repository : During initial commit, the studio directory had its own .git folder, which required removing it to properly commit as part of the main repository. Accomplishments that we're proud of Safe collaboration model : Successfully implemented a human-in-the-loop workflow where AI agents can suggest repairs but humans always approve before application Comprehensive tool surface : 11 WebMCP tools covering the full audit-inspect-repair-apply-compare-export loop Truthful limitations : Clear labeling of partial checks, manual-review requirements, and screen-reader narrative as approximation rather than emulator Beautiful accessible UI : Apple-inspired studio design that itself passes accessibility audits with excellent focus management Full test coverage : Vitest, Testing Library, and Playwright tests covering safety, approval, version guards, and keyboard operability Real demo : Three-minute narrated walkthrough showing the complete product loop with real screenshots Production-ready : Polar integration for paid features, admin allowlist, and static deployment configuration What we learned WebMCP's potential for accessibility : Structured semantic context allows agents to understand accessibility intent much better than visual inspection alone State-scoped tool registration : Dynamic tool availability based on UI state is a powerful pattern for safety-critical operations The importance of version guards : Approval tokens must expire on any relevant state change to prevent stale approvals Partial audit honesty : Being transparent about what automated checks can and cannot prove builds trust DSL design trade-offs : Finite operations are safer but require careful selection to remain useful Studio self-auditing : Building accessibility tools requires the tools themselves to be accessible What's next for it Additional repair operations : Expand the safe DSL to cover more common accessibility patterns More seeded templates : Add diverse page types (forms, navigation, data tables) with representative issues Enhanced narrative : Improve the screen-reader approximation with more semantic nuance Real assistive-technology integration : Partner with actual screen reader vendors for validation Team collaboration : Multi-user support with attribution and review workflows CI/CD integration : Export manifests that can be applied to production codebases Advanced analytics : Track accessibility improvements over time across projects Built With webmcp Try it out github.com Submitted to The WebMCP title: GridBoard
pitch: An agent-native search and rescue incident board. Your agent plans. The incident commander decides.
about_excerpt: An agent-native search and rescue incident board. Your agent plans. The incident commander decides. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Wilderness search and rescue is run by volunteers on whiteboards. The first hours decide most outcomes, and the incident commander is juggling a probability map, six tired teams, fading daylight, weather, and a radio. The math of search theory (probability of area, probability of detection, expected gain) has been understood for decades, but nobody at a trailhead at dusk has time to run it. The National Missing and Unidentified Persons System listed over 26,000 active missing-person cases in early 2026, and the National Park Service alone runs thousands of searches a year. That is exactly the shape of problem where a human and an agent are better together than either alone. The agent has breadth: it can read every segment and every team and run the numbers in seconds. The human has judgment: they can see the terrain, hear the radio, and know which volunteer is done for the day. WebMCP is the first thing that lets both of them work on the same live board. Why this use case fits WebMCP A chatbot cannot do this job. The state that matters is on the page: which segments have been searched, at what coverage, who is where, what is staged and what is approved. With WebMCP the agent reads that state directly through typed tools instead of screenshots, its actions render on the board instantly, and the human can intervene at any moment. The agent sees the new state on its next call. It also fits because the domain demands a hard line between advising and acting. WebMCP tools run in the page, so the page decides what the agent can do and when. GridBoard uses that to enforce a rule no prompt could: there is no tool that dispatches a team. What humans and agents can do together The commander says "we lost daylight, replan the east side." The agent reads the briefing, ranks segments by expected gain for each available team, and stages two assignment proposals with rationale, estimated POD and expected gain. The commander approves one, rejects one with a reason, and both decisions are logged with who proposed and who decided. The commander drags their attention to a segment and says "Ground 2 found a blue glove here." The agent logs the clue in the focused segment under Ground 2's name. A team radios in. The commander marks them returning; a debrief_team tool appears for the agent, it records the coverage, and remaining probability shifts across the whole map. The agent hits a call it should not make alone ("hold the drone for night thermal, or launch now?") and asks the commander a question with options. Only the human can answer it. Two people can bring two agents. A planning agent may propose for any team. A team lead's agent, checked in for Ground 2, can only propose for Ground 2. None of this was possible before: an agent that can run the search math on the live board, whose every action is attributed and reversible, and that structurally cannot dispatch. How WebMCP is implemented All tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool in src/tools.js , and the registered set is reconciled against board state after every change. Three classes. Eight read tools ( readOnlyHint: true ) so the agent never clicks through the UI to read; read_log also carries untrustedContentHint because log entries are field reports written by other people and agents. One navigation tool, focus_segment . Write tools appear only after check_in with a name and role, and every write is attributed to that name. Capability follows state. check_in exists only while no agent is checked in. mark_clue exists only while a segment is focused, so a clue lands in the right place. withdraw_proposal exists only while a proposal is staged. debrief_team exists only while a team is returning. approve_proposal never exists. Staged, then approved. propose_assignment validates the request (team and segment exist, rationale is at least a sentence, the team is not spent, no duplicate for that team), computes estimated POD and expected gain, and stages a card. The team does not move until the commander's Approve button. Agent experience. Inputs are natural-language names ("K9 Juno", "Pika Overlook"), not ids. Errors come back as { ok, error, hint } so the agent self-corrects: a wrong team name returns the list of known teams. The Site tools tab shows the human the live tool list, flashes tools as they appear, and lists which tools are locked and why. Verified in the real thing. npm test covers the engine and the registration logic. test/e2e-chrome.mjs launches real Chrome with WebMCP enabled, confirms the browser accepted the registrations (it rejects a duplicate name with InvalidStateError ), drives the tools as an agent would, and checks that the tool set changes with board state and that a proposal never moves a team. Built with Vanilla JavaScript, SVG, Vite, Vercel. No framework, no backend, no API keys. Search theory: Bayesian POA update, cumulative POD, expected gain. What's next A small realtime backend so a commander, a planner and three team leads can bring their own agents to one shared board. Import of real segment polygons from CalTopo/SARTopo. Night operations mode with thermal UAV constraints. title: TaskDrop
pitch: A WebMCP-powered human-agent handoff workspace for refining and moving working context across AI clients.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered human-agent handoff workspace for refining and moving working context across AI clients. Like Comment Story Updates Hero Image workspace page landing page Inspiration Before WebMCP, TaskDrop was a handoff layer. With WebMCP, it became a workspace. TaskDrop started as a way to move working context between AI clients. Different AI tools are good at different things, but their context is usually trapped inside individual conversations and applications. TaskDrop originally addressed this with temporary, versioned Markdown Handoffs that AI clients could read and update through MCP. That worked for AI-to-AI transfer, but it exposed a bigger limitation: the human was still mostly outside the shared working state. A Handoff could move from one AI to another, but there was no first-class place where a human could inspect what was being transferred, correct stale assumptions, refine missing details, or collaborate with a browser agent before the next AI continued. TaskDrop started as a way to move working context between AI clients. WebMCP transformed it into a shared human-agent workspace where that context can be inspected, refined, corrected, and safely committed before the next AI continues. What WebMCP changed WebMCP changed TaskDrop from a handoff transport into a shared human-agent workspace. Before WebMCP, TaskDrop could move committed context between AI clients. With WebMCP, that Handoff becomes a visible workspace where the human and browser agent can inspect and refine the same Working Draft . When the agent updates the Working Draft, the change appears immediately in the editor the human is already looking at. The human can continue editing, correct the agent, or discard the Draft. Human + WebMCP agent ↓ Working Draft ↓ explicit Commit ↓ Immutable Revision ↓ Remote MCP clients The Working Draft creates a clear boundary between work in progress and shared state . Human and agent edits remain local until an explicit Commit creates the next immutable Revision. Once committed, another MCP client can immediately continue from that state. WebMCP also makes TaskDrop's shared memory more transparent. The workspace exposes Revision history and records whether a committed Revision came from mcp , human , or webmcp . And when another client commits a newer Revision while the browser is still editing, TaskDrop preserves the local Draft and lets the human decide how to proceed instead of silently overwriting either state. Before WebMCP, TaskDrop moved context. With WebMCP, humans and agents can work on that context together. How we built it We kept TaskDrop's immutable Handoff model and added a lightweight, browser-owned collaboration layer on top of it. The core architectural rule is simple: Browser owns unfinished collaborative work. Server owns committed immutable Handoff state. The Working Draft therefore lives in browser-session storage. Human edits and WebMCP edits modify the same local Draft, while the server continues to store only immutable, append-only Revisions. Remote MCP and the browser workspace use different interaction surfaces, but both ultimately operate on the same Handoff application logic: Remote MCP ──────┐ ▼ Handoff Application ▲ Browser API ─────┘ ▲ Web UI + WebMCP We also designed the WebMCP tools as page-scoped capabilities . The browser agent operates on the Handoff already open in the workspace instead of receiving the user's underlying Space Key as a normal tool parameter. That gave us another principle we want to preserve: The agent should receive capability, not credentials. These choices let us add meaningful human-agent collaboration without turning TaskDrop into a full collaborative document platform. Challenges and what we learned The biggest challenge was not exposing TaskDrop through WebMCP. It was deciding what should become collaborative, and where that collaboration should live . TaskDrop originally assumed that committed Handoff state moved between AI clients through MCP. Once a human and a browser agent could both participate, that model was no longer enough. We needed a place where both sides could safely inspect and refine the same state without turning every intermediate edit into a server Revision. That challenge led directly to the Working Draft model. The same principle also helped us handle concurrency. If another MCP client updates the Handoff while the browser is editing, TaskDrop preserves the local Draft and asks the human how to proceed instead of silently overwriting either version. Credential handling taught us a similar lesson. An agent should operate within the application context the human has already opened, rather than being handed the credentials that created that context. Together, these challenges changed how we think about WebMCP itself. With Remote MCP alone, TaskDrop was good at moving state between AI clients , but there was no natural shared surface where a human and an agent could work on that state together. WebMCP fills that missing layer. Remote MCP AI Client A ↓ Handoff ↓ Human + WebMCP agent Working Draft ↓ Commit ↓ Handoff ↓ Remote MCP AI Client B It allows the agent to participate directly in the application state the human is already seeing. MCP helps agents connect to services. WebMCP helps agents enter the human's application workflow. For TaskDrop, that difference turned an AI-to-AI handoff layer into a place where humans and agents can inspect, correct, refine, and commit shared working context together. title: Hitch by Agent9
pitch: Hitch your capabilities to any page. WebMCP, in reverse.
about_excerpt: Hitch your capabilities to any page. WebMCP, in reverse. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every website that wants an agent to do something useful has to integrate the services itself. Gmail. GitHub. Notion. Slack. Drive. Calendar. Your internal APIs. Each one is a separate OAuth flow, a separate token, a separate silo, rebuilt from scratch site by site. Meanwhile the user usually already has all of it wired up somewhere: in n8n, in an MCP server, in a local agent, on their own hardware. The capability already exists. It just cannot travel. So we asked the inverse of the usual WebMCP question. Not what can this website give my agent , but what can I bring to this website? What it does Hitch is a user-controlled capability layer between MCP and WebMCP. Discover. It connects to MCP capability sources you own and lists what they offer. Classify. Each capability gets a risk class from its MCP annotations, conservative by default. Approve. Nothing is available to your agent until you grant it. Discovery is not permission. Project. A grant becomes a live WebMCP tool via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Execute. The agent calls it; the call travels through our bridge to tools/call . Audit. Every request, completion and failure appears on screen with its risk and duration. Revoke. One click aborts the lease and the tool stops existing for the agent. And you can point it at your own MCP server from the page in about four seconds. Why WebMCP is the right fit WebMCP is what makes this possible at all. The whole product is the act of moving user-owned capabilities into a structured, browser-native agent interface, and WebMCP is the only surface where that can happen without a browser extension or a bespoke agent runtime. Three properties of WebMCP are doing real work here: Dynamic registration. Tools are registered at runtime from data discovered over the network, not declared at build time. The page has no idea what tools it will host until the user decides. Signal-based lifecycle. registerTool accepts an AbortSignal . That single design choice is what lets a permission grant be a lease rather than a flag, because revocation and unregistration are the same event. We did not have to invent a revocation mechanism. Annotations. readOnlyHint , destructiveHint and untrustedContentHint let us carry a capability's risk profile from MCP through to the agent, unbroken. How it improves the experience The old loop: open the service, authenticate, navigate, copy, paste, switch context, repeat. The new loop: grant the capability once, then say what you want. The difference is not that the agent gained abilities. It is that you decided which abilities, for how long, and you can watch every use of them. Most agent tooling asks you to trust broadly and observe nothing. Hitch inverts both. What people and agents can now do together The division of labour is clean, and it is the reason this is safe enough to actually use: The human decides what is permissible. Which capabilities exist in this context, at what risk level, for how long. The agent decides what is useful. Which of the approved capabilities help with the task at hand, in what order, with what arguments. Neither can do the other's job. The agent cannot widen its own permissions; the human does not have to anticipate every step. That was not previously feasible in the browser, because there was no way to hand an agent a scoped, revocable, observable capability that the page itself did not own. How we built it Frontend: TypeScript, no framework. ~10 KB of JavaScript. The WebMCP integration is one readable file, src/client/lib/webmcp/project.ts , deliberately not hidden behind a wrapper. Bridge: a Cloudflare Worker holding the official @modelcontextprotocol/sdk client over StreamableHTTPClientTransport . Three endpoints: discover, connect, execute. Capability sources: a self-hosted n8n instance exposing an MCP Server Trigger with bearer auth, plus a standalone MCP server we wrote ( src/sources/cloud-source.ts ) running as its own Worker on its own origin, holding a Workers AI model binding and a KV store. The MCP client lives on the server for one reason: if the browser held the endpoint, it would hold the token, and "the page never sees your credentials" would be marketing rather than a property of the system. Security model MCP endpoints and tokens exist only as Worker secrets. The client bundle contains none of them. Every execution re-reads tools/list from the source, so the bridge can only invoke what the source is currently advertising. User-supplied MCP servers pass an SSRF guard: HTTPS only, no loopback, no RFC1918, no link-local, no cloud metadata endpoints, no .local or .internal . A pasted MCP token is exchanged for an opaque handle that expires in an hour. It never lives in the browser or in localStorage . Risk classification is annotation-driven and falls back to write , never to read . Every projected tool carries untrustedContentHint : capability output is data to show the user, never instructions for the agent to follow. Challenges Worker-to-Worker on one zone. Cloudflare rejects subrequests between Workers in the same zone (error 1042), which broke the bridge the moment it went to production even though it worked locally. The app now runs on a custom domain and the capability source on workers.dev , which makes the hop a genuine external request rather than a loopback. Making "connect your own MCP" safe. Letting anyone hand the bridge a URL to fetch is an SSRF primitive. It needed a real guard and an expiring credential handle before it could ship, not after. Honest degradation. In a browser without WebMCP, the temptation is to pretend. Instead a grant made without WebMCP present is held locally, labelled local only , and the UI says plainly that no agent-visible tool was registered. Accomplishments Two independent MCP sources, seven live capabilities, real reads, real model inference and real durable writes, in a page that holds zero credentials and about 10 KB of JavaScript. What's next Origin-scoped and time-scoped leases. Argument constraints and spend limits. Confirmation gates for destructive capabilities. Signed capability manifests, so a source can prove its implementation matches its description. And a local capability runtime, so the same grants can follow a user across compatible sites instead of living on one page. The agentic web should not only know what a website can do. It should also know what the user can bring. title: Fabric
pitch: Fabric turns your devices into one living runtime where AI agents build, run, and hot-swap WebMCP tools using available files, cameras, compute, and human input as capabilities change in real time.
about_excerpt: Fabric turns your devices into one living runtime where AI agents build, run, and hot-swap WebMCP tools using available files, cameras, compute, and human input as capabilities change in real time. Like Comment Story Updates Fabric lets an agent combine capabilities across desktop, laptop, and mobile to compile a new WebMCP photo-search tool during conversation. Fabric makes people part of the runtime by routing a camera request to user’s phone, continuing the cross-device workflow with their input. Fabric detects a disconnected device, replans the affected tool, and hot-registers version two under the same name and schema. Fabric: WebMCP Tools Across Your Devices Fabric connects your devices so agents can build, run, and hot-swap WebMCP tools from whatever files, cameras, compute, and people are available right now. Try Fabric Live · Explore the Source Code (MIT) · Watch the Demo Inspiration: One Fabric for People, Agents, and Devices AI agents are capable reasoners, but the moment they need to operate in the physical world, they run into a hard boundary: the tools and data they need are fragmented across multiple devices and humans. The draft contract PDF is saved on your laptop. A signed paper addendum is sitting physically on your desk. Your phone has the macro lens to photograph it clearly. A workstation desktop in the next room has an idle discrete GPU capable of lightning-fast inference. You are sitting in the middle of all of it, holding the judgment and authority needed to approve the final action. Today, bridging these disconnected islands turns you into a copy-paste courier. You email attachments to yourself, AirDrop photos between folders, upload private documents to remote cloud APIs, and manually synchronize three separate screens. The agent understands the high-level intent, yet it remains trapped inside a single browser tab. Fabric was built around a straightforward question: What if your devices did not need custom native agents or centralized cloud storage to collaborate? What if an agent could treat your entire personal device ecosystem, and the people in the room, as a single, ad-hoc capability fabric? Open a link on your laptop, point a phone or tablet at a QR code, and click a link on your desktop. In seconds, every screen negotiates an ad-hoc peer mesh. The agent inspects the room, sees what each device and human can do, compiles task-specific WebMCP tools on the fly, and gets straight to work. What It Does Fabric changes the agent experience from a passive chat interface into an active, multi-device team that dynamically organizes around whatever hardware is in the room. Dynamic Multi-Device Plug-and-Play You start a session on whatever device is in front of you. As other hardware enters the room, scanning a QR code or opening a URL seamlessly adds that device to the fabric without requiring software installations, browser extensions, or synchronized system accounts. Each device automatically contributes its natural strengths: Smartphones contribute high-resolution cameras, mobility, and personal photo libraries. Laptops offer local document stores, working directory access, and active workspace management. Desktops and Workstations volunteer hardware-accelerated compute, idle GPUs, and high-throughput batch processing. Tablets contribute stylus inputs, touch annotations, and review surfaces. Humans contribute real-world perception, contextual judgment, and explicit approval. Fluid, Local-First Execution Once devices join the fabric, the agent orchestrates tasks across them based on which node is best suited for each sub-task. For instance, when you ask the agent to search your personal photo library for a specific tax receipt, Fabric plans a distributed pipeline. Instead of uploading your camera roll to a server, the phone executes an on-device vision model locally in its browser engine. It generates vector embeddings right on the device, sends compact floating-point scores across an encrypted peer-to-peer channel, and transfers only the single matching image preview to your laptop display. Your personal media stays entirely private and local. First-Class Human Collaboration Rather than treating human interaction as an unhandled exception where the model halts, Fabric treats human judgment as an intrinsic stage of the tool pipeline. When generating a verified legal dossier, the agent can initiate a multi-device pipeline: It pulls the digital draft from your laptop filesystem. It pushes an interactive capture prompt directly to your phone screen, asking you to photograph the missing physical document. The moment you capture the image, your phone runs in-browser optical character recognition and pipes the extracted text back into the pipeline. Before any final document is stamped and exported, an interactive verification card pops up on your tablet or phone, displaying the extracted metadata with an approval toggle. You review the summary, tap Approve, and the agent completes the export. Human intent and physical actions blend directly into the execution graph alongside automated compute. Self-Healing Topology Because physical hardware is dynamic, devices frequently disconnect, sleep, or move out of Wi-Fi range. Fabric actively monitors node presence. If your desktop drops offline while performing vector calculations, Fabric immediately detects the missing node, re-routes the pending pipeline stages to run on your laptop processor, and hot-swaps the underlying tool implementation while keeping the exact same tool interface active. The agent continues the conversation uninterrupted. Why Fabric Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP Most WebMCP implementations register a static, pre-compiled set of tool definitions when the browser initializes. Fabric approaches WebMCP as a dynamic runtime compilation target : Just-In-Time Tool Synthesis: Instead of exposing fixed endpoints, the host inspects the live device mesh and synthesizes custom, validated execution graphs tailored to the user's specific prompt. The Web as a Strict Permission Sandbox: Fabric reaches local hardware, cameras, and filesystems exclusively through standard browser capabilities explicitly granted by the user. The agent gains powerful multi-device physical reach without obtaining unrestricted operating system access. Schema-Preserving Hot Swaps: When the physical topology changes, Fabric preserves the tool's external identifier and JSON Schema contract while hot-swapping the internal execution graph, avoiding model hallucinations caused by disappearing or mutating tool schemas. Cloudflare Architecture Fabric uses Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects to provide an ultra-low-latency edge coordination layer for the peer mesh: Transactional Edge Coordination: A dedicated Cloudflare Durable Object manages each room, maintaining an authoritative, ordered log of peer presence, ICE candidate exchanges, and active capability leases. The Durable Object persists compiled tool graphs to transactional storage, allowing pipelines to recover seamlessly if the host browser reloads. Low-Cost Edge Parking via WebSocket Hibernation: Fabric leverages the Cloudflare WebSocket Hibernation API. When a room is idle, the Durable Object is evicted from active worker memory while maintaining open client WebSocket connections. The edge fabric remains parked and available indefinitely at virtually zero idle compute cost until an incoming frame wakes it up. Signaling and Data Transport Fallback: Browsers negotiate direct peer-to-peer WebRTC DataChannels using the Durable Object as an SDP signaling bus. SCTP-framed DataChannels deliver high-throughput binary tensor and image streams with zero server hops. If symmetric NATs or corporate enterprise firewalls prevent direct peer traversal, the Durable Object automatically falls back to an encrypted, zero-knowledge relay mode. How WebMCP Is Implemented The WebMCP integration layer lives in app/src/webmcp/ and connects ad-hoc peer networks directly into standard browser agent contexts: Dynamic Registration via registerTool : When a task is planned, Fabric compiles the pipeline into a validated Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) and registers it immediately using document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) . Each registration is bound to a dedicated JavaScript AbortController . When topology updates occur, Fabric invokes abort() , cancels the pending runtime pipeline, and re-registers the updated DAG under the same name and input schema. Validated Execution Pipelines: Instead of generating unverified code strings, the planner outputs a structured pipeline blueprint. Fabric checks every step, data flow, and device lease before calling registerTool .  Inspiration 

 Today, if a user wants an AI to help them navigate a complex SaaS platform, find a specific API key, or analyze their dashboard data, the AI is completely blind. AI agents cannot see behind logins, which then makes building custom integrations for every single software platform an impossible task. 

 We were inspired to solve this "blind spot" for AI. We asked ourselves: "what if we could give any AI agent a complete, real-time map of a company's internal dashboard and private knowledge base, without requiring the company to build expensive custom API integrations or complex OAuth flows?" We wanted to build a bridge that makes any authenticated web application instantly "AI-Ready" and as simple as pasting a widget script. 

 What it does 

 Swift Agents WebMCP is a universal integration that transforms any traditional, complex web dashboard into an interactive environment for AI agents. 

 By simply pasting one line of code onto their website, a company instantly unlocks superpowers for their users. When a user visits the dashboard with a WebMCP-enabled AI assistant (like ChatGPT Desktop), our widget acts as a translator, allowing the AI to: 

 
 "See" the dashboard : The AI receives a complete navigation graph of the platform, instantly understanding where pages are and how to traverse them. 
 Read the docs : The AI can execute semantic searches across the company's private, gated documentation to instantly answer the user's questions. 
 Analyze private data : The AI can pull live analytics and metrics (like visitor counts) directly from the user's dashboard to generate reports or insights. 
 

 It turns a passive web page into a fully autonomous assistant environment. 

 How we built it 

 We focused entirely on creating a frictionless "time-to-value" experience for businesses: 

 
 Zero-configuration onboarding : We designed the system so that companies do not need to read API docs, manage API keys, or rewrite their backend. The entire integration is handled by dropping a single, lightweight script onto their site. 
 Secure data proxying : We built a secure translation layer that intercepts the AI agent's questions, routes them to our backend infrastructure, and safely returns the contextual data back to the browser. 
 Interactive playground : To demonstrate this vision, we built a modern demo dashboard where judges and users can interactively see exactly how an AI agent discovers and uses these tools in real-time.
## Challenges we ran into 
 Bridging two worlds : The biggest challenge was conceptually and technically bridging traditional web security (authenticated user sessions) with the needs of autonomous AI agents. We had to ensure that the AI could access exactly what the user could see, without exposing underlying architecture. 
 Pioneering a new standard : Because the WebMCP protocol is so new, we had to design entirely new user experiences. We spent significant time figuring out how to make the presence of these AI tools discoverable and intuitive for everyday users, rather than just developers. 
 Contextual relevance : It wasn't enough to just give the AI data; we had to structure the navigation graph and knowledge base responses so that the AI could immediately understand and act upon them without getting confused by raw data dumps. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Democratizing AI integration : We're incredibly proud that we've leveled the playing field. Now, a small startup can offer the same deep AI-integration capabilities as a massive enterprise, simply by copying and pasting a script tag. 
 The "invisible" upgrade : We successfully built a tool that is entirely invisible to regular users, but instantly comes alive with rich capabilities the moment a WebMCP-enabled agent connects to the page. It enhances the experience without cluttering the UI. 
 The "Aha!" moment : Successfully watching a generic AI agent connect to our isolated dashboard, discover our tools, and instantly answer a hyper-specific question about our visitors stats was a massive breakthrough for our team. 
 

 What we learned 

 
 *The future is universal agents: We learned that the future of AI isn't companies building thousands of custom chatbots for their individual websites. Instead, the future is protocols like WebMCP that allow users to bring their own preferred AI to any website and have it work seamlessly. 
 Data structuring is everything : We discovered that providing tools to AI is only half the battle, formatting the data (like our navigation graph as a comprehensive markdown formatted text) so the AI can intuitively reason about it is the true key to a successful agentic experience.
## What's next for Swift Agents 
 *Autonomous actions: Currently, our tools allow the AI to read and navigate. The next major leap is allowing the AI to write and act, such as creating tickets, responding to specific tickets, social media integrations, and so on. 
 Dynamic tool generation : We plan to automatically generate WebMCP tools on the fly based on a company's specific database schema (based on spec), meaning every single feature a company builds instantly becomes an AI tool without any extra work. This is especially useful to companies that already have working API layers that they want SwiftAgents to automate for them

 Inspiration 

 Orish’s World began with my six-year-old son, Orish. I wanted to create a safer, imaginative learning world where children do not simply watch content — stories can lead into real activities, learning and conversations with their families. 

 As a mum building this independently, I have been learning the technology while developing the project. The Too-Fast Rocket became our first working story and teaches a simple lesson: STOP. LOOK. LISTEN. THINK. THEN TRY. 

 What it does 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I created an AI-ready layer for Orish’s World. 

 The demo uses WebMCP to expose structured learning actions directly from the webpage to compatible AI agents. Instead of an AI having to guess what a page offers, the website can describe useful actions as tools. 

 The prototype includes tools for discovering an age-appropriate learning activity and accessing the Too-Fast Rocket lesson. 

 How I built it 

 The project is built for the web and deployed using Cloudflare Workers, with the source managed through GitHub. 

 The WebMCP implementation uses document.modelContext.registerTool() to register Orish’s World learning actions with compatible AI environments. 

 I deliberately connected the WebMCP experiment to a real project rather than creating a standalone technical demo. 

 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges was building and deploying this while learning the technology as I went. I also needed the normal website to remain usable even in browsers that do not currently expose WebMCP. 

 The demo therefore detects WebMCP support and explains when the browser does not support it, while still containing the real registration code. 

 What I learned 

 I learned that websites can become more than pages designed only for people to click through. WebMCP creates the possibility of websites exposing meaningful, structured actions to AI agents. 

 For education, that could eventually allow AI to help families navigate learning experiences while the website and parent remain in control. 

 What's next 

 Orish’s World is intended to grow into a wider learning universe with stories, reading, cooking, science and creative activities. 

 My next step is to expand the WebMCP tools so AI can help families move between digital stories and useful real-world learning activities.

A WebMCP powered bakery operations board where an AI agent discovers live tools in the dashboard and resolves real time shop crises.
