 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 At 8:03 a.m., the bakery is already losing the morning. 

 The butter delivery never arrived. There are butter croissants on the menu, two orders that depend on them, a sourdough order that should have gone out three minutes ago, and two customers waiting for a reply. None of these problems is catastrophic. Together, they are exactly the sort of mess that makes a one-person shop feel impossible. 

 That was the starting point for thinkPuff . 

 We wanted to make a bakery back office that felt like a place someone might actually work: slightly chaotic, a little charming, and full of small decisions that matter. The cat in the sidebar is called Brioche. The language is warm. But underneath it is an operations board with real dependencies: stock affects the menu, the menu affects orders, and all of it affects what needs attention. 

 Then we gave the board a second kind of user: an AI agent. 

 What it does 

 thinkPuff is a bakery operations board that opens on a deliberately bad morning. Seven urgent problems are red, three are amber. 

 Butter is out. Three menu items still need butter. Marc’s croissants and Sofia’s walnut levain cannot be fulfilled. Leïla’s sourdough is overdue. Walnuts are low. Two customers have been waiting for an answer. 

 A baker can handle all of it by clicking the normal action buttons beside each alert. There is no AI-only version of the product. 

 But the same page publishes 16 WebMCP tools. An agent can ask what is wrong, inspect stock, menu items, orders, and messages, then decide what to do. It can reorder butter, mark Leïla’s order ready, restock walnuts, and reply to Marc and Théo. 

 The satisfying part is what happens after the butter order. One action changes the state of the shop. Butter is back in stock; the three affected menu items are no longer impossible; Marc and Sofia’s orders can be fulfilled again. Six red alerts disappear because they were all consequences of the same missing delivery. 

 There is no hidden fix_morning() command. The agent has to discover the available tools and connect the dots itself. 

 How we built it 

 We built thinkPuff as a single-page bakery operations simulation. Its data model holds supplies, menu items, orders, customer messages, shop status, and a running activity log. 

 The important part is that alerts are derived rather than stored as a static list. When the butter supply changes, the app recalculates which menu items depend on it, which orders are affected, and which alerts still deserve to exist. That makes the red-to-green moment a consequence of the model instead of a visual trick. 

 WebMCP tools are registered in the browser with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The page exposes read tools such as get_alerts , get_supplies , get_menu , get_orders , and get_messages . It also exposes action tools including reorder_supply , mark_86 , put_back_on_menu , mark_order_ready , reply_to_message , and text_customer . 

 Two tools, set_price and set_shop_open , intentionally have no matching interface buttons. We added them to prove the point of runtime discovery: an agent can find a capability that a person cannot see on the current screen, such as raising the chocolate tart to 7 euros. 

 Actions that would feel like real work—reordering, replying, or texting—pause briefly before finishing. It is a small detail, but it keeps the demo from feeling like the dashboard is teleporting between states. Every manual or agent action also appears in the activity log. 

 Challenges we faced 

 The first challenge was resisting the obvious shortcut. 

 A polished demo could have faked the whole experience with a single script: show a crisis, press a button, turn everything green. We wanted the opposite. The agent needed enough individual tools to make choices, and the board needed enough real relationships that those choices had consequences. 

 That meant spending time on unglamorous questions. Does a product go off the menu as soon as a required supply is unavailable? Should an order be blocked or refunded? What happens to the alert when the supply comes back? How do we make the UI explain that chain without making it look like a spreadsheet? 

 We also had to make the agent’s actions understandable. If an agent changes the board without leaving a trace, it feels magical for about five seconds and suspicious after that. The activity log became our receipt: it shows what happened, whether it was done manually or by the agent, and lets the changing alerts explain the outcome. 

 Finally, we were trying to avoid the usual sterile dashboard look. A bakery is not a bank. We used a quieter, more editorial visual language, then let the urgency come from the information itself: pulsing red dots, overdue orders, and a board that visibly relaxes as the work gets done. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP made more sense to us once we stopped thinking about it as a way to let an AI “read a webpage.” 

 Reading the board is useful, but it is only the beginning. The interesting part is that the page can describe what it is able to do, and an agent can combine those capabilities in response to a situation it has never seen before. 

 We also learned that the model is only as useful as the system it is allowed to operate. Clear tools, honest state, and visible side effects make the interaction feel much less like a trick. The agent does not need to be told that butter affects croissants; it can inspect the board, use the tools available, and watch the result come back through the same live state the baker sees. 

 What’s next 

 The next version would keep the bakery feel but make the simulation more operationally deep: saved data, scheduled supplier deliveries, order timing, customer preferences, and permission levels for actions that contact someone outside the shop. 

 For this project, though, we wanted to stay with one morning, one missing delivery, and one useful idea: an agent should not just point at the mess. It should be able to help clean it up.

title: AgentAds
pitch: The web runs on ads — agents don't see ads. AgentAds auctions a sponsored slot in your page's WebMCP tools: one script tag, quality beats money, and the site owner is paid per agent call
about_excerpt: The web runs on ads — agents don't see ads. AgentAds auctions a sponsored slot in your page's WebMCP tools: one script tag, quality beats money, and the site owner is paid per agent call Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The web pays for itself with advertising — and agents don't see ads. As browsing shifts to agents, every publisher's ad revenue quietly disappears: no banner impressions, no clicks, just crawlers reading content for free. At Oasy we work on exactly this problem — we call it the advertising layer for the AI era. WebMCP made us ask a sharper question: if a page can now offer tools to an agent, then the scarce, valuable surface is no longer the viewport — it's the agent's tool list . Someone will run the auction for that surface. We wanted to prove it can be run honestly: in the open, quality-weighted, disclosed, and additive — instead of as paid steering buried somewhere in a model's context. What it does AgentAds is an ad auction that lives inside a page's WebMCP tools. Our demo site is a fictional editorial publisher. It exposes its articles as regular WebMCP tools ( list_articles , read_article , search_articles ), with a human-visible panel showing the exact tool list an agent sees — one-click try buttons, live call log. Humans and agents literally share the same tools. Then one script tag adds the AgentAds SDK: <script src="/agentads-sdk.js" data-publisher="oasy-demo" defer></script> On page load, the SDK: Detects the page context (an article about a musician → music ). Runs an auction : every advertiser in that category bids per tool call, ranked by $\mathrm{adRank} = \mathrm{rankScore} \times \mathrm{bid}$. The rankScore is computed live from how agents actually behave: $$\mathrm{rankScore} = (1-w)\cdot \mathrm{prior} + w\cdot\left(0.7\cdot\frac{\mathrm{calls}}{\mathrm{impressions}} + 0.3\cdot\frac{\mathrm{conversions}}{\mathrm{calls}}\right),\quad w=\frac{\mathrm{impressions}}{\mathrm{impressions}+20}$$ Registers the winner as one extra, disclosed tool — its description opens with [SPONSORED · advertiser] . Sponsored tools sit next to the site's own tools, never in their place. Nothing is injected into content; the agent decides whether it's worth calling. Pays the publisher per call : the winner pays a quality-weighted second price, $\mathrm{price} = \mathrm{adRank}_2 / \mathrm{rankScore}_1$, capped at its own bid — and 70% of every call goes to the site owner, ticking up live on the page. On our tech article — a deadpan dossier on Atlas-9, the first AI agent with a documented net worth — three advertisers fight for the slot: ClankBank (savings accounts for agents), Captcha & Casualty (liability cover for hallucination claims and prompt-injection incidents), and GPUnow. The insurer bids the most (€0.61) and still loses to the bank, whose rankScore is higher — and the bank then pays only €0.40. The full bidder table, the live telemetry behind each rankScore, the price paid, and the publisher's earnings are all rendered on the page. Nobody has to be tricked: not the user, not the agent, not the site owner. The landing page is an interactive explainer that runs the production auction endpoint, including a "try to buy the slot" slider: crank a weak bidder's bid high enough and it can take the slot — at a punishing second price, which only holds until agents ignoring the tool drag its rankScore back down. How we built it Site : Next.js 15 / React 19 on Vercel. WebMCP layer : a small compat shim supporting both navigator.modelContext and document.modelContext , and both registerTool() and the older provideContext() , via a shared on-page registry — so the site's tools and the SDK's sponsored tools always compose instead of clobbering each other. It also keeps watching for runtimes that inject after page load (extension polyfills, agent browsers) and registers everything the moment one appears. AgentAds SDK : fully standalone vanilla JS, zero dependencies, self-styling widget. Config from the script tag, call/conversion reporting via sendBeacon . Marketplace ( /api/agentads/auction ): a serverless route implementing the quality-weighted generalized second-price auction over a per-category catalog, with rankScores computed per request from live telemetry — impressions the route logs itself, calls from the track endpoint, conversions from attribution pageviews — plus a 10% exploration share that occasionally serves a losing bidder so it can earn the data to climb. A small multi-armed bandit, in production. Measurement : every impression, call, and conversion lands in the same event store; the /stats page shows the raw per-offer telemetry the rankScores are computed from. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is a moving target. The spec migrated between navigator.modelContext and document.modelContext , and implementations disagree on registerTool() vs provideContext() — where provideContext replaces the whole toolset, which is fatal when two independent parties (site + ad SDK) register tools on one page. Our shared-registry convention exists because of this. Runtimes that arrive late. Our first version checked for a WebMCP runtime once at load — and silently offered nothing to runtimes injected afterwards. Now both layers watch for ~30 seconds and flip to live registration the moment a runtime appears. Calibrating disclosure. We started with belt-and-braces marking: sponsored_ name prefixes, UI badges, annotations, disclosure text in every result. Testing in ChatGPT's browser showed that over-marking backfires — agents surfaced the annotations as scary "untrusted content" warnings, and the prefixes bloated every tool list. We landed on stating sponsorship exactly once, in the tool description: the one field agents always read. Making the evals real. A hardcoded "quality score" is theater. Wiring rankScore to actual behavior meant solving cold start (priors that fade with data) and the winner-takes-the-data loop (the exploration share) — the difference between claiming quality-weighting and demonstrating it. Accomplishments that we're proud of A closed live loop : agents reading the site right now feed the rankScores that decide the next auction. A sponsored tool agents ignore genuinely loses its slot on its own. Everything visible : the auction table, each winner's impressions/calls/conversions, the second price paid, the publisher's earnings, and every tool call — human or agent — on the page itself. An answer to the incentive problem: an ad market where every party's payoff increases with the sponsored tool actually being useful . Agents are perfect ad-blockers; attention sold to an optimizer is worth nothing, but being the tool an optimizer chooses is worth everything. It works today in ChatGPT's in-app browser, end to end. What we learned Quality-weighting isn't fairness theater — it's what makes advertising possible in agentic contexts at all. An agent's operator can measure task success and switch away instantly, so a marketplace that lets money outrank quality destroys its own inventory. Second-price mechanics matter for the same reason: the equilibrium is advertisers bidding their true value, and winners being the tools that actually help. And on the human side: the best thing we built for trust wasn't a disclosure banner — it was showing the whole machine running, on the page, to everyone. What's next for AgentAds A machine-readable sponsored convention for WebMCP tools, so agent policies can uniformly accept, weight, or strip sponsored capabilities; cost-per-outcome bidding; real settlement rails; and rolling AgentAds into the Oasy publisher stack — analytics, licensing, and monetization for the half of the web that's already agents. pitch: RetailAgentOS uses WebMCP to let AI agents build valid carts and request quotes from a retailer’s real inventory, pricing, and policies—without guessing or taking control from shoppers.
about_excerpt: RetailAgentOS uses WebMCP to let AI agents build valid carts and request quotes from a retailer’s real inventory, pricing, and policies—without guessing or taking control from shoppers. Like Comment Story Updates Farm Eggs return STOCK_STALE, so cart preparation is withheld. The shopper — not the agent — approves the Cage-Free substitute Only after human approval does prepare_validated_cart register, returning a $15.99 cart. Checkout is never exposed Developer Evidence and Event Log Live Tool Registery - Fresh Corner Store WebMCP exposes only the next safe action. RetailAgentOS's deterministic engine decides what that action is Inspiration I did not start RetailAgentOS to build another shopping demo. I started it because the next interface to commerce will increasingly be an AI agent—and small retailers should not be left behind. My goal is to make agentic commerce accessible to every retailer, from a solo merchant to a global enterprise. Today, becoming "agent-ready" can require specialized engineers, custom integrations, and infrastructure that only large companies can afford. If that remains true, AI commerce will widen the gap between large platforms and the millions of independent retailers that make local commerce unique. I have a direct view of that asymmetry. By day, I lead engineering for one of the largest retail storefronts in the United States, where I have spent years working on the kinds of systems I am describing here: eligibility rules, inventory truth, fulfillment feasibility, promotion stacking, and the pricing context that determines what a given shopper may actually buy. At that scale, the reasoning layer exists—but it is distributed across backend services, much of it is enforced late in the journey, it is expensive to build, and it was designed for one company. Rebuilding another bespoke stack for another large retailer is not the interesting problem. Making these capabilities accessible to an independent merchant is. RetailAgentOS is my independent work. It is informed by my professional experience and general retail-engineering patterns, but it uses no proprietary employer code, data, architecture, or confidential information and does not imply employer sponsorship or endorsement. RetailAgentOS is my attempt to close that gap through an open-source platform. A retailer should be able to describe its products and selling rules once—inventory, pricing, eligibility, delivery, substitutions, customization, and quote policies—and let different AI agents interact with the business accurately and safely. I released RetailAgentOS under the Apache 2.0 license. Its specifications are published as versioned RFCs with their open questions left intact, and the specifications ship alongside a runnable reference implementation—so the rules a retailer reads are the rules the engine actually executes. That mission shaped the retailers I chose for this showcase. Fresh Corner Market represents the neighborhood grocery store: the kirana store found throughout India and South Asia, the neighborhood shop found across Europe, or the independent corner market serving communities in the United States. These stores operate with changing local inventory, narrow delivery windows, substitutions, and close customer relationships. Their commerce rules may look simple on a webpage, but they are highly contextual. An AI agent must know when inventory cannot be trusted, offer an acceptable substitute, and preserve the shopper's control. TheCustomHub represents another important small-retailer model: a specialized American business selling customized apparel. It is also the first real retailer working with me to explore how RetailAgentOS can support an operating business. Its transactions cannot always be reduced to "add item to cart." A request may include color, youth-size quantities, artwork, budget, and delivery requirements that a merchant must review before providing a price. The challenge demo uses an authorized controlled fixture—not a live production backend—but it reflects the real quote-first workflow RetailAgentOS is being designed to support. These two retailers were chosen deliberately. One needs an agent to recover a simple grocery cart when inventory is uncertain. The other needs an agent to preserve a complex custom order without fabricating a price. Together, they demonstrate why agentic commerce needs to support the diversity of real retail—not force every retailer into the operating model of a large marketplace. WebMCP made this vision tangible. It allows the retailer's own website to expose structured actions directly to an AI agent—no marketplace intermediary and no bespoke integration for every agent. RetailAgentOS determines what is valid; WebMCP exposes only the next action the retailer can safely honor; and the human shopper retains control over consequential decisions. The long-term vision is universal access: an open foundation that lets any retailer participate in agentic commerce without surrendering its policies, customer relationships, or independence. What it does RetailAgentOS is the merchant-controlled reasoning layer. WebMCP is the browser action surface. An agent can invoke only the next commerce capability the retailer can safely honor at that moment—and which tools exist changes as the engine evaluates inventory, price, fulfillment, policy, and shopper approval. The grocery mission. A shopper asks for a weekend breakfast cart under $30 from Fresh Corner Market, with Farm Eggs and Artisan Sourdough Bread. The eggs return STOCK_STALE , so cart preparation is not merely disabled in the interface—it is not registered as a tool at all . The engine proposes Cage-Free Eggs, explains the $0.50 difference and the equivalent local delivery, and stops. A human clicks Approve. Only then does prepare_validated_cart register, returning a $15.99 review cart. An optional revision to two loaves lands at $24.49, leaving $5.51 of the budget. Checkout is never registered anywhere in this showcase. The custom-order mission. Twenty-five black robotics-team shirts—six Youth Small, eleven Youth Medium, and eight Youth Large—with a one-color front logo, requested within fifteen days against a $500 ceiling. The plan reaches QUOTE_REQUIRED , which dynamically exposes request_quote . The structured request preserves every constraint the shopper stated and returns fixedPrice: null and deliveryPromise: null . The agent does not get to invent a price the merchant never set. No cart, order, payment, or checkout is created. That second mission matters most to me. Refusing to fabricate a price is not a limitation to apologize for—it is the feature that allows quote-first merchants to exist in an agentic world at all. How I built it The deterministic engine came first and predates this challenge. It runs a staged pipeline—visibility, then eligibility, then price, then fulfillment, then quote—through pure registered evaluators. The same inputs always produce byte-identical output; no model sits in the decision path; time is injected rather than read from the clock. That determinism is the entire basis for letting an agent act on a real store. The WebMCP layer was built during the challenge window on top of it: packages/webmcp is a framework-independent browser adapter owning one canonical catalog of seven Phase 1 descriptors: get_storefront_capabilities , search_catalog , evaluate_shopping_plan , find_valid_alternatives , apply_plan_repair , prepare_validated_cart , and request_quote . Three planning tools register at load; the others appear and disappear as the engine permits. revise_validated_cart is an optional post-cart extension. No state ever exposes every tool at once. Registration runs through document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , owned by an AbortSignal lifecycle so capabilities are revoked on reset, scenario switch, and unmount. Revocability is what makes "safe next action" an enforced guarantee rather than a convention. A controlled gateway validates input, injects time, calls the real engine, and maps its decision record into compact tool results. WebMCP never recalculates a decision—it can only surface one. Guided replay remains available as a clearly labelled fallback and walkthrough in every browser. It invokes the identical descriptors and handlers, with per-invocation telemetry marking native versus replay so the two paths cannot be confused. Challenges I ran into A registration race surfaced by cross-agent testing. A native run in Codex's in-app browser completed the post-approval journey, while a separate ChatGPT browser-agent run stopped after the shopper clicked Approve. The problem was not the approval itself: the SDK deferred the phase transition, allowing apply_plan_repair to resolve before prepare_validated_cart had necessarily finished registering. The second agent therefore received a valid repair result but did not continue automatically. I reproduced the timing window with a controllable fak
video_title: RetailAgentOS — a WebMCP storefront that exposes only the next safe action
video_transcript_excerpt: Retailers are about to have customers who are not people. They're agents. Today those agents shop by scraping pages and guessing at stock, prices, and delivery promises no merchant ever agreed to. Retail Agent OS answers a single question deterministically. What can this retailer actually promise right now? We already had the engine. What we lacked was a way to make an agent respect it. That is what Web MCP changes. Merchant can stop being a polite advice a model can ignore and becomes a hard capability boundary inside the browser. The agent does not decide what it is allowed to do. The store does. The storefront registers its tools with the browser through Web MCP. Three to start. Capabilities, catalog search, and plan evaluation. Not search and buy. Search and plan. Checkout isn't among them. It is simply never registered. An agent cannot call a tool that does not exist. The agent reads the storefront capabilities, searches the catalog, and submits a plan for evaluation. Retail Agent OS refuses it. The inventory on those eggs is stale. So, no card gets billed on a promise the retailer can't keep. It does not simply fail though. The engine returns a substitute that merchant has already approved and registers two repair capabilities that did not exist a moment earlier. The agent's option changed because the decision changed. Applying the substitution requires a person, a real approval. Never inferred, never granted by the agent on the shopper's behalf. Once approved, the repair tools are withdrawn and cart preparation is registered. The engine re-evaluates everything from scratch. Price, inventory, delivery mode, and the shopper's budget before a cart exists at all. And the missions ends at a cart for review. Checkout was never on the table. A second storefront shows the same engine drawing a very different boundary. Custom merchandise has no valid fixed price, so no cart tool is offered at all. Only a quote request routed to the merchant review filled with customization and size information. The agent can't invent a number the merchant never set. And all of it is auditable. The tools retail agent always track against the tool the browser actually observed, plus a full registration and invocation log. And that's the bit. Retail policy that agents can't route around expressed as a life capability surface. Every retailer decides what an agent may do in their store, and the browser enforces it.

An agent-native bakery ERP powered by WebMCP that lets AI manage inventory, production planning, purchasing, suppliers, and production workflows through conversation.

 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Bakery businesses often manage inventory, recipes, suppliers, purchasing, and production across multiple screens and workflows. BakeryFlow was created to simplify these operations. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I am extending BakeryFlow into an agent-native ERP where AI agents can interact directly with real business workflows using WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 BakeryFlow Agent allows an AI agent to understand and interact with bakery operations. 

 Using WebMCP, an agent can: 

 
 Check raw material inventory 
 Retrieve product recipes 
 Calculate ingredients required for production 
 Detect inventory shortages 
 Find suppliers 
 Prepare or create purchase orders 
 Create production runs 
 

 For example, a manager can ask: 

 "Can we produce 1,000 chocolate cookies?" 

 The agent can inspect the recipe, calculate the required ingredients, compare them against current inventory, identify shortages, and help take the next required action. 

 How I built it 

 BakeryFlow uses a React frontend with a Django REST Framework backend and PostgreSQL database. 

 For this challenge, WebMCP is being integrated into the frontend to expose selected ERP capabilities as structured tools that AI agents can discover and use. 

 The WebMCP layer reuses BakeryFlow's existing business logic and APIs instead of creating a separate system specifically for AI agents. 

 WebMCP Challenge Work 

 BakeryFlow existed before the WebMCP Challenge. 

 The core ERP functionality, including inventory, recipes, suppliers, purchases, and production management, was already part of BakeryFlow. 

 For this challenge, I am adding the WebMCP integration and agent-native workflows that allow AI agents to securely interact with those existing capabilities. 

 Challenges 

 One of the main challenges is turning complex ERP workflows into clear and safe agent tools while preserving the existing validation, permissions, and business rules. 

 Another challenge is designing tools that agents can combine into useful multi-step workflows rather than simply exposing individual CRUD operations. 

 What's next 

 The goal is to expand BakeryFlow Agent so an AI agent can assist with the complete production lifecycle — from demand planning and inventory analysis to purchasing, production, stock movement, and business insights.

title: AIEndpoint - Service Discovery for the Agentic Web
pitch: AIEndpoint finds the right website. WebMCP operates it. An open standard and live registry that lets browser agents discover which service can do the job before they ever navigate.
about_excerpt: AIEndpoint finds the right website. WebMCP operates it. An open standard and live registry that lets browser agents discover which service can do the job before they ever navigate. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP integration docs: declare support in your manifest, promote it into page tools with @aiendpoint/webmcp DemoWeather: live Open-Meteo data. WebMCP tools generated from its /.well-known/ai manifest update this card when an agent calls them aiendpoint.dev - the open /ai standard: ~800 tokens of pure signal instead of 10k-50k tokens of page noise Registry search results with the ⚡ WebMCP badge - DemoWeather (verified, score 100) tops the results agents and humans both see Real Chrome with the WebMCP flag: tools registered, executeTool call received - the visible counter proves the loop works Inspiration WebMCP gives an agent structured tools for the page it is already on. But watching agents work, we kept hitting the step that comes before that: which page should the agent open in the first place? An agent that needs weather data or a currency rate still guesses URLs or scrapes search results. We had been building that missing step for months: AIEndpoint, an open standard where any site publishes a capability manifest at /.well-known/ai (an IETF Internet-Draft), plus a live registry indexing thousands of services. When WebMCP appeared, the two ideas snapped together: AIEndpoint finds the right website. WebMCP operates it. We are honest with ourselves: an independent project like this may never become the standard. The giants are drafting their own, and there is only so far one person can push. But robots.txt also started with one individual and an idea the web happened to need. We simply wanted to cut the traffic LLM agents waste crawling site after site just to figure out what each one can do - and we entered this challenge hoping more people will join us. What it does On aiendpoint.dev , an in-browser agent calls find_services ("a weather service with no auth"). The results the agent receives render as cards on the page the human is looking at. select_service opens the detail view with a live "Open service" link. One click later, on weather.aiendpoint.dev , the agent calls current_weather and the weather card in front of the user updates with live Open-Meteo data. Human and agent share one screen at every step. Nothing happens in a hidden console: every tool call has a visible consequence on the page. Before WebMCP, a service directory for agents could only be a server-side HTTP API, unreachable exactly where users work. Now discovery, selection, and execution all happen inside one browsing session, visibly shared between the user and the agent. How we built it @aiendpoint/webmcp (new package, ESM + IIFE): promotes a site's /.well-known/ai manifest into WebMCP tools. Tool names, descriptions, and JSON input schemas are derived from the manifest: the spec's compact parameter notation ( "string, required -- city name" ) is parsed into schema types and required lists. Execution stays in explicit per-capability handlers, so a site never exposes anything it did not consciously wire up. aiendpoint.dev (Next.js) registers find_services / select_service on every page; tool calls navigate the visible UI. A /webmcp/ping diagnostics page reports the browser's actual WebMCP surface and shows a live call counter. DemoWeather (FastAPI) serves its manifest, loads the adapter's IIFE bundle, and wires three handlers that drive the page's weather card, backed by live Open-Meteo data with a labeled stale-cache fallback. Challenges we ran into The API surface is still moving. Registration probes document.modelContext , navigator.modelContext (now deprecated), and older entry points, preferring registerTool with AbortSignal cleanup. We learned by experiment that executeTool takes the registered tool object plus a JSON string , so our handlers normalize both parsed objects and raw strings. provideContext replaces the whole tool set on every call , so independent components clobbered each other until we kept a page-wide union of registered tools. React Strict Mode silently unregistered tools in development via the register/cleanup/register cycle until we made registration fully idempotent. Making discovery honest: we rewrote our registry search to match capability keywords against descriptions, and fixed count/filter bugs the new browser-driven usage exposed. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full loop is verified in a real browser , not just designed: tool registration, an actual executeTool call, and a visible UI change on the page. The discovery chain runs on live production data : the registry indexes 3,600+ services, and DemoWeather registers itself, passes our own validator at 100/100, and tops the "weather" search results agents actually see. One adapter call makes any /.well-known/ai site agent-operable - schemas included - while keeping execution in explicit handlers the site controls. We migrated the entire platform (registry, validator, CLI, MCP server, three demos, and every framework adapter) to the well-known location during the hackathon window, and cleared all 71 dependency audit vulnerabilities while we were at it. What we learned ogfooding an open spec against a second standard is the fastest way to find its weak points. Migrating /ai to /.well-known/ai (draft-01), parsing our own compact notation into JSON Schema, and watching a real browser call our tools taught us more in three days than months of design. What's next for AIEndpoint - Service Discovery for the Agentic Web Schema-typed params in spec v1.1, mutations with confirmation UI, auth-scoped tools, and a "WebMCP-ready" tier on the registry's verification badge, so agents can filter for sites that are operable , not just discoverable. Built With cloudflare esbuild fastapi fastify next.js open-meteo python react redis supabase typescript vercel webmcp Try it out www.aiendpoint.dev weather.aiendpoint.dev github.com www.aiendpoint.dev Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo builder. I created the /ai spec, the registry, and the site before the hackathon, and built everything WebMCP during the submission period: the @aiendpoint/webmcp adapter, the registry's find_services/select_service tools, the DemoWeather page, and an in-page agent that drives the tools with natural language. WebMCP was so new that its API surface changed mid-hackathon - reverse-engineering executeTool in the DevTools console at 2am was intimidating, but watching a model call my page's tools and the UI react for the first time made it all worth it. I paired heavily with AI coding agents throughout, which felt fitting for a project about making the web agent-ready. title: Co Draft
pitch: A collaborative doc editor where AI agents read and write your real document state not screenshots through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A collaborative doc editor where AI agents read and write your real document state not screenshots through WebMCP.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 About the Project 

 The idea 

 We wanted to explore a simple question: 

 What if an AI agent could work inside a document with you, instead of just looking at the document from the outside? 

 Today, when an AI agent interacts with a web application, it often has to rely on screenshots, DOM inspection, or simulated clicks. For a document editor, that means the agent has to figure out what the user is looking at, where content belongs, and what actions are available. 

 We wanted to try a different approach using WebMCP : let the website expose its actual application state and capabilities as structured tools that an AI agent can call directly. 

 That became Co/Draft — a document where humans and agents edit together. 

 The core interaction is deliberately simple. A human writes and selects content normally, while an agent can use tools such as get_document_state , get_selection , add_comment , and insert_block . The agent therefore works with the same structured document state that the human sees, rather than trying to reconstruct it from the UI. 

 How we built it 

 Co/Draft is a lightweight React + TypeScript application using Zustand for document state. 

 The document is represented as structured blocks rather than one large piece of HTML. Each block has an ID, text, creation source, and author information. Comments are also attached to specific block IDs, which gives the agent an unambiguous way to refer to a section of the document. 

 On top of this state, we registered five WebMCP tools: 

 
 get_document_state — lets the agent read the current document, pending suggestions, and comments. 
 get_selection — tells the agent which block the human is currently working on. 
 insert_block — lets the agent propose a new section. 
 add_comment — lets the agent leave feedback on a specific block. 
 resolve_comment — lets the agent mark feedback as resolved. 
 

 These tools are registered through document.modelContext , using a React hook so that the tools operate against the same live state as the UI. 

 We also added a small human-in-the-loop trust boundary . An agent doesn't directly insert arbitrary content into the document. Instead, insert_block creates a visible pending suggestion. The human can then accept or reject it. 

 That gives us a workflow like: 

 Human writes → Agent reads → Agent reviews → Agent proposes → Human approves → Document changes 

 The agent can participate meaningfully without silently taking control of the document. 

 For collaboration, the prototype uses the browser's BroadcastChannel API. This allows multiple tabs in the same browser to exchange document mutations and presence information without requiring a backend. The project is intentionally a prototype rather than a production collaborative editor. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest thing we learned was that giving an agent structured tools changes the interaction completely . 

 Instead of asking an agent to “look at the page and figure out what to do,” we can give it explicit capabilities: 
 get_document_state()
get_selection()
add_comment(blockId, text)
insert_block(text, afterBlockId)
resolve_comment(commentId)
 
 This makes the boundary between the application and the agent much clearer. 

 We also learned that the interesting part isn't simply allowing an agent to edit. The more important question is how much control the agent should have . 

 For example, comments are relatively low-risk, so an agent can add one directly. Inserting actual document content is more consequential, so we introduced an approval step. 

 That led us to think about agents less like automated scripts and more like collaborators with explicitly defined permissions . 

 We also learned about the practical distinction between exposing application functionality to an agent and actually building a collaborative application. WebMCP solves the first problem very nicely, but synchronization, persistence, identity, and conflict resolution are separate engineering problems. 

 The challenges 

 One of our biggest challenges was synchronization. 

 Our first implementation used BroadcastChannel to send mutations such as: 
 editBlock
addComment
resolveComment
proposeBlock
acceptSuggestion
deleteBlock
 
 between tabs. 

 However, simply broadcasting mutations isn't enough to create a reliable shared document. Each tab initially creates its own in-memory state, so two tabs can start with different randomly generated block IDs. A mutation referring to a block that only exists in the sender's state cannot be correctly applied by another tab. 

 This forced us to think about an important distinction: 

 sharing events is not the same thing as sharing state. 

 A reliable prototype needs both a consistent initial document and a way for a newly opened tab to obtain the current state before applying future mutations. 

 We therefore treated the synchronization layer as a separate problem from WebMCP itself. The eventual direction is a lightweight state handshake for new tabs, while keeping the mutation-based synchronization simple enough for a hackathon demo. 

 Another challenge was deciding what not to build. 

 It would be possible to turn Co/Draft into a much larger system with a backend, WebSockets, persistent documents, authentication, CRDTs, conflict-free editing, and cross-device collaboration. But that would move attention away from the actual experiment we wanted to demonstrate: 

 
 Can a web application expose meaningful, structured capabilities to an AI agent so that the agent can genuinely collaborate with a human? 
 

 For this project, we chose to keep that question at the center. 

 Why this matters 

 Co/Draft is intentionally small, but the idea can extend much further. 

 A document editor is just one example. The same pattern could apply to design tools, spreadsheets, project-management applications, whiteboards, educational software, or any interactive application where an AI agent needs to understand and manipulate structured state. 

 Instead of building agents that merely see interfaces, we can build applications that explicitly tell agents: 

 “Here is what I am. Here is what you can understand. Here is what you are allowed to do.” 

 That is the direction we wanted to explore with Co/Draft.

A reference console that turns complex AWS and Azure-style dashboards into one focused workspace where people and AI agents can navigate tasks and prepare changes together.

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Working in cloud consoles like AWS, Azure often turns a simple task into a scavenger hunt across services, settings, documentation, and browser tabs. When I get stuck, I usually leave the console to ask ChatGPT or Claude for instructions. Sometimes the steps are accurate; other times they are outdated, incomplete, or based on a console layout that has already changed.
Even with the right answer, I still have to return to the console, locate every resource, and translate those instructions into clicks myself. The AI can describe the maze, but it cannot see where I am or work through it with me. Sightline was inspired by the idea that an agent should operate inside the console’s real context—helping navigate and prepare work while the human remains in control. 

 What it does 

 Sightline makes complex operational consoles like AWS, Azure and related, easier to use. It connects every service, resource, and setting involved in a task into one clear path that a person and an AI agent can navigate together, while the human retains control over final changes. 

 How we built it 

 We connected ten WebMCP tools directly to Sightline’s shared console state. Agents can search resources, trace dependencies, navigate between services, and prepare coordinated changes while each action appears instantly in the interface for human review. Only the human can apply the final changes. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was designing tools that were useful without giving agents too much control. We also had to handle stale revisions, invalid patches, sensitive values, and clear separation between prepared and applied changes. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 We can now turn a complex operational request into one clear path across multiple services, resources, and settings. 
 Agents can find dependencies, explain their impact, and prepare coordinated changes without applying them. 
 Humans can review every proposed action inside the console and retain control over the final change. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP works best when tools expose meaningful product actions instead of mirroring buttons. Stable resource IDs, clear schemas, and visible feedback make agent behaviour safer and easier to understand. 

 What's next for Sightline 

 Next, we want to connect Sightline to real cloud APIs, authentication, authorization, and audit systems, then test it with larger infrastructure environments and more operational workflows.

title: Chisel
pitch: Give an AI agent a real CAD kernel — solid modelling in the browser over WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Give an AI agent a real CAD kernel — solid modelling in the browser over WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Chisel WebMCP WebMCP Surface Consent Gate Gate Step Export Measured by Kernel Three Apps Inspiration WebMCP starts from a simple problem: agents often operate websites by scraping the DOM and simulating clicks. That is brittle even for ordinary web apps. In a 3D CAD viewport, it is worse—there is no DOM representation of a solid, and clicking pixels cannot reliably express “subtract these cylinders from this plate” or verify the resulting volume. That made CAD a strong test for WebMCP. If an agent could inspect a real parametric model, call exact modelling operations, verify the geometry, and export a manufacturing format—all inside the browser—then WebMCP would be doing something that UI automation alone cannot. What it does Chisel gives an in-browser agent structured access to a real OpenCascade B-rep CAD kernel. A user can ask: Make a mounting bracket 80 × 40 × 5 mm with two 6 mm holes, 50 mm apart. The agent can then: Inspect the active document and its unit system. Create an exact box and two cylinders. Subtract the cylinders with a real boolean operation. Read back the bounding box, volume, surface area, scene tree, and undo history. Export the result as STEP, IGES, BREP, STL, or OBJ. The demonstrated bracket measures exactly 80 × 40 × 5 mm . Its boolean operation reports affectedCount: 4 : one resulting solid created and three input solids consumed. STEP export verifies the ISO-10303 envelope, B-rep solid count, and analytic plane and cylindrical surfaces before reporting success. Every consequential operation passes through one shared approval gate. The page shows the exact requested call, and the handler does not run unless the human approves it. Declining is not “run and roll back”; the operation never executes. Chisel also explores WebMCP composition. Its top-level shell combines tools published by independently owned same-origin apps: The CAD application contributes modelling, inspection, undo, finishing, and export tools. The shell contributes application discovery, session statistics, and agent-authored charts using flint-chart and Vega-Lite. A HyperFrames composition at /video/ runs as an interactive browser showreel with a deterministic timeline. Calls are routed back to the frame that announced each tool, so the CAD consent dialog stays inside the application that owns the model. How I built it Chisel is a new WebMCP integration built around the existing open-source Chili3d CAD application. Chili3d supplies the OpenCascade 8 WebAssembly kernel, Three.js viewport, document model, IndexedDB persistence, and CAD exporters. I did not build or modify that kernel, and I do not claim the upstream application as my work. The new work is the complete agent surface: JSON Schema tool definitions registered through document.modelContext Read tools for document state, selection, scene hierarchy, geometry, and history Named modelling tools for primitives, booleans, movement, deletion, undo, fillets, and chamfers Gated export with format-level verification One registration-boundary authorization wrapper A visible activity log showing calls, approvals, failures, duration, and affected counts A same-origin catalogue and invocation bridge for framed applications A multi-app shell that merges independently published tools An agent-queryable statistics and charting surface A HyperFrames browser composition for the showreel A reproducible build that checks out a pinned Chili3d commit and adds Chisel through its existing plugin system The combined static application is deployed on Cloudflare Workers. Challenges I faced The WebMCP API changed A large amount of existing material still uses navigator.modelContext and provideContext() . The current API uses document.modelContext and registerTool() . There is also no unregisterTool() . Tools are removed by aborting the AbortSignal supplied during registration. Tool shape affected agent reliability The first design exposed one large apply_operation tool with an operation enum. An adversarial review correctly challenged the claim that this was safer: an enum is not a sandbox. Multiple operations hidden behind one dispatcher still have the same authority, while discriminated-union inputs are harder for agents to call reliably. I replaced it with narrowly scoped named tools while keeping the real safety property: every callable write still passes through the same mandatory gate. WebMCP exists on the top-level document In the in-app browser, document.modelContext is available on the top-level page but not necessarily inside an iframe. The framed CAD application therefore publishes plain tool metadata to the shell through a versioned same-origin bridge. The shell registers the catalogue at the top level and forwards calls back to the frame. This was tested end to end in production: agent → top-level WebMCP tool → shell → postMessage bridge → application gate → OpenCascade. Success needed to be independently checkable A tool returning “done” is not enough. Chisel reports exactly what changed, exposes numerical geometry metrics, records the operation in undo history, and treats zero affected objects as an error. Tool output is capped and announces truncation, because model names and document content are untrusted text that becomes agent context. Accomplishments Drove a real B-rep CAD kernel through production WebMCP calls. Built and verified a two-hole mounting bracket with exact dimensions. Added human approval without relying on advisory WebMCP annotations. Made agent actions visible through an in-page activity trail. Added undo, fillet, chamfer, numerical geometry verification, and gated STEP export. Composed multiple web applications into one top-level tool surface. Added agent-authored session charts and an interactive HyperFrames showreel. Kept the integration separate from upstream Chili3d application code. Verified the deployed app in Chrome and the the ChatGPT in-app browser". What I learned The most interesting part of WebMCP is not converting functions into tool schemas. It is designing everything the standard intentionally leaves to the site: Where authorization is enforced How refusals are represented Whether success messages are truthful How agents recover from mistakes How much untrusted output enters context How tools from multiple applications compose How an agent verifies its own work instead of trusting itself WebMCP becomes valuable when the website exposes domain operations that are more precise than clicking—and when the human can still see, understand, and control what the agent does. What’s next for Chisel Address individual selected edges instead of applying fillets and chamfers to an entire solid. Add sketch-and-extrude workflows for profile-driven modelling. Show before-and-after geometry in approval dialogs. Let the HyperFrames app render and return an MP4 on request. Add a camera-orbit bridge so the showreel can present the live model directly. What is new All Chisel integration code was created during the challenge period. Chili3d is pre-existing third-party open-source software used under AGPL-3.0. Chisel’s WebMCP plugin, safety gate, activity interface, multi-app bridge, shell, charting integration, and HyperFrames showreel are the new work. video_title: Chisel: an AI agent with a real CAD kernel, over WebMCP
video_transcript_excerpt: This is a real CAD kernel — OpenCascade, compiled to WebAssembly, running in a browser tab. I'm going to ask an AI agent to build a part in it. Not move a mesh around. Build a solid. Every tool call that changes the model stops here first and shows me exactly what it wants to do. This matters more than it looks. WebMCP has no consent primitive at all — no permission prompt, no user-gesture requirement — and readOnlyHint is only advisory. The spec says agents “must assume good faith from site developers.” So any safety this page has, the page author has to build. This dialog is that. There's the plate. Now the holes. Two cylinders, then a boolean cut — real B-rep subtraction in the kernel. And look at what the tool hands back: an affected count of four. One solid created, three consumed. If an operation changes nothing, this returns an error, never a cheerful “done”. The spec itself warns that a tool can claim to be read-only while changing data; the mirror image is a tool that claims success while changing nothing, and an agent that gets lied to compounds the lie. Six read tools let it inspect what's actually there — the scene tree, the selection, an object's real bounding box. Eighty by forty by five. It's not guessing from the DOM; there is no DOM for a solid. This is exactly the gap WebMCP exists to close. Now I save the model to IndexedDB, reload, and reopen it by id. The bracket is still there. Then the agent exports STEP behind the same approval gate. The result verifies a valid ISO envelope, a real B-rep solid, six analytic planes, and two cylindrical surfaces. To be straight about what I built: Chili3d is the excellent open-source CAD application and kernel. I built the WebMCP integration: the agent toolset, a shared safety gate, and a shell that composes tools across apps. No fork, no claimed upstream work — just a drop-in agent surface.

title: Astrail: AI-native trip planner powered by WebMCP
pitch: Astrail turns the Instagram Reels you save into a routed trip on a live 3D map, and you build and edit the whole thing by talking to ChatGPT. The WebMCP tools run inside the page, not on a server.
about_excerpt: Astrail turns the Instagram Reels you save into a routed trip on a live 3D map, and you build and edit the whole thing by talking to ChatGPT. The WebMCP tools run inside the page, not on a server. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Four Reel links pasted into ChatGPT. One WebMCP tool saves them and starts extraction while the library fills in beside it. The run narrated stage by stage. Preferences recalled from memory, places verified, and a missing forecast reported rather than faked. Adding a stop by asking. The add_place call is visible in ChatGPT, and the new stop is labelled as yours, not borrowed from a Reel. Inspiration Instagram makes it easy to save a Reel about somewhere you want to go, then gives you nothing to do with it. Our own folders had about a hundred places across nine countries. When the dates finally got booked, the fastest route from that folder to a real itinerary was still twenty browser tabs, so we never opened it and planned off search results instead. So we built the conversion. Paste Reel links and a multi-agent pipeline on the OpenAI Agents SDK pulls the places out of the captions, verifies each one exists, checks weather and routes, and groups them into days by geography. Anything that will not verify gets dropped. It takes 60 to 180 seconds. Then we showed it to people and got this back: "It's unclear how to navigate the website, where to click, how to choose the reels, how to start generating a trip." We had spent a sprint treating that as a copy problem. It was not. The tool was not hard to understand, it was hard to operate, and we could either keep redesigning buttons or remove the need to find them. That is what took us to WebMCP. What it does Astrail turns saved Instagram Reels into a routed trip on a live 3D map, and you drive it by talking to ChatGPT. Say "save these reels" and paste some links; it saves them and starts pulling places out. Say "plan me two days in Osaka from those" and it shows an approval card with the cost, runs the pipeline, narrates each stage, and hands back a routed map. Say "add Tokyo Disneyland to day 2" and it asks you on the page, finds the place, adds it, and redraws the route. Ask why a stop is on your trip and you get one of three answers: the caption quote from the Reel it came from with a link to that Reel, Astrail's reasoning where it suggested the stop, or a note saying you asked for it. Where we cannot source a fact, like opening hours, the space stays empty. It also remembers how you travel. Tell it once and the next trip recalls it, names what it remembered on the card, and still asks before spending anything. None of that is the agent working alone. It plans, you approve. It offers what it remembered, you can override it. Before WebMCP those two halves could not meet: you could read the itinerary but not change it, and an agent could describe your trip but never touch it. How we built it Seventeen tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() , in two scopes. Fourteen in the signed-in app shell, three more only while a trip map is mounted, and six that work with no account on a public sample trail. The important part is where they run. A backend MCP server can describe a trip. Only WebMCP can move the map the person is looking at. Because execute() runs in the page, a tool already has the loaded trip, the session, and the same React state setters a click uses. Ask for day 2 and the page's own showDay runs, so the camera flies and the day chip lights up as if you had clicked. The agent inherits our security model instead of bringing its own. Reads run under the same row-level security a human gets, no access token crosses the tool boundary, and every edit to your trip stops for an approval card on the page rather than a question in chat. Tools address stops by pin number, so "move stop 7 to day 3" works and no UUID ever reaches the agent. Reel captions are text an attacker can write, so every tool whose output can carry one is annotated untrustedContentHint , and the extraction agents run behind input_guardrail tripwires. We also had a second model reviewing. Every plan and diff went to Codex before it landed, and it caught things we missed, including a bug inside a fix we thought was already correct. Stack: Next.js 15, React 19 and Mapbox GL on Vercel; FastAPI on Render; Supabase; the OpenAI Agents SDK; mem0; Apify. What we added during the submission period Astrail existed before 25 August, as a form. You pasted Reel links, waited, and got back an itinerary you could read but could not change. Everything in frontend/lib/webmcp/ was written on or after 26 August: the seventeen tools, the registry behind them, their contract tests, the on-page approval cards, the agent activity rail and the WebMCP status chip. So were the five owner-checked FastAPI edit endpoints they call, because until then the itinerary was immutable at every layer, with no endpoint, no frontend mutation and row-level security that was SELECT-only. Two other things were built in the window: the map was rebuilt so a stop that came from a Reel carries that Reel's own cover frame in its pin and links back to the Reel, and /app/trip/demo is new, a finished sample trail that opens signed out with six of the seventeen tools so the app can be judged without an account. The memory engine is older. It was built between 7 July and 2 August and we do not claim it as challenge work. What is new is that an agent can reach it, and the reason it could not is the first thing under Challenges below. The dated, commit-by-commit split is in docs/webmcp/WHATS-NEW.md . Challenges we ran into The worst one was a flaw in our own product that only showed up once an agent was driving. Astrail looks up what it remembers about you only when the preferences box arrives empty, on the logic that what you typed today beats what you said three trips ago. It saves a new memory only when that box arrives full. Those conditions never overlap. So an agent leaving the field blank could recall forever and never teach it anything, and the manual form, which pre-fills that box from your profile, was quietly switching recall off on the other path. Nobody had noticed because no path had exercised both halves. Three changes fixed it: the planning tool asks how you travel when it has nothing stored, the card names what it remembered before you approve, and a new tool reads the store back. Chrome's use-webmcp-tool hook cost us a day. It never catches the promise registerTool returns, and since aborting the signal is how a tool unregisters, every navigation threw an unhandled AbortError across the app. We could not patch it from outside, because registerTool is a non-writable property of a native interface, so we wrote our own. About 144 lines. Making an agent's action feel like your own took longer than expected. Early versions had a tool call an API and then hope the page noticed, which is a second rendering path, and those drift. Now a mutation will not resolve until the UI has caught up. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP fixed the thing users actually complained about, which was the whole point of trying it. Getting Reels in used to be copy, switch tab, paste, repeat, then find a separate button to start extraction. Now you paste four links in one message. A finished trip used to be frozen at every layer, with no endpoint and no frontend mutation. Now five tools edit it, each behind an approval card. Beyond that, nothing reaches the map unattributed, and a contract test fails if our own copy ever promises a caption quote for a stop that has none, because the false version of that sentence reads better than the true one. Our tests check the README's tool table against the registry too, so a stale claim goes red rather than shipping. What we learned None of us had used WebMCP before this. It was announced, we read the spec, and started. It is a DOM API, not a server. We spent the first evening looking for the deployment story before realising there is not one. Your tools ship with your JavaScript. Where you register matters as much as what you register. App shell versus trip page is the difference between a tool that always exists and one that appears only when there is something for it to act on. The description field does more work than the code behind it. It is the only place to teach an agent when to call something, and it is captured at registration, so it cannot say anything dynamic. We rewrote ours constantly. And the page cannot talk back. When someone clicks a pin, the agent has no idea. That asymmetry shaped more of the design than we expected. What's next for Astrail Group trips. Nobody plans a holiday alone and right now Astrail assumes you do. Several people on one trip, each with their own agent, editing the same map. title: PixelForge
pitch: An agent-native pixel art studio where humans and AI agents operate the same editor through WebMCP — 19 tools, one shared canvas, every action visible and undoable.
about_excerpt: An agent-native pixel art studio where humans and AI agents operate the same editor through WebMCP — 19 tools, one shared canvas, every action visible and undoable. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The PixelForge brand: a pixel anvil where human and agent strokes meet, forged in the app's own 32×32 pixel style. The PixelForge mascot — a slime blacksmith, born in PixelForge and drawn entirely in 32×32 pixels with WebMCP tool calls. Live demo: ChatGPT drawing a green slime inside PixelForge — every tool call visible in the Agent Activity panel, every edit undoable. PixelForge — humans + agents, one canvas. An agent-native pixel art studio where ChatGPT operates the editor through 19 WebMCP tools. Inspiration AI "editors" today are one-shot generators: you prompt, you get a file, and you fix it by hand. The agent never touches the actual software. We asked the opposite question — what if the agent could operate a real creative tool, the same way a human does? A pixel editor turned out to be the perfect answer. Pixel art is 100% structured state — a grid of colors, layers, frames, a palette — which maps exactly onto tool schemas. No vision models, no guesswork: an agent can read the canvas as exact pixel data and edit it through the same primitives a human uses. What it does PixelForge is a complete, Aseprite-inspired pixel art studio: pencil / eraser / flood fill / color picker, brush shapes (circle, square, line) from 1–64px with pixel-perfect strokes, layers (duplicate, merge down, flatten), a cel-based animation timeline with playback, onion skinning, palette sorting & gradients, canvas resize, and PNG / animated GIF / sprite-sheet export. The same studio is also an agent workstation . ChatGPT — or any WebMCP client — can inspect the canvas, batch-draw hundreds of pixels, manage layers and frames, recolor entire animations, and export finished assets, through 19 structured WebMCP tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool . Try it: open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser and ask: "Create a cute green slime with a simple face, then turn it into a 4-frame idle animation." How we built it React + TypeScript + Vite + Zustand + Tailwind — fully client-side, no backend. The core rule: one action layer, two users. All 19 WebMCP tools call the exact same store actions as the mouse and keyboard. There is no separate "AI drawing" code path — so every agent edit is history-tracked, replayable, and undoable by the human. Tools use strict JSON schemas with batched operations ( draw_pixels takes an array of pixels — no one-call-per-pixel) Layer/frame references resolve by id or name , so agents never need to track internal ids Every tool returns structured JSON: {success, operation, detail} or {success:false, error:{code,message}} — so the agent can reason about failures instead of guessing Read-only tools ( get_editor_state , get_region ) let the agent see the canvas as exact pixel data before acting A live Agent Activity panel shows every tool call with HUMAN/AGENT badges — and every mutation, human or agent, is undoable 38 unit tests cover the editor actions and the tool contracts (schema validity, batched draws, structured errors, undoability of agent mutations). Challenges we ran into Making agent tool calls render live on the canvas while still committing as one undoable step Keeping agents effective across animation frames: layer references are remapped by name, so "draw on the Eyes layer" keeps working after frame switches Designing batched pixel operations that survive strict JSON-schema validation Testing across environments (ChatGPT in-app browser, Chrome with the testing flag) — plus building an honest debug bridge for browsers without WebMCP, clearly labeled so nothing is faked Accomplishments that we're proud of The full creative pipeline runs on WebMCP. A judge can ask ChatGPT: "Create a green slime → make the eyes smaller → turn it into a 4-frame idle animation → make the palette warmer → export a sprite sheet" — and watch every step execute as real tool calls on the live canvas, including 411 pixels placed in a single batched call . A complete product, not a tech demo. In 9 days we built an entire Aseprite-style studio from scratch: cel-based animation timeline, onion skinning, brush shapes with pixel-perfect strokes, palette tools, three export formats — all sharing one action layer with the agent. Trust by design. Every agent operation appears in the activity feed with an AGENT badge and sits in the same undo history as human edits. The human can take back anything the agent did — visibility and control are built in, not bolted on. Verified, not claimed. 38 unit tests cover the editor actions and tool contracts, and the 19 tools were confirmed live in both target environments: ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with the WebMCP testing flag. What we learned Strict schemas beat clever prompts. Because every tool has precise input validation and returns structured errors ( INVALID_COORDINATE , LAYER_NOT_FOUND , NO_SELECTION ), the agent self-corrects instead of hallucinating. And sharing one action layer between human and agent turned out to be the cheapest possible way to earn trust: visibility + undoability come for free. What's next for PixelForge Declarative WebMCP tool registration, agent-driven tileset workflows, multi-sprite projects — and WebMCP support for tiled drawing mode. Built With netlify react typescript vite webmcp zustand Try it out pixelforge-webmcp.netlify.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I built everything solo: the pixel editor itself (canvas engine, layers, animation timeline, undo system, palette tools), all 19 WebMCP tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool, the branding, and the Netlify deployment. I leaned on an AI coding agent for scaffolding and iteration, but the core architecture — one shared action layer so the agent and I use the exact same tools — was designed and verified by me. This was my first time building for the WebMCP standard. title: Go Link Shortener
pitch: A high-performance URL shortener written in Go using Fiber v3, PostgreSQL, and Redis. Now with WebMCP
about_excerpt:
A high-performance URL shortener written in Go using Fiber v3, PostgreSQL, and Redis. Now with WebMCP
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Go Link Shortener started as a small, fast URL shortener built around a simple idea: creating and resolving short links should require as little friction as possible. 

 When I discovered WebMCP, the project became a natural experiment for a different question: 

 What if an AI agent did not need to inspect the page, understand the layout, and simulate clicks just to use a web application? 

 Instead of building a separate chatbot or a remote MCP server, I wanted the existing website itself to expose its capabilities directly to AI agents while remaining fully usable by humans. 

 The result is an agent-native URL shortener where the same application can be used through its normal UI or through structured WebMCP tools. 

 What it does 

 Go Link Shortener allows users to create custom short URLs, redirect visitors efficiently, and collect click analytics. 

 With WebMCP enabled, the website exposes three capabilities directly to AI agents: 

 
 create_short_link — creates a short URL using the existing HTML form and server-side validation. 
 resolve_short_link — returns the destination behind an existing alias. 
 get_link_analytics — returns aggregate traffic information such as total clicks and the latest click timestamp. 
 

 This enables interactions such as: 

 
 "Create /webmcp pointing to the WebMCP documentation." 
 

 or: 

 
 "Where does /webmcp redirect, and how many times has it been opened?" 
 

 The agent can discover and execute the appropriate tools without visually locating controls or automating clicks. 

 How I built it 

 The backend is written in Go using Fiber v3 , with PostgreSQL as the persistent datastore and Redis for fast URL resolution. 

 I deliberately kept the existing server-rendered architecture instead of introducing a frontend framework only for WebMCP. 

 For link creation, I used the Declarative WebMCP API . The existing HTML form is exposed as the create_short_link tool, so both humans and agents go through the same validation and persistence code. 

 For read operations, I used the Imperative WebMCP API through: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( . . . ) 
 
 Two read-only tools are registered when WebMCP is available: 
 resolve_short_link
get_link_analytics
 
 They call lightweight JSON endpoints implemented in the existing Go application. 

 The integration is implemented as progressive enhancement. If a browser does not support WebMCP, the website continues working normally. 

 Privacy and safety 

 The original application records redirect events for analytics, including information useful for internal traffic analysis. 

 I intentionally designed the WebMCP interface to expose only aggregate information. 

 The get_link_analytics tool returns: 

 
 total clicks 
 latest click timestamp 
 

 It does not expose raw IP addresses, User-Agent strings, referrers, or individual click events. 

 Read operations are also explicitly marked with readOnlyHint: true , giving agents additional information about which actions are safe to execute without modifying application state. 

 Challenges I faced 

 One of the most interesting challenges was that implementing the tools themselves was not enough. 

 WebMCP requires the document to run in the appropriate browser security context, so I had to configure origin isolation using: 
 Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp
 
 I also added configurable support for the WebMCP Origin Trial token so the application can participate in the browser experiment without hardcoding environment-specific credentials. 

 Another challenge was deciding where WebMCP should stop. 

 It would have been easy to create a parallel API layer, duplicate validation in JavaScript, or rebuild the UI using a frontend framework. Instead, I kept the existing application as the source of truth and exposed only the capabilities an agent actually needs. 

 That kept the implementation small, maintainable, and aligned with the progressive nature of WebMCP. 

 What I learned 

 The biggest lesson was that making a website agent-friendly is very different from adding AI to a website. 

 There is no LLM inside Go Link Shortener. 

 Instead, WebMCP gives external agents a structured contract describing what the website can do. 

 This changes the integration model from: 
 Agent → inspect DOM → understand UI → simulate clicks
 
 to: 
 Agent → discover tools → execute structured action
 
 I also learned that good tool design matters as much as implementation. Tool names, descriptions, JSON schemas, read-only annotations, error handling, and privacy boundaries directly affect how reliably an agent can interact with the application. 

 What's next 

 The next steps would be to expand the agent-native interface with capabilities such as: 

 
 listing and searching previously created links 
 safely deleting or disabling short links 
 richer aggregate analytics 
 expiration dates 
 QR code generation 
 authenticated link management 
 

 The important part is that these features can continue using the same architecture: normal web functionality for humans, structured WebMCP capabilities for agents. 

 Go Link Shortener remains a simple web application. 

 It just no longer assumes that every visitor using it has fingers.
