title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: NetLab
pitch: A browser-based network simulator where people and AI agents troubleshoot the same live network together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A browser-based network simulator where people and AI agents troubleshoot the same live network together through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Website opened inside ChatGPT Browser ChatGPT Diagnosing with the help of WebMCP tools NetLab Network Creation NetLab exposed WebMCP Tools used by ChatGPT ChatGPT highlighting the faulty node in network through the highlight_node tool ChatGPT fixing the faulty node through the WebMCP Tool Inspiration Network simulators are great for learning because you can experiment with routers, IP addresses, gateways and routes without needing physical networking hardware. But when something breaks, the experience is still very manual. A topology may look perfectly fine while one incorrect gateway or missing route prevents two machines from communicating. You then have to open devices one by one, inspect their interfaces and routing tables, run tests, and work backwards until you find the problem. That felt like a good place to explore WebMCP. Instead of building another chatbot inside a simulator, I wanted to see what would happen if the simulator itself became understandable and operable by an external AI agent , while the user continued working in the same interface. That became NetLab . What NetLab does NetLab is a lightweight browser-based network simulation lab. A user can: create PCs and routers connect and disconnect devices configure IPv4 addresses and CIDR prefixes configure default gateways configure router interfaces add and remove static routes load working and intentionally broken network labs run connectivity tests see the forward and return packet paths inspect exactly where and why routing fails The networking behavior is handled by NetLab itself. It has a deterministic client-side simulation engine for IPv4 addressing, subnet logic, gateways, directly connected networks, static routing and bidirectional reachability. In other words, the language model does not decide whether a network works. ChatGPT reasons about the result; NetLab decides the result. Why WebMCP fits this use case A network simulator contains much more state than what is immediately visible on the canvas. Two routers may look correctly connected while their interface addresses or routing tables make communication impossible. Without structured access, an agent would have to inspect the UI, open individual devices, read form fields, understand what each control represents and then attempt to operate the application through the interface. With WebMCP, NetLab exposes meaningful networking capabilities directly. The current site tools are: get_topology get_device_state test_connectivity highlight_device add_static_route remove_static_route This allows ChatGPT to work with the actual network state rather than infer it from screenshots. For example, in the included Broken Static Routing Challenge : PC-01 cannot reach PC-02. ChatGPT reads the live topology. It runs NetLab's connectivity simulator. It inspects the relevant router. It identifies the missing return route. It can highlight that router directly in the user's canvas. When asked, it adds the missing static route. It runs the simulator again and NetLab verifies that connectivity now succeeds. The important part is that the human and the agent are not working with separate copies of the network. They are both operating the same live lab state . If the human changes the network manually, the next tool call sees that change. If the agent modifies a route, the user immediately sees it in the same inspector. How I built it I first built NetLab as a normal network simulator before adding WebMCP. The application uses a visual topology canvas for manipulating devices and connections, while the network itself is represented as structured client-side state. The simulator implements the core Layer-3 logic separately from the UI so that both human actions and agent actions can reuse the same behavior. At a high level: Human UI → Application actions → Shared lab state → Network simulator and: WebMCP tools → Application actions → Shared lab state → Network simulator This was important because I did not want a separate "AI version" of NetLab's behavior. The WebMCP tools are registered using the imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Read tools expose concise networking state instead of React or framework internals, and write tools reuse the same application actions used by the normal interface. Everything currently runs client-side. NetLab does not require a backend or an embedded AI model. Challenges The first challenge was scope. It would have been very easy to turn this into an attempt to recreate Packet Tracer, which was neither realistic nor necessary for the idea I wanted to demonstrate. So I deliberately kept the networking scope focused on PCs, routers, IPv4, CIDR, default gateways and static routing. This was enough to make troubleshooting real without pretending NetLab was a full network emulator. The second challenge was keeping the simulator trustworthy. Connectivity needed to come from deterministic network logic rather than from the AI. That meant handling forward and return paths, subnet checks, next-hop resolution, static-route matching and useful failure conditions correctly. The third challenge was WebMCP itself. Tool design mattered more than simply exposing lots of functions. I kept the surface intentionally small and domain-specific so an agent could clearly understand when to inspect the network, when to run a simulation and when to make a routing change. Testing was also interesting because WebMCP is still emerging. I verified the tools directly in Chrome with WebMCP testing enabled and then tested the full human-agent workflow inside ChatGPT's in-app browser. What I learned The biggest thing I learned from this project is that making a web application "agent-native" is not the same as adding AI to it. The useful part is deciding which pieces should remain deterministic application logic, which capabilities should be exposed as tools, and where the human should stay in control. For NetLab: the simulator owns networking truth WebMCP exposes structured capabilities the agent reasons over those capabilities the human still sees and controls the live workspace That division ended up being much more interesting than simply asking an LLM to operate the UI. What's next NetLab is intentionally a small Layer-3 simulator today, but the same interaction model could extend much further. Future versions could explore switches, VLANs, ARP, DHCP, NAT, dynamic routing protocols and richer challenge generation. More interesting to me is the collaborative side: an agent could generate troubleshooting labs, guide a learner without directly giving away the answer, explain packet behavior step by step, or validate a network design while the user continues modifying it manually. For this challenge, I wanted to get the core idea right first: a network simulator where a person and their agent can inspect, troubleshoot and change the same executable environment together. I also designed and implemented the six site tools that let ChatGPT inspect, diagnose, highlight, modify, and re-test the same live network used by the human. title: Scopebox
pitch: Turn human intent into the live capability boundary for web agents. Scopebox lets agents act only inside explicitly framed fields and request the smallest scope expansion when needed.
about_excerpt: Turn human intent into the live capability boundary for web agents. Scopebox lets agents act only inside explicitly framed fields and request the smallest scope expansion when needed. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP gives web agents a powerful new ability: websites can expose native tools that agents can call directly. That raises a second question: Who decides what the agent is allowed to change right now? Scopebox explores a simple answer: The agent can only touch what the human frames. Instead of giving an agent a fixed set of write capabilities, Scopebox turns a human visual selection into the live capability boundary. The demo uses a deliberately small six-field launch board so that this interaction is easy to see, but the pattern is meant to generalize to CMSs, CRMs, admin dashboards, forms, and internal tools. What it does Scopebox separates broad visibility from narrow write authority. The agent can inspect the whole page, but initially has no write capability. A human can frame specific fields, such as Headline and Description. The page then dynamically exposes WebMCP write tools that are valid only for that exact scope. If the agent discovers that another field must change, it cannot expand its own authority. It requests the smallest necessary scope expansion and waits. The human can either keep the current scope or explicitly expand it. When the human approves an expansion: the capability boundary changes, only the newly granted field becomes writable, the pending WebMCP request resolves, and the agent continues automatically in the same turn. No extra chat message such as “I pressed it” is required. When the bounded changes are ready, the agent can submit them for review, but it cannot accept its own review, publish, or deploy. The final decision remains human. How we built it Scopebox is a small JavaScript WebMCP prototype built around a canonical application state. The visible Launch Board is intentionally not an ordinary editable form. Agent mutations must pass through the registered WebMCP capability surface. The main control mechanisms are: Dynamic WebMCP capabilities The tools exposed to the agent change with the current human frame. At Scope v0, the agent can inspect the workspace and active scope. After the human frames writable fields, write and scope-expansion capabilities become available. Exact scopeVersion binding Write capabilities are bound to the exact scope version under which they were granted. A stale capability fails closed with HOLD / SCOPE_STALE . Mixed in-scope and out-of-scope updates fail atomically rather than partially applying. Human-gated scope expansion request_scope_expansion creates a visible Human decision surface and remains pending while the human decides. Approval resolves the same Site-tool call and lets the agent continue automatically. Denial preserves the existing scope. Timeout, cancellation, replacement, and stale-request paths fail closed. Exact reviewId binding Human review actions are bound to the exact active review ID. Missing review identity fails with HOLD / REVIEW_ID_REQUIRED . A stale or mismatched review fails with HOLD / REVIEW_STALE . Review submission also closes the write tools until the human either returns the change set to draft or accepts it. Canonical field surface Normal browser editing does not create hidden or “ghost” agent edits. The canonical application store wins over DOM-only mutations, and the agent must use the scoped WebMCP write capability to change canonical state. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not creating a tool call. It was preserving the meaning of human authority across a live interaction. A scope-expansion request originally behaved like a normal short-lived tool call. Refreshing the registered capability surface could cancel the very request that was waiting for the human. We changed the continuation model so that capability registration is deferred while the Human decision is in flight. The pending call now resolves with the exact Human decision, after which the agent re-inspects the new scope and continues in the same turn. Another challenge was separating what the browser can display from what the agent is actually authorized to mutate. Making the Launch Board canonical and non-editable through ordinary browser form interaction closed that gap. Accomplishments The final prototype demonstrates: dynamic WebMCP capabilities driven by a Human visual frame exact scope-version binding atomic failure for out-of-scope edits Human-only scope expansion automatic same-turn continuation after Human approval exact review-ID binding stale review and stale scope fail-closed behavior write-tool closure during Human review Return to Draft and Accept flows canonical protection against browser-only ghost edits a live public deployment tested through ChatGPT's in-app browser The final validation suite passes 21 tests with 0 failures . What we learned WebMCP is not only a way to give agents more tools. Because tools can be registered dynamically, the capability surface itself can become part of the user interface. That makes it possible to treat human intent as something operational rather than merely conversational. The Human gesture does not just tell the agent what the user wants. It changes what the agent is technically capable of doing. What's next The Launch Board is only one example. The same interaction pattern could be applied anywhere a web application contains actions that should remain bounded by explicit Human intent: CMS content fields CRM records and deal stages administrative permissions internal operations tools structured forms approval workflows Different interfaces can expose different capability surfaces while keeping the same rule: The agent can only touch what the human frames. title: AdGate
pitch: AdGate creates ad opportunities for the AI-native era: pay a small fee for instant AI access, or unlock the same insight free through a sponsor-supported experience. Which do you choose?
about_excerpt: AdGate creates ad opportunities for the AI-native era: pay a small fee for instant AI access, or unlock the same insight free through a sponsor-supported experience. Which do you choose? Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The arrival of AI agents is dramatically changing how people consume web content. In the past, people would visit and read websites one by one. Today, AI can collect information on their behalf by scraping sources such as technical blogs. This is a great user experience for end users. However, it can also mean that website operators and the businesses that advertise on those sites lose their opportunity to reach users. This product was inspired by that problem. I wanted agents to be able to use a publisher’s structured capabilities while keeping people clearly in control of how access is granted. By combining WebMCP with x402, I wanted to explore a model where users who value convenience can make a micropayment for a nearly automated experience, while users who do not want to pay can access premium content by viewing a short advertisement. What it does For this project, I created a fictional recipe website. It includes a WebMCP-compatible tool called analyze_recipe , which provides more detailed analysis as a premium feature. There are two ways to access the premium feature: View an owned sponsor message (advertisement) for eight seconds. Explicitly approve a 0.01 testnet USDC x402 payment on Base Sepolia. Both paths authorize the same protected analysis endpoint. The original tool invocation then resumes with one structured result containing a recipe summary, nutrition notes, practical suggestions, and a general-information disclaimer. The same gate is also used by the visible Analyze this recipe button, so people and agents use one coherent product flow rather than separate experiences. I felt WebMCP was a good fit because agents can discover and invoke typed, page-owned capabilities instead of scraping a page or guessing which buttons to click. Users can make an important decision in the middle of the same invocation without losing the shared context. How we built it The React/Vite frontend registers analyze_recipe with document.modelContext.registerTool , with a navigator.modelContext compatibility fallback. A shared GateCoordinator keeps one request alive while the page renders the sponsor or payment experience, propagates cancellation, and resolves the result exactly once. The x402-enabled resource server, built with Hono, manages authorization and canonical deterministic analysis. Sponsor sessions, single-use grants, and their consumption state are stored in a named Cloudflare Durable Object. For the payment path, the app displays Base Sepolia terms before wallet access and then uses x402 exact-payment authorization. An optional Hono/viem facilitator verifies and settles the testnet payment. The browser never holds a private key, and the AI never controls the wallet. I used Codex to turn product decisions into executable specifications, build the frontend/server/facilitator boundaries, write focused tests, diagnose lifecycle and payment-receipt issues, create fake-host browser journeys, and run the final release checks. Human decisions remained explicit for product scope, payment policy, security constraints, deployment, and publication. Both the frontend and backend are deployed on Cloudflare. Challenges we ran into One challenge was deciding how to combine WebMCP and x402, as well as who should manage the wallet and where it should be managed. For the smoothest user experience, a server-managed wallet such as Privy could be a good option. However, this project focuses on WebMCP, where people and AI work together in a visible browser environment. For that reason, I deliberately chose a conventional MetaMask wallet for this demo. This is only a choice for the current demo. In the future, I believe the product should support WalletConnect and allow users to choose flexibly between wallet options such as MetaMask and Privy. With this architecture, I separated the responsibilities of AI and human interaction. The AI handles the process automatically up to the payment step. As the human-in-the-loop, the person reviews the payment details. If they decide not to pay, they can view an advertisement and be guided to premium access instead. Designing this architecture was the most difficult part of the project. Accomplishments that we're proud of Although the development period was short, I am proud that I was able to learn WebMCP and combine it with x402 and Cloudflare technologies to turn this idea into a working product. I spent more time than usual thinking through the idea and designing the architecture. It is a very simple demo, but I am proud that I was able to build it as a new advertising model for the AI-native era. What we learned The biggest lesson was gaining a practical understanding of WebMCP. Building with it helped me understand how it differs from MCP. Because WebMCP is based in a visible browser environment, I think it makes it easier to build products with a clear separation of responsibilities between people and AI. I also found this to be highly compatible with x402. What's next for AdGate Next, I would like to expand this gate to other structured publisher resources, such as news, research, and creator tools. To make it more broadly useful, I would like to build a dashboard for sponsors and make the supported blockchains and assets more flexible. For production, the payment path would need authentication, rate limits, monitoring, treasury controls, stronger key management, and evaluation of production payment rails. I would also like to explore privacy-preserving sponsor measurement and observability while maintaining a clear boundary for explicit human choice. title: OpenAct
pitch: A confirmation-first WebMCP agent for screen reader users. The screen reader stays the interface; WebMCP is the actuator.
about_excerpt: A confirmation-first WebMCP agent for screen reader users. The screen reader stays the interface; WebMCP is the actuator. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP can expose higher-level page actions, but putting agent-oriented tools into the accessibility tree would make them appear as page content to screen readers. OpenAct explores the indirect model instead: an agent can reason about available actions while the screen reader remains the user's interface. What it does An NVDA user describes an action in natural language. OpenAct discovers native WebMCP tools, or conservatively infers tools when native tools are unavailable. It proposes exactly one call, presents an accessible and editable confirmation dialog, executes only after explicit confirmation, and speaks the result. The demo is a fictional Northstar City permit workflow with two equivalent routes: /baseline : a keyboard and screen-reader-operable form without WebMCP. /instrumented : the same form with four native tools registered through document.modelContext . The tools are save_property_details , save_project_details , review_application , and submit_application . Why WebMCP OpenAct uses WebMCP as an action layer rather than another interface a screen reader must navigate. Native tools give an agent structured actions and schemas while the user keeps the familiar NVDA interaction model. This makes higher-level assistance possible without placing agent-only content or metadata in the accessibility tree. How it works One shared action definition generates both the accessible HTML form and each WebMCP tool. A parity test fails the build if their labels, required fields, enums, or schemas drift. The Chrome MV3 extension discovers page tools and enforces authorization. The NVDA add-on owns the reasoning layer, confirmation dialog, settings, speech, and a standard-library localhost relay. The relay binds to 127.0.0.1 and pairs through a one-time code. At runtime, the NVDA add-on uses the OpenAI Responses API with a configurable model that defaults to gpt-5.4-mini . It sends bounded context with store: false and requires a strict call , clarify , or refuse decision. The model can propose an action, but it cannot authorize or execute one. Safety and accessibility Every call requires confirmation. Unknown reversibility is treated as irreversible. HMAC covers the call ID, tool name, timestamp, and canonical arguments. Expired, replayed, invalid, or retargeted confirmations are rejected. A kill switch blocks new requests and clears queued work. The autobridge fails closed on ambiguous, stale, unnamed, or unsupported controls. Telemetry is metadata-only and excludes utterances, arguments, form values, API keys, and unrestricted URLs. No agent-oriented text or metadata is added to the accessibility tree. The visible form remains fully usable without OpenAct. Verification The repository includes unit, property, cross-language, browser, accessibility, native Chrome, coverage, and mutation checks. Native verification drives all four tools in installed Chrome 151 with WebMCP enabled and no injected modelContext . Axe reports zero automated violations on the tested routes and states. Honest limits WebMCP does not make an inaccessible website accessible. It exposes actions, not missing labels, keyboard support, structure, or comprehension. This prototype has not been validated with disabled participants and makes no measured task-completion claim. Northstar City and all demo data are fictional. The native page round trip is verified in Chrome. ChatGPT's in-app browser and the complete packed extension, relay, and installed NVDA path remain pending manual verification. title: GrandGrandMCP
pitch: Book a doctor's appointment just by talking — no forms, no dropdowns. WebMCP lets an AI agent do it for you, and it asks if something's unclear instead of guessing.
about_excerpt: Book a doctor's appointment just by talking — no forms, no dropdowns. WebMCP lets an AI agent do it for you, and it asks if something's unclear instead of guessing. Like Comment Story Updates GranGrandMCP Inspiration Booking a medical appointment online is a perfect example of that barrier. It's a routine task for most people, but for someone elderly, or unfamiliar with dropdowns and date pickers, a five-field form can be genuinely frustrating. We wanted to see what that experience looks like when an agent can act on someone's behalf — and, just as importantly, when it knows to ask instead of guess. What it does GrandGrandMCP is an appointment-booking calendar where a person can type or speak a plain-language request — "book me a doctor's appointment for tomorrow morning" — and an AI agent finds an open slot, books it, and drops it onto a visual calendar next to the user's existing personal events (bank errands, birthdays). If the agent doesn't have a detail it needs, like the patient's name, the app pauses mid-booking and asks — a single, friendly follow-up question instead of silently making something up. How we built it A single Cloudflare Worker serves both the frontend and the API from one origin, backed by D1 for storage — appointments and personal calendar events both persist there, so the agenda survives a page reload. The frontend registers three tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : search_available_slots , book_appointment , and check_appointment_status , each with a JSON Schema describing its inputs. book_appointment 's execute callback checks whether a patient name was provided. If not, it calls client.requestUserInteraction() — a WebMCP feature that pauses the agent's tool call and lets the page ask the person directly, right under the calendar, before completing the booking. Voice input uses the browser's native SpeechRecognition API, so a request can be typed or spoken. The calendar itself is a minimalist, pastel-themed UI built from scratch, with no framework — just HTML, CSS, and vanilla JS. Challenges we ran into executeTool() doesn't return what you'd expect. When calling our tools through Chrome's native document.modelContext.executeTool() (with the WebMCP flag enabled), the result came back wrapped in MCP-style content blocks instead of the plain object our own execute() function returns. We didn't catch this until a booking confirmation printed undefined for the date and time — which led us to write a small normalization layer that unwraps both shapes transparently. Fragile natural-language parsing. Our first attempt at pulling a patient's name out of a sentence used a regex anchored on the word "for" — which broke as soon as a message contained "for" twice (e.g. "...for John Smith for Saturday"). We replaced it with a capitalized-name heuristic, and more importantly, leaned on requestUserInteraction so the tool itself doesn't need to be clever about parsing — it can just ask. State that quietly wasn't persisting. Early on, the calendar looked complete, but personal events were only seeded in JavaScript memory, and booked appointments weren't being re-fetched from D1 on page load. Everything looked right until a refresh made it obvious. What we learned WebMCP is at its best when it replaces genuine friction — not when it's added to a flow that would work the same without it. The most valuable primitive we used wasn't tool registration itself, it was requestUserInteraction : the ability for a tool to pause and loop a human back in is what makes an agent feel collaborative instead of either fully autonomous or fully manual. What's next I want to expand this idea to other fields for someone elderly, not just medical. title: SupplyPilot
pitch: Procurement agents that search, compare, and prepare purchases — while humans keep the final say.
about_excerpt:
Procurement agents that search, compare, and prepare purchases — while humans keep the final say.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Why SupplyPilot 

 Small-business owners often spend hours comparing suppliers, checking trust, balancing warranty and delivery requirements, and preparing purchases. SupplyPilot turns that fragmented workflow into a structured human-agent collaboration. 

 What it does 

 A user can ask for something concrete such as “Find me 5 reliable laptops under $2,500 with at least a 1-year warranty.” SupplyPilot ranks marketplace offers using supplier verification, requirement fit, availability, budget, warranty, delivery speed, and rating. The agent can compare the shortlist, refine constraints, request a simulated quote, prepare a purchase draft, and retrieve order status. 

 Why WebMCP is the right fit 

 SupplyPilot does not make an agent guess through buttons and page structure. The site exposes procurement capabilities directly with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , giving a WebMCP-aware agent structured inputs and deterministic outputs for marketplace search, supplier inspection, comparison, draft creation and revision, quote requests, purchase confirmation, and order tracking. 

 That creates a cleaner UX: the person states the business goal, the agent handles the repetitive procurement steps, and the website remains the source of truth for marketplace state. 

 Human control is deliberate 

 The most important boundary is the purchase itself. The agent cannot approve its own spending decision . If it calls confirm_purchase before the human explicitly approves the active draft in the SupplyPilot UI, the tool returns HUMAN_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED . Only after the person presses Confirm Purchase can the agent complete the simulated order. 

 This demonstrates what people and agents can do together that is difficult with ordinary web automation: the agent can reliably operate a structured procurement workflow while the human retains authority at the highest-risk step. 

 Demo flow 

 
 Search for 5 reliable laptops under $2,500 with at least a one-year warranty. 
 Compare and refine the shortlist. 
 Prepare a purchase draft. 
 Attempt agent confirmation and show HUMAN_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED . 
 Human approves the exact draft in the UI. 
 Agent completes the simulated order and checks status. 
 

 Implementation 

 SupplyPilot is a zero-build HTML/CSS/JavaScript application deployed over HTTPS on Netlify. Marketplace records are deterministic demo data so judges can reproduce the same workflow reliably. No real payment is processed.

title: Consilium WebMCP
pitch: Your browser agent can understand your goals, show evidence, and help you plan your goals and aspirations with you, of course, always being in control.
about_excerpt: Your browser agent can understand your goals, show evidence, and help you plan your goals and aspirations with you, of course, always being in control. Like Comment Story Updates 4 Meet Maya: a persistent WebMCP personal OS where goals, history and agent actions stay grounded, inspectable and user-controlled. Goals & Projects: six life areas become structured WebMCP state, clear goals, durable context and agent-ready actions. Progress & Patterns: longitudinal memory surfaces evidence-backed trends, counterevidence and what should change next. Morning Brief: D1 history + Vectorize retrieval turn yesterday’s evidence into today’s ranked, explainable priorities. Journal & Reflection: structured daily memory captures outcomes, failures and adaptations so the agent learns over time. Consult the Council: Workers AI combines personal history with verified advisor texts, preserving citations and disagreement. Library & Advisors: user-appointed, source-bounded advisors keep AI guidance grounded in verified public-domain evidence. Transparency & Analytics: every WebMCP call exposes inputs, evidence, confidence and state effects—no hidden mutation. Inspiration Useful advice needs more than just relying on ones own thinking. A useful system that is a companion in ones daily life needs to remember what happend with your goals and how you pursued them and understand your feelings and life as it evolves toward achieving what you aspire to in different areas of your life. Consilium is a system that I have been working on for quite a while before this challenge. I started to develop it to help me understand my life and my decisions better by using advice I used to apply, or try to apply from books that inspired me. For this challenge, I wanted to show how a browser agent can work with my system through the exciting new technology, WebMCP, without of course, it replacing my role or taking over decisions or becoming some kind of to-do planner. What it does I didnt want to show any of my private thoughts or details for this challenge, so I created the demo using a fictional demo person called Maya. She is a freelancer like me (actually, I am a teacher moonlighting as a developer), and she is balancing work, family responsibilities and limited energy, drawing loosely on pressures I know from my own life and from trying to build my business at night and teaching during the day. Her goals, her progress, the journal and evening reflection run across six connected areas: physical, mental, spiritual, social, financial and vocational. In my original system I associate areas with different advisors. For this demo, I kept the council to three authors that are in the public-domain. Each advisor, or council member, is represented by a book author whose work I want to keep applying over time. In the past, I would have read a book once and then slowly lost the benefit or didn't know how to apply most effectively in my life. The browser agent can read the current goals, look at the history of my goals and recognise patterns, and consult my, or in this demo, Maya's appointed council. My actual system vectorises book passages so that relevant parts can be retrieved when I consult that advisor. I chose Marcus Aurelius (Meditations), Epictetus and Sun Tzu (Art of War) for this demo, but I have Stephen Covey, Musashi, Carl Jung and others in my actual council. I used a small selection of public-domain books so I could provide inspectable book excerpts and locations (I ran into issues before where AI would hallucinate advice etc. So, I make it literally show me where it's getting the advice from). Personal records and book passages used for advice are retrieved separately and resolved against canonical D1 records, but on my actual system I am using Postgres to store everything. Advice given isnt something that automatically changes my plans and goals etc. For the demo, the agent stages an action and then the person reviews the text. A separate commit turns the approved action into a tracked "Today" goal. An evening reflection is in the form of my journaling habit and records readiness, six plain-English answers and a status for every active goal I have today. Missed goals require an explanation and adaptation of the progress and influence how the advice unfolds over time, so if I miss something or just don't have time or can't be bothered, the system carries that forward and adjusts priorities etc. The WebMCP Component The human interface and browser agent operate on the same session records. Typed tools expose context, history, patterns, appointments, goals, progress through the goals, the journal, evening reflection, morning brief, consultation, inspection and proposals. Twelve tools are registered for this demo. There is a 13th one, commit_proposed_action. It is available only while the session has a pending proposal. Its availability is not consent. I need the browser agent to obtain human approval, then the server separately checks ownership, proposal state and one-use commitment. How I built it The page registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool, JSON schemas and annotations. I setup a Cloudflare Worker that serves the interface and API (Totally impressed by these Cloudflare workers, actually the whole suite is really amazing). D1 owns application records, source text and audit state. Workers AI produces BGE query embeddings, Vectorize retrieves filtered candidates, on my home system I use ChromaDB for this part and the server resolves their IDs back to canonical records. Each council consultation attempts one bounded Workers AI structured response. If that output fails validation, the system labels and then uses the deterministic fallback instead. Validation checks its shape, council member/advisor-owned evidence references and quoted source phrases. Reflection synthesis and morning-brief generation are transformations of recorded evidence, not extra model deliberation. The browser agent is separate from the application's Workers AI inference. Challenges and current limitations Getting a useful recommendation is not enough. I found it really challenging to keep where it came from, its uncertainty, session ownership and the approval boundary visible at all times. My latest rehearsal rejected malformed model output and displayed a labelled fallback and thats not presented as successful fresh AI reasoning. The demo and the video must preserve the actual result mode. The source packs are super small for the demo, which kind of breaks my heart, because i really wanted to show the coolness of being able to "plug in" a book and then have advice grounded in that author's actual writing, but I kept it small for this demo, after all, its about the WebMCP, not my existing system. Exact quote identity does not prove that every interpretation is correct. This is not a system operating on complete-book understanding, and therefore isnt a hallucination-free system. I ran into heaps of problems with AI generated advice inventing or misattributing sources. That is why I started storing the source passages separately and making the system resolve retrieved IDs back to the original text. But again, I really wanted to represent my system and its use of WebMCP as clearly as possible here for you to see. Believe me though, it's super cool. What I learned The useful boundary is between understanding, proposing and applying. Memory was a big thing for this system and being able to use all the information I collected about myself in my reflections and progress challenges matters because outcomes and counterexamples affect the next plan of attack when working towards goal achievement, rather than just filling a history panel with data that isnt being used to make my journey better. Pre-existing work and demo data The original Consilium system, the visuals and workflows have been in development by me for quite some time. The Cloudflare adaptation and WebMCP edition have their own public history. The repository's PREEXISTING.md shows reused work and the challenge-specific changes. This demo uses fictional personal records and public-domain excerpts, not the original private journals or full vector library (it's around 23,000 vectors). Its frozen fictional timeline is disclosed in the interface. Try it I hope you can give the live application a go in a WebMCP-capable browser. You dont need an account for the demo. Ask the browser agent to read the goals and history, then explain one pattern with both supporting evidence and a counterexample, without changing anything. Inspect a council result's actual generation mode, trace and exact excerpts. Request the proposal and approve its text only if you want it committed. The repository's DEMO.md supplies more testing instructions. title: Rove
pitch: Rove turns open-web shopping into a shared workspace where people and browser agents research, refine, and save real retailer finds together.
about_excerpt: Rove turns open-web shopping into a shared workspace where people and browser agents research, refine, and save real retailer finds together. Like Comment Story Updates Threads of Clothes you saved Clothes and Styles for you by Agent Update Profile Welcome and Profile setup More Clothes List of Saved Prompts and their finds Inspiration Shopping across the open web is fragmented. Products live across dozens of retailer tabs, useful recommendations disappear inside chat transcripts, and the human often cannot refine an agent’s work without starting over. That inspired Rove: a shared fashion research workspace where a person and a browser agent work on the same shopping mission. The agent handles open-web research while the human stays in control of preferences, budgets, product review, selective replacement, and the final cart. What it does Rove turns a natural shopping request—such as “Find three shirts, three pants, sneakers, and a fragrance for four days in Cancún under C$450”—into a structured research mission. The browser agent can: Read the user-approved style profile. Translate the request into quantities, categories, occasions, and budgets. Claim prioritized retailer research targets. Browse live retailer pages. Progressively publish grounded products with direct images and canonical links. Enrich products with availability, pricing, materials, and variants. Report research progress and unresolved needs. Add exact products to the shared cart. At the same time, the human can: Watch products arrive progressively. Filter and compare recommendations. Inspect retailer provenance. Accept the complete edit or replace only selected items. Request completely fresh research without duplicate links. Save completed prompts and accepted products locally. Manage a cross-retailer cart called “Your Thread.” Rove keeps completed missions separate from the current mission, so previous research remains useful without confusing the active task. How we built it Rove is a client-only application built with Nuxt 4, Vue 3, strict TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and the imperative WebMCP API. It registers 17 tools through document.modelContext , covering profile setup, mission planning, retailer scheduling, candidate publication, product enrichment, recommendation review, research history, and cart management. The most important architectural decision was giving the interface and WebMCP tools the same typed domain action layer. Agent actions do not update a separate hidden system: they produce the same visible state changes as human actions. A deterministic research scheduler ranks retailer targets based on: Requested categories and quantities. Remaining unmet needs. Style and occasion relevance. Department compatibility. Per-item and overall budgets. Retailer capabilities. Scarce categories such as fragrance. Published candidates pass through validation for retailer domains, canonical product URLs, mission identity, budgets, duplicate history, and required imagery. Recommendation order combines relevance, budget fit, profile alignment, availability, freshness, and retailer diversity. The application uses browser-local persistence and requires no backend, database, account, API key, embedded chatbot, or OpenAI API call. It is deployed as a static Netlify application and remains usable when WebMCP is unavailable. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making agent research behave like a reliable product workflow instead of an open-ended chat. Retailer information is inconsistent. Some products have sizes and colours, while fragrances and accessories may have neither. We had to introduce category-aware variant handling so a perfume could not accidentally inherit an invalid clothing colour or size. Selective replacement was another difficult problem. When the user rejected one product, the system initially risked replacing or hiding accepted products. We redesigned the review workflow so accepted products remain visible and only explicitly rejected items become new research targets. We also had to solve duplicate prevention across repeated missions. Rove now retains previously surfaced and accepted product links so “research again” can use past preferences as context without relisting the same products. Product imagery created additional complexity because retailer image URLs vary and can fail after publication. We added direct-image validation, visible fallbacks, and consistent image framing so missing or differently sized assets do not break the interface. Finally, we had to balance a sophisticated agent workflow with a simple human experience. Mission state, research queues, replacement context, saved history, and the cart all needed to remain understandable without exposing internal orchestration details. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that Rove feels like a complete fashion product rather than a WebMCP demonstration screen. Key accomplishments include: Seventeen working WebMCP tools with closed schemas and clear annotations. One shared action boundary for human and agent operations. Progressive multi-retailer research with visible state changes. Quantity-aware and budget-aware mission fulfilment. Selective product replacement without disturbing accepted items. Fresh research that avoids previously listed links. Category-aware cart variants for clothing, fragrance, and accessories. Saved missions with locally preserved prompts and accepted edits. A polished, responsive, accessible Rove interface. A deterministic test suite with 68 passing tests, strict type checking, and verified production builds. What we learned We learned that useful agent experiences depend more on state design and tool contracts than on one large prompt. Small, purpose-built tools with explicit schemas gave the browser agent clearer responsibilities and made failures easier to understand. A persisted state machine also made the collaboration resilient: the agent could report what it had completed, what remained unresolved, and what it should do next. We also learned that human control must be visible. Users need to see what the agent changed, preserve decisions they already approved, and request corrections without restarting the entire workflow. Most importantly, WebMCP works best when it is integrated into the product’s real domain model. The tools should not sit beside the application—they should operate the application. What's next for Rove Next, we want to expand Rove with: More retailer adapters and stronger regional availability support. Better price and inventory freshness indicators. Optional, privacy-conscious cross-device synchronization. Visual style references and wardrobe-aware recommendations. Stronger accessibility and mobile interaction testing. User-controlled retailer preferences and sustainability signals. Cleaner retailer checkout handoffs while keeping purchasing on official retailer sites. Evaluations that measure duplicate rate, budget adherence, research completion, and recommendation acceptance. Our long-term vision is for Rove to become the open-web workspace where people and agents build confident shopping decisions together. title: Waypoint
pitch: Live Support Co-browsing via WebMCP & PartyKit
about_excerpt: Live Support Co-browsing via WebMCP & PartyKit Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration & Why WebMCP is the Right Fit Traditional co-browsing tools stream DOM trees or broadcast video feeds over WebRTC. That architecture grants support representatives raw access to customer screens, exposing credit card numbers, passwords, and private inputs. WebMCP provides a structured alternative: typed tool contracts registered directly on document.modelContext . Waypoint maps customer support to WebMCP tools. Because WebMCP tools exist only on the document that registered them, execution remains structurally confined to the customer's local session. Representatives cannot touch the DOM or execute actions unilaterally; they interact solely through declared schemas. WebMCP turns an intrusive, high-risk screen share into a bounded execution interface. What It Does & How It Creates a Better User Experience Waypoint is a zero-trust co-browsing and remote support platform built on WebMCP and edge WebSockets. Instead of sharing screens or streaming DOM mutations, the customer and support rep connect through a shared tool interface: Zero Privacy Invasion : Customers never surrender their screen or expose unrendered form fields to a representative. Explicit Human Consent : When a representative proposes a fix (such as an address correction or coupon code), the customer sees a native modal showing the exact arguments before deciding to approve or reject it. Kilobytes Instead of Megabytes : By replacing video feeds with lightweight JSON protocol events over WebSockets, Waypoint drops bandwidth consumption from 2.4 MB/s (WebRTC) to 0.8 KB/s. Sessions stay fast and responsive even on unstable mobile connections. Zero Software Installation : Customers do not need browser extensions or screen-sharing desktop agents. Support operates entirely within standard browser capabilities. Read-Only State Streaming : Tools marked with readOnlyHint: true stream safe state updates (cart totals, items, active errors) to the rep's console with zero bandwidth overhead and zero screen recording. What People and Agents Can Do Together That Was Difficult Before Before WebMCP, co-browsing forced an all-or-nothing choice: either give a remote human total control over your screen, or manually follow verbal instructions over phone or chat. Browser AI agents faced a similar hurdle, relying on fragile DOM scraping or screen vision to click around. Waypoint unifies the peers, and browser AI agents around the same tool boundary: An agent inspects cart state using get_order_details and helps configure the order. When an issue requires human escalation (such as an expired coupon code or tricky shipping validation), a human representative connects to the exact same tool space through an edge relay. The representative proposes a structured resolution, which appears natively in the customer's tab for explicit approval. Both human representatives and AI agents operate under the same rule: neither can bypass the customer's approval gate or run unauthorized code on the customer's machine. How We Implemented WebMCP & Architecture Tool Registration : In the customer tab, we register three distinct tools that their agent calls: get_order_details : Marked with readOnlyHint: true to provide an immutable snapshot of items, totals, and active errors without requiring human gating. update_shipping_address : Defined with JSON Schema properties ( name , street , city , zip ) to handle delivery validation. apply_promo_code : Defined with a code property to validate discounts and surface checkout errors. Local Handlers : Each tool definition includes an async execute(args) callback that executes strictly inside the customer's UI state. Schema Serialization & Edge Relay : When a support session opens, the customer tab queries document.modelContext.getTools() , serializes the schemas, and sends them to a PartyKit WebSocket relay. The relay routes messages blindly without storing tokens or user data. Dynamic Console & Approval Gate : The support console receives the schemas and renders input forms on the fly. Submitting a form sends an action_proposed event. The customer tab listens to this event, presents an approval modal, and only invokes the tool once the customer clicks Approve. Challenges We Ran Into AI Prompt Leaks vs Neutral Tool Schemas : During testing with Chrome's MCP Tools extension, descriptions like "If expired, use SUMMER2026" (an oversight) introduced a side effect; the agent updates the code input after it was previously written with the explicit code referenced in the user prompt. Simply removing the additional statement in the tool description prevented the re-write issue. Handling disconnections cleanly required explicit bidirectional teardown. When either the customer or rep leaves, the PartyKit room purges its cached state and immediately notifies the peer, preventing orphaned sessions. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of Co-browsing without screen sharing : Running a full support session requires mere kilobytes of JSON events instead of megabytes of continuous media frames. Structural Confinement : The support agent physically, or digitally, cannot take unauthorized actions. Execution stays locked to the customer's action Unifying AI and Human Interfaces : Interweaving WebAPIs to build tools for AI browser agents that can replace traditional screen sharing software. What We Learned How WebMCP can unlock & further the interaction between humans &a agents Once an application defines its capabilities as structured WebMCP schemas, building secure collaboration features becomes seamless than trying to mask sensitive inputs over an open video feed. title: Archive Evidence Room
pitch: Turn any webpage's history into cited evidence. A WebMCP agent finds comparable captures, inspects archived diffs, and pins findings with their sources to a caseboard shared with you.
about_excerpt: Turn any webpage's history into cited evidence. A WebMCP agent finds comparable captures, inspects archived diffs, and pins findings with their sources to a caseboard shared with you. Like Comment Story Updates The final finding stays beside its cited excerpt, ready for human review, source checking, and Markdown export. A scoped question becomes live coverage across public archives, with Arquivo.pt selected for comparison. The Evidence Room connects four WebMCP tools to one caseboard that the agent and the person can inspect together. One selected window becomes a bounded diff with both source captures and an explicit untrusted text warning. Index records produce six exact capture windows before any archived page body is downloaded. Why I built it Web archives contain real evidence, but working with them still feels like manual archaeology. Find snapshots, open a pile of tabs, compare dates, copy URLs, then try to remember which version actually proved the point. I wanted to ask a browser agent a sharper question: "How did this page change, and can you show me the exact captures that prove it?" This project also has some history. @agntn/archives started in April 2025 as one TypeScript interface over several web archives. It gradually gained caching, lazy provider loading, typed metadata and more sources. In 2026 it grew into a proper agent tool: first native OMP and Pi extensions, then an MCP server, archived body reads, pagination, capture diffs and finally a Nuxt explorer running on Cloudflare Workers. The WebMCP Challenge was a good reason to build the missing piece. Not another chat box, and not four aliases for buttons. I wanted the page itself to become a shared investigation room for a person and an agent. What it does Archive Evidence Room registers four native WebMCP tools through document.modelContext : scope_archive_case defines one historical question and checks which archives have evidence. find_change_windows finds consecutive captures without downloading archived bodies. inspect_archive_change reads one selected pair and returns a short cited diff. pin_archive_finding records whether that diff supports, contradicts or only adds context to the question. Every call updates the same visible caseboard. The agent can do the repetitive archive work, but the person still sees the dates, original URL, provider, underlying Memento archive, diff and final interpretation. No invisible research session and no uncited answer at the end. WebMCP is progressive enhancement here. Without the experimental browser API, the full workflow still works by hand. How I built it The UI is Nuxt 4, Vue and Docus. The server runs on Cloudflare Workers. I used the existing cached /api/coverage , /api/snapshots and /api/diff routes instead of creating a second archive backend for the hackathon. Those routes call the same @agntn/archives executors already used by MCP, OMP and Pi. Discovery is index first. The room requests between 3 and 12 capture records, groups them by exact URL and provider, keeps Memento captures inside the same underlying archive, then ranks useful windows. Archived bodies are fetched only after someone chooses a window to inspect. The result is much faster and much kinder to public archive infrastructure than reading everything up front. The caseboard keeps provenance all the way through. A diff can resolve to captures slightly different from the index rows, so the final citation comes from the diff result, not stale listing metadata. Findings store the interpretation beside the evidence instead of mixing both into one generated paragraph. What was hard Public web archives disagree about almost everything: timestamp formats, URL normalization, replay endpoints, metadata and failure behavior. Even www , default ports or letter case in a path can quietly produce the wrong pair. Memento adds another trap because one provider can return captures from several underlying archives. A plausible diff between unrelated records would be worse than no result, so I made the pairing rules deliberately strict. Cancellation was more subtle. Browser abort signals had to travel through $fetch , Nitro, cache misses and the archive executor. Sharing one cached promise also shared one caller's cancellation with another caller. That was wrong. Each cache miss now owns its request and one closed tab cannot kill another investigation. The other problem is trust. Archived HTML can contain instructions written specifically to manipulate an agent. Treating that as normal tool output would be ridiculous. The room exposes only a bounded text excerpt, marks it as untrusted, renders it as escaped text and keeps it separate from the finding written by the agent. What I learned The useful WebMCP abstraction is not "let the agent click my UI." It is a small protocol with state the user can inspect. caseId and changeId make the steps explicit, while the shared board makes mistakes visible. I also learned that archive research needs honest negative results. No capture in one bounded query does not mean a page never existed. A partial diff cannot prove text was absent outside the compared prefix. The product gets better when those limits stay visible instead of being polished into confidence. For the final smoke test I used sive.rs : seven captures became six safe windows, one exact archived diff and a finding pinned with both capture URLs. The public page does not preload this result because the caseboard belongs to the current browser session. Open the Evidence Room and ask the browser agent to investigate how sive.rs changed between 2020 and 2022 to reproduce the flow. We asked: What if web applications treated autonomous AI agents as first-class citizens? What if an e-commerce and hardware co-design platform exposed its entire feature set natively via structured, typed, in-browser protocol endpoints?

What it does

Hardware Co-Design Studio: Users and AI assistants collaboratively configure high-performance hardware (e.g., neural keypads, cybernetic rings, biometric dials) across materials, finishes, custom laser engravings, and dynamic RGB illuminations.

Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Escrow Security: High-stakes operations like cart checkouts require explicit human approval via cryptographic confirmation modals, preventing unauthorized autonomous transactions.

title: Boardify
pitch: Boardify turns the infinite whiteboard into an agent-native canvas where humans and browser AI co-architect systems via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Boardify turns the infinite whiteboard into an agent-native canvas where humans and browser AI co-architect systems via WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates canvas assets library workflow template notes template er template cloud workflow template tables export shapes code and dsl deployment and sharing Inspiration We've all experienced the frustration of whiteboarding complex software architecture. You open a spatial tool like Miro or Excalidraw, stare at an empty canvas, and wrestle with "blank canvas paralysis." Meanwhile, your AI assistant is confined to a narrow linear chat sidebar in another window. To bridge this gap, engineers have spent years copying code snippets, describing layout ideas in prose, switching tabs, manually drawing boxes, pasting brand logos, and routing arrows. Previous attempts to give AI agents spatial capabilities relied on vision screen-scraping : taking a screenshot of the browser, passing it to an LLM to guess $(x, y)$ pixel coordinates, and synthesizing simulated mouse clicks. This approach is fundamentally flawed—it introduces 3,000ms+ roundtrip latency, breaks across different device pixel ratios and monitor resolutions, and frequently causes cards to collide or overlap. Spatial thinking is inherently non-linear, multi-dimensional, and relational—represented mathematically as a directed graph $G = (V, E)$. Chat interfaces force this multidimensional thought process into a 1-dimensional string of tokens. When the OpenAI & Google WebMCP Challenge was announced, we realized that browser-native agents no longer need to be blind or clumsy. By establishing window.document.modelContext , browser applications can expose structured, type-safe APIs directly to the host model. We asked ourselves: "What if an AI didn't just talk to you about your architecture—what if it pulled up a chair directly at your whiteboard, read the graph in sub-20ms, placed typed SQL tables, routed bezier wires, and untangled layout physics alongside you?" That was the spark for Boardify . What It Does Boardify is the first agent-native spatial whiteboard built from the ground up for the WebMCP standard. It is a shared collaborative workspace where humans bring intuition, taste, and high-level strategy, while browser agents bring speed, scale, and architectural execution. Key capabilities include: 24 First-Class WebMCP Tools: Directly exposed on document.modelContext with strict JSON Schema definitions, encompassing node creation, wire connections, SQL schema tables, tech stack logos, checkpoints, and graph layout physics. Agent Ghost Cursor & Tactile Feedback: Real-time visual agency. When an agent runs a tool, a pulsing Ghost Cursor sweeps across the canvas with an active action badge (e.g., AGENT · tool: add_entity_table ), accompanied by mechanical pop animations and sound design. Instant Relational ERD Generation: Prompt the agent with "table users and orders" , and it creates complete SQL database entity cards equipped with primary keys, foreign keys, data types ( UUID , VARCHAR , TIMESTAMP ), and relational wire linkages. Curated Architecture Vector Logo Library: Over 1,800+ tech logos (Next.js, Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL, Docker, AWS, Stripe, etc.) searchable and spawnable by the agent in milliseconds. Physics-Based Auto-Tidy & Smart Flow: Clean algorithms for topological DAG ordering, force-directed untangling, and semantic clustering. Zero-Friction Multi-Format Export: 1-click export of visual diagrams to clean Markdown documentation, Mermaid flowchart code, structured JSON state, or high-res PNG. Dual-Mode WebMCP Execution: Hooks natively into Chrome Canary ( #enable-webmcp-testing ) and ChatGPT in-app browser sessions, while offering an interactive AI Agent Studio and DevTools console polyfill for standard desktop browsers. How we built it Boardify was engineered using a high-performance, modern web stack tailored for 60fps spatial manipulation: Frontend Core: Next.js 15 (App Router) with React 19, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. Graphics & Spatial Engine: Infinite zoom-and-pan canvas combining HTML5 viewport transforms with high-efficiency SVG Bezier curve rendering. WebMCP Integration Layer ( src/lib/webmcp.ts ): Complete implementation of the WebMCP specification. When the canvas mounts, it registers 24 typed tools to window.document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Multi-Provider LLM Client: Native client adapters for Google Gemini ( gemini-2.0-flash with multi-version fallback across v1beta and v1 ), OpenAI ( gpt-4o-mini ), Anthropic ( claude-3.5-sonnet ), alongside an offline heuristic synthesis engine. ### The Mathematics of Spatial Whiteboarding (LaTeX) Camera Projection & Viewport Transforms: To translate between user screen coordinates $(x_s, y_s)$ and the infinite 2D world space $(x_w, y_w)$, we compute affine viewport transformations using scale factor $C_z$ and pan offsets $(C_x, C_y)$: $$\begin{pmatrix} x_s \ y_s \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} C_x \ C_y \end{pmatrix} + C_z \begin{pmatrix} x_w \ y_w \end{pmatrix}$$ The inverse projection (Screen-to-World) executed during pointer events and agent cursor positioning is: $$\begin{pmatrix} x_w \ y_w \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{x_s - C_x}{C_z} \ \frac{y_s - C_y}{C_z} \end{pmatrix}$$ Cubic Bézier Dynamic Cable Routing: Every wire connecting two nodes $P_0 = (x_0, y_0)$ and $P_3 = (x_3, y_3)$ is generated as a smooth cubic Bézier spline $B(t)$ parameterized over $t \in [0, 1]$: $$B(t) = (1-t)^3 P_0 + 3(1-t)^2 t P_1 + 3(1-t) t^2 P_2 + t^3 P_3$$ where intermediate control points $P_1 = (x_0 + \Delta x \cdot \kappa, y_0)$ and $P_2 = (x_3 - \Delta x \cdot \kappa, y_3)$ dynamically scale with horizontal separation $\Delta x = x_3 - x_0$ using stiffness coefficient $\kappa = 0.45$. Force-Directed Physics Layout (Spring-Embedder): Our tidy_force_directed tool models notes as charged particles exerting repulsive Coulomb forces and edges as Hookean springs with equilibrium length $L$: $$F_{\text{repulsive}}(u, v) = \frac{k^2}{|p_u - p_v|} \cdot \hat{r} {uv}, \quad \text{where } k = \sqrt{\frac{\text{Width} \cdot \text{Height}}{|V|}}$$ $$F {\text{attractive}}(u, v) = \frac{|p_u - p_v|^2}{k} \cdot \hat{r}_{vu}$$ System states are updated over discrete iterations via velocity-Verlet numerical integration: $$p_i^{(t+\Delta t)} = p_i^{(t)} + v_i^{(t)}\Delta t + \frac{1}{2}a_i^{(t)}\Delta t^2$$ converging in $O(|V|^2 + |E|)$ time to a minimum-energy, crossing-minimized diagram. Directional DAG Smart Flow: Hierarchical diagrams are arranged using topological level sorting. We compute the longest path for each vertex $v \in V$ in $O(|V| + |E|)$: $$\text{Level}(v) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \text{in-degree}(v) = 0 \ 1 + \max_{(u, v) \in E} \text{Level}(u) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ Vertices are partitioned into horizontal columns $C_\ell = {v \in V \mid \text{Level}(v) = \ell}$ and laid out left-to-right to preserve intuitive cause-and-effect flow. Challenges we ran into Spatial Collision & Viewport Bleed: When agents spawn multiple cards, placing them blindly resulted in cards overlapping existing notes or landing far below the fold on compact laptop viewports. We solved this by developing an outward radial spiral search in findFreeSpot() paired with synchronous bounding-box camera framing ( fitView(true, allNodes) ), guaranteeing that generated items appear immediately within the user's active viewport without disrupting existing work. React 19 State Batching vs. Real-Time Tool Execution: When an agent called multiple tools in rapid succession (e.g. creating 4 nodes and 3 links), unbatched state updates caused intermediate render passes where references to newly created nodes were not yet committed to nodesRef.current . We re-architected tool execution into atomic batch commits , accumulating additions in memory and applying them in a single cohesive render cycle. Passive Event Listener Constraints on Infinite Canvas: Modern browsers treat wheel events as passive by default to optimize scrolling performance. However, an infinite canvas must intercept wheel to implement pinch-to-zoom and multi-directional trackpad panning with e.preventDefault() . We resolved this by binding native non-passive DOM event listeners directly to the container ref with { passive: false } , completely eliminating browser console errors. Multi-Model API Evolution: During development, the legacy gemini-pro endpoint was retired in Google's v1beta API. We built a resilient multi-version client adapter in src/lib/llm-client.ts that auto-migrates stored keys to gemini-2.0-flash , sanitizes quotation marks and whitespace, and provides automatic fallback across v1beta and v1 REST endpoints. What we learned WebMCP Eliminates the Prompt Engineering Tax: Instead of writing 500-word system prompts telling an LLM "format your output as JSON with x, y, width, and height" , WebMCP provides typed JSON Schemas directly through the browser. The agent interacts with our app through clean function calls
